parses: superlative, nom. fem. sing. or neut. pl.

tolleris.parse: pres. pass. indic., 2nd sing. or fut. pass. indic., 2nd sing.

vulnerātus: perf. pass. part., nom. sing. masc.
ea: she; or “that” when it modifies a noun
agitātus: perf. pass. part., nom. sing. masc.
doctī: perf. pass. part., nom. pl. masc.
expugnābimus: we will storm, we will capture
superātae: perf. pass. part., nom. pl. fem.
necātus: perf. pass. part., nom. sing. masc.
dēlectāta: perf. pass. part., nom. sing. fem.
appellātum: perf. pass. part., nom. sing. neut.
probāta: perf. pass. part., nom. pl. neut.
vocātus: perf. pass. part., nom. sing. masc.
fontibus: fountains, springs (abl. pl., from fōns, fontis)
fontes: fountains, springs (voc. pl., from fōns, fontis)
mutari: to be changed (pres. pass. infin. of mūtō)
peregrinantis: roaming (acc. pl. of the present participle)
fecit: he/she made (perf. act. indic. of faciō)
vixerunt: they have lived (i.e., they are dead)
caveo: beware of, be on one’s guard against
iuvenis: young; (as a noun) a young man
pars: part; pl. partēs, partium political party, faction
recipio: take back, receive; mē recipiō withdraw, retreat
provincia: province (a territory governed by a Roman magistrate)
committo: commit, entrust; proelium committō begin battle
finitimus: neighboring; (as noun) fīnitimī, -ōrum m. pl. neighbors
hispanus: Spanish; (as noun) Hispānus, -ī m. a Spaniard
inquam: say (a highly defective verb, typically used to introduce direct speech; inquit and inquiunt “he/she/it says/said” and “they say” are also common forms)
quidem: indeed, at least, at any rate
nequidem: not even (e.g., nē rēx quidem “not even the king”)
talis: such, of such a kind (of quality)
tantus: so large, so much, such, such (so) great (of quantity)
pro: in front of; on behalf of
ut: in order that or to, so that (purpose clause); that (result clause)
ne: in order that … not, so that … not, lest (negative purpose clause)
dummodo: provided that, so long as, if only
supplicium: punishment (especially capital punishment); exact punishment from someone, punish someone
studeo: be eager for, be devoted to; study
littera: letter (of the alphabet); (pl.) letter, epistle; literature
haereo: stick to, cling to, remain fixed
consulo: (with acc.) consult, ask the advice of; (with dat.) look out for (the interests of)
quin: (with subjunctive) that, from; (with relative clause of characteristic) who … not

LA1.la: Laudās fortūnam et vītam antīquae terrae.
LA1.en: You praise the fortune and the life of the ancient land.
LA1.note: From Horace, Sermones 2.7.22–23. The subject is IN the verb. Antīquae means “ancient” and modifies terrae.

LA2.en: The sailors do not love the land.
LA2.note: Nautae is nominative plural here, because amant is plural.

LA3.en: We will see the queen tomorrow.

LA4.en: The girls were carrying the money.
LA4.note: Puellae could also be genitive: “They were carrying the girl’s money.” The plural verb favors “the girls.”

LA5.en: Today I prepare dinner for the poet.
LA5.note: Poētae could be dative (“for the poet”) or genitive (“the poet’s dinner”). The verb is first person, so poētae cannot be the subject.

LA6.en: The goddess gives fortune to the poet.
LA6.note: With dat (“gives”), poētae is most likely the person who receives: the indirect object.

LA7.en: You (pl.) were praising the lives of the poets.

LA8.en: Yesterday the farmer was seeing the land.

LA9.en: The woman will always give dinner to the girls.

LA10.la: Agricola nautārum mēnsam puellīs et fēminīs dēmōnstrat.
LA10.en: The farmer points out the sailors’ table to the girls and women.

LA11.en: He (she) often praised the queen’s fortune.

LA12.en: The farmers will save the poet’s life.

LA13.la: Puellae et fēminae cēnam agricolīs dabant.
LA13.en: The girls and women were giving dinner to the farmers.

LA14.en: The goddess points out the money to the sailors.

LW1.en: The farmer always loved the land.

LW2.en: Today the sailors see the land of Italy.

LW4.la: Puellae fēminīs et deae cēnam crās parābunt.
LW4.en: The girls will prepare dinner for the women and the goddess tomorrow.

LW5.en: Yesterday you loved the queens’ money.

LW6.en: The woman will always give money to the girl.

LW7.en: The sailors of Asia do not see the land.

LW9.en: The queen of Rome was preparing dinner for the farmers.

LW10.la: Dea fēminās mox monēbit et servābit.
LW10.en: The goddess will soon warn and save the women.
LW10.note: Two verbs share the subject and the object. Treat one verb at a time.

LW11.la: Rēgīna crās pecūniam agricolae et nautīs dabit.
LW11.en: The queen will give money to the farmer and the sailors tomorrow.

LW12.la: Puellae puellīs et nautīs fortūnam semper dēmōnstrābant.
LW12.en: The girls were always pointing out fortune to the girls and sailors.

LW13.la: Semper, ō rēgīna, terrās Rōmae servō.
LW13.en: Always, O queen, I save the lands of Rome.
LW13.note: Ō rēgīna is a vocative (direct address). The subject is IN the verb.

LW14.en: Today we praise Rome. Tomorrow we will work.

LB1.en: The gods save and love me.

Dī: The book glosses Dī as “gods,” nominative plural.
mē: The book glosses mē as “me,” accusative singular.

LB2.en: You (pl.) were answering the slave-girls’ letters yesterday.

LB3.en: The farmers often helped the woman.

LB4.en: I was waiting for the money.

LB5.en: Julia was able to see the shore of the fatherland.

LB6.la: Turba rēgīnam salūtat, sed rēgīna nōn videt.
LB6.en: The crowd greets the queen, but the queen does not see (it).

LB7.en: The poet will praise the shore of the island.

LB10.en: The girls show the way to the slave-girl.
LB10.note: Puellae and ancillae can each be nominative plural or dative singular. Because the verb is plural, one of them is the subject.

LB11.en: Fortune ought to help the farmer.

LB12.en: I was standing and looking at the water.

LB13.la: Fortūnam et fāmam rēgīnae dare possum, sed dare nōn dēbeō.
LB13.en: I can give fortune and fame to the queen, but I ought not to give (them).
LB13.note: Rēgīnae is most likely dative with dare, but it could be genitive with fāmam.

LB15.en: The fame of the fatherland will always be able to remain.

LC1.en: Preserve the sound way of life!
LC1.note: From Seneca, Epistulae Morales 8.5. Sānam means “sound” and modifies viam.

LC2.en: Will I sail to Ephesus soon?
LC2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Plautus, Bacchides 775–776. Ephesum is accusative singular of Ephesus.

LC3.en: Tomorrow I will stay in the cottage.

LC4.la: Ambulāte, ō nautae! Per portam properāre dēbēmus.
LC4.en: Walk, sailors! We ought to hasten through the gate.

LC5.la: Mēnsam ē casā movēbant et cēnam in herbā parābant.
LC5.en: They were moving the table out of the cottage and preparing dinner on the grass.

LC6.en: You (pl.) were always able to frighten the farmer.

LC7.en: Tomorrow they will work under the stars.

LC8.la: Epistulam dē fāmā patriae ā rēgīnā portābam.
LC8.en: I was carrying a letter about the fame of the fatherland from the queen.
LC8.note: Dē fāmā patriae means “about the fame of the fatherland.”

LC9.la: In silvā nōn labōrābam. Sum agricola.
LC9.en: I was not working in the forest. I am a farmer.

LC10.la: Iuvā, ō agricola! Portā vaccam ex aquā!
LC10.en: Help, farmer! Carry the cow out of the water!

LC12.la: Errābis trāns viam, per iānuās, et in casam.
LC12.en: You will wander across the road, through the doors, and into the cottage.

LC13.en: The slave-girl was hastening out of the cottage.

LC14.la: Fēminae trāns viam per silvam ad portam errābunt.
LC14.en: The women will wander across the road, through the forest, to the gate.

LD1.la: Bellī perīculum nōn erat in Siciliā.
LD1.en: There was no danger of war in Sicily.
LD1.note: From Cicero, In Verrem 2.5.42. Erat can be translated “there was.”

LD2.la: Nōn ad bellum vōs nec ad perīculum vocō.
LD2.en: I call you neither to war nor to danger.
LD2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Tacitus, Historiae 1.38. Vōs means “you” (accusative plural) and nec means “nor.”

vōs: The book glosses vōs as “you,” accusative plural.
nec: The book glosses nec as “nor,” a conjunction.

LD3.la: Nōn est discipulus super magistrum, sed perfectus erit sīcut magister.
LD3.en: A student is not above the teacher, but he will be fully trained like his teacher.
LD3.note: From Luke 6.40. Super + accusative means “above,” perfectus means “perfected,” and sīcut means “just as.”

LD4.la: Fēcit Dominus Deus caelum et terram.
LD4.en: The Lord God made the sky and the earth.
LD4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Genesis 2.4. Fēcit means “made” and caelum means “sky.” Deus is in apposition to Dominus.

LD5.la: Agricola cum fīliābus per portam casae ambulat.
LD5.en: The farmer walks with his daughters through the gate of the cottage.

LD6.la: Deus rēgīnam Āsiae iuvābit quod servīs pecūniam saepe dabat.
LD6.en: God will help the queen of Asia because she often gave money to (her) slaves.

LD7.la: Discipulus magistrum sed nōn librōs amābat.
LD7.en: The student loved the teacher but not the books.

LD8.la: Agricola, dā rosās puellīs! Sunt cum fīliābus.
LD8.en: Farmer, give roses to the girls! They are with (their) daughters.

LD9.la: Domine, pugnā et fortūnam in proelium nunc portā!
LD9.en: Master, fight and carry good fortune into the battle now!

LD10.la: Amīcō dē poētae fortūnā crās respondēbit.
LD10.en: He will answer (his) friend about the poet’s fortune tomorrow.

LD11.la: Ex aquā cum deō properābat dea.
LD11.en: The goddess was hastening out of the water with the god.

LD12.la: Marcus, poētae fīlius, vītam magistrī servāre potest.
LD12.en: Marcus, the poet’s son, can save the teacher’s life.

LD13.la: Ad īnsulam servus erat et in terrā pecūniam cēlābat.
LD13.en: A slave was near the island, and he was hiding money in the ground.
LD13.note: Ad īnsulam shows nearness here, not motion.

LD14.la: Agricola ad agrōs aquam portat et vaccās servābit.
LD14.en: The farmer carries water to the fields and will save the cows.

LD15.la: Ō puerī, ē casīs properāte et proeliō parāte.
LD15.en: O boys, hasten out of the cottages and prepare for battle!

LD16.la: Crās in īnsulā Mārcus erit cum amīcīs, puerō et puellā, quod in agrō labōrābit.
LD16.en: Tomorrow Marcus will be on the island with his friends, a boy and a girl, because he will be working in the field.
LD16.note: Puerō and puellā are in apposition to amīcīs.

LE1.en: Hello, do you have dinner today?

LE2.en: The lives of good men are in danger.
LE2.note: From Cicero, de Republica 3.26. Bonōrum is an adjective used as a noun: “of good men.”

LE3.la: Pius Aenēās tibi, ō magna Iūnō, mactat, et sacrīs cum vaccīs stat ad āram.
LE3.en: Pious Aeneas sacrifices to you, great Juno, and stands at the altar with sacred cows.
LE3.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 8.84–85. Pius means “pious” and tibi is the dative singular of “you.”

tibi: The book glosses tibi as “to you,” dative singular.

LE4.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiārēs 6.18.5. Mē is the accusative singular of “me.”

mē: The book glosses mē as “me,” accusative singular.

LE6.la: Cum magnō agricolā nōn pugnābit parvus poēta.
LE6.en: The small poet will not fight with the large farmer.

LE7.la: Dominī nostrī vaccam sacram in altā arā mactābant.
LE7.en: Our masters were sacrificing a sacred cow on the high altar.

LE8.la: Herī in silvā longā et lātā multae ferae erant.
LE8.en: Yesterday there were many wild animals in the long, wide forest.

LE9.la: Parva via per magnam silvam errat ab oppidō meō ad albam casam tuam.
LE9.en: A small road wanders through the large forest from my town to your white cottage.

LE10.la: Dēmōnstrā, servē miser, tuō dominō magnum perīculum.
LE10.en: Show your master a great danger, wretched slave!

LE11.la: Magnam silvam vītō quod multae ferae cēnam bonam exspectant.
LE11.en: I avoid the large forest because many wild animals are waiting for a good dinner.

LE12.la: Ad oppidī portam altam, magna āra stat.
LE12.en: At the high gate of the town stands a large altar.

LE13.la: In casā tuā saepe est Mārcus, amīcus tuus.
LE13.en: Marcus, your friend, is often in your cottage.

LE14.la: In agrō lātō parva fīlia mea cum miserīs labōrābat.
LE14.en: In the wide field my small daughter was working with the wretched (people).
LE14.note: Miserīs is an adjective used as a noun: “with the wretched.”

LF1.en: Noah was building an altar for the Lord.
LF1.note: From Genesis 8.20. Nōē is nominative singular. Dominō is a dative of interest: “for the Lord.”

LF2.la: Virginēs Vestālēs cum puerīs et cum puellīs aquā ē fontibus lavābantur.
LF2.en: The Vestal Virgins, with boys and with girls, were being bathed with water from the fountains.
LF2.note: From Tacitus, Historiae 4.53. Aquā has no preposition. An ablative of a thing with no preposition is an ablative of means: “with water.”

Virginēs: The book glosses this as “Vestal Virgins,” nominative plural.

LF3.la: Sacrī fontēs et ōrae grātae, valēte!
LF3.en: Farewell, sacred fountains and pleasing shores!
LF3.note: From Martial, Epigramma 4.57.7. Fontēs is vocative plural. Valēte is a plural command: “be well,” that is, “farewell.”

LF4.en: They are able, because they seem to be able.
LF4.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 5.231. In the passive, especially with an infinitive, videō can mean “seem.”

LF5.la: Cibus et novum vīnum dominō ā servō dabantur.
LF5.en: Food and new wine were being given to the master by the slave.

LF6.la: Mactābitur alba vacca in ārā ab agricolā laetō.
LF6.en: A white cow will be sacrificed on the altar by the happy farmer.

LF7.la: Potest incitāre, mī fīde serve, equōs pigrōs?
LF7.en: Can he rouse the lazy horses, my faithful slave?
LF7.note: There is no stated subject: “he” is understood. Mī is the vocative singular of meus.

LF8.la: Dominus avārus multum aurum et argentum sub terrā cēlābat.
LF8.en: The greedy master was hiding much gold and silver under the ground.

LF9.la: Laetus erat servus fīdus, sed misera erat ancilla pigra.
LF9.en: The faithful slave was happy, but the lazy slave-girl was wretched.
LF9.note: Laetus and misera are predicate adjectives: they follow sum and describe the subject, just as a predicate nominative names it. Like a predicate nominative, they are in the nominative case.

LF10.la: Aurum et argentum Mārcō ā deīs dantur.
LF10.en: Gold and silver are given to Marcus by the gods.

LF11.la: Per fenestram ab ancillā pulchra lūna vidētur.
LF11.en: The moon is seen through the window by the beautiful slave-girl.

LF12.la: Ō medice nōte, ad nostram patriam properā quod multī aegrī sunt.
LF12.en: O famous doctor, hasten to our fatherland because many are sick.
LF12.note: Aegrī is a predicate adjective: it follows sum and describes the subject multī (“many”), just as a predicate nominative would name it.

LF13.la: Argentum et gladius ā fīliō tuō ad magistrum portābuntur.
LF13.en: Silver and a sword will be carried to the teacher by your son.

LF14.la: Multae īnsulae et patriae ā nautīs avārīs superābantur.
LF14.en: Many islands and fatherlands were being conquered by greedy sailors.

LG1.la: Malum est cōnsilium quod mūtārī nōn potest.
LG1.en: The plan is bad because it cannot be changed.
LG1.note: From Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 17.14.4. Malum is a predicate adjective. Mūtārī is a passive infinitive (“to be changed”). Quod can also be “which”: “A plan that cannot be changed is bad.”

LG2.en: Give, and it will be given to you.
LG2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Luke 6.38. Datē is a plural command.

LG3.note: From Terence, Hecyra 605. Mī is the vocative of meus. Veniam is accusative singular: “mercy, pardon.”

LG4.la: Id grātum est mihi, quod sum tibi amīcus.
LG4.en: It is pleasing to me because I am a friend to you.
LG4.note: From Catullus, Carmen 68.9. Grātum is a predicate adjective. Both mihi and tibi are datives: “to me,” “to you.”

LG5.en: Caesar was breaking camp away from the town.
LG5.note: From Caesar, de Bello Civili 3.80.7. Castra movēre means “to break camp.”

LG6.la: Tū dē tēctō nihil probābās, sed ego multa.
LG6.en: You approved of nothing about the building, but I approved of many things.
LG6.note: Dē tēctō means “about the building.” In the second clause, probābam is understood.

LG7.la: Ab ancillā fīdā cibus et vīnum parābantur.
LG7.en: Food and wine were being prepared by the faithful slave-girl.

LG8.la: Ego tē servābam, sed tū grātus nōn erās.
LG8.en: I was saving you, but you were not grateful.
LG8.note: Grātus is a predicate adjective: it follows sum and describes the subject, tū.

LG9.la: Cōnsilium nostrum, ō rēgīna, probā et nōbīs aurum et argentum dā.
LG9.en: O queen, approve our plan and give us gold and silver.

LG10.en: The master’s fortune always helps the slave.

LG11.la: In īnsulā fīdī sociī sunt rēgīnae.
LG11.en: The queen has faithful allies on the island.
LG11.note: Rēgīnae is a dative of possessor. The thing possessed, sociī, is the subject: “Faithful allies are to the queen.”

LG12.la: Ā tēctō nostrō albīs equīs portāberis.
LG12.en: You will be carried from our house by white horses.
LG12.note: Albīs equīs has no preposition and names the means: horses are things, not persons, so this is not an agent.

LG13.la: Ad portam tēctī stābat agricola laetus.
LG13.en: The happy farmer was standing near the gate of the house.
LG13.note: Ad portam shows nearness here, not motion.

LG14.la: Hostia in ārā albā ā vōbīs mactābitur.
LG14.en: A sacrificial victim will be sacrificed on the white altar by you (pl.).

LG15.la: Lēgātī, quod morbus in castrīs erat, medicum culpābant.
LG15.en: The lieutenants were blaming the doctor because there was disease in the camp.

LH1.la: Crās ad casam amīcī meī, agricolae Mārcī, cum fīliābus meīs ambulā.
LH1.en: Tomorrow walk to the house of my friend, the farmer Marcus, with my daughters.
LH1.note: Fīliābus is the dative and ablative plural of fīlia. Agricolae Marcī is in apposition to amīcī meī.

LH2.en: The sailor is always saved by fortune.
LH2.note: Fortūnā is a thing, not a person, so it is an ablative of means.

LH3.la: Nōs servābit quod longōs gladiōs portābit.
LH3.en: He will save us because he will carry long swords.
LH3.note: The subject of both verbs is in the endings: “he.”

LH4.la: Nigrīs in silvīs ā nōbīs ferae malae vītābuntur.
LH4.en: Bad wild animals will be avoided by us in the black forests.

LH5.la: Ex agrīs ā dominō puerī fugābantur.
LH5.en: The boys were being chased out of the fields by the master.

LH6.la: Poēta pulcher magnā in casā ad viam erat.
LH6.en: The handsome poet was in a large cottage near the road.

LH7.la: Saepe lātō in agrō agricola manēbat et multam aquam equīs dabat.
LH7.en: The farmer often stayed in the wide field and gave much water to the horses.

LH8.la: Iūlia, fēmina Mārcī, ad iānuam nunc stat et ā mē salūtātur.
LH8.en: Julia, the wife of Marcus, now stands near the door and is greeted by me.
LH8.note: Fēmina Mārcī is in apposition to Iūlia.

LH9.la: Miser sum quod mihi nōn est pecūnia.
LH9.en: I am wretched because I do not have money.
LH9.note: Miser is a predicate adjective. Mihi … est pecūnia is a dative of possessor: “Money is not to me.”

LH10.la: Ego et amīcus meus cibum tuum nōn probāmus.
LH10.en: My friend and I do not approve of your food.
LH10.note: The first person comes first in Latin.

LH11.la: In altā ārā dominus meus multās hostiās et albās mactābat quod deī fīliō aegrō longam vītam et fortūnam dabant.
LH11.en: On the high altar my master was sacrificing many white victims because the gods were giving a long life and good fortune to the sick son.
LH11.note: Albās modifies hostiās: “many and white victims.”

LH12.la: Puella parva ancillae tuae albās rosās in hortō dēmōnstrābit.
LH12.en: The little girl will show white roses to your slave-girl in the garden.

LH13.la: Magnōs deōs et deās, ō discipule bone, rogā.
LH13.en: Ask the great gods and goddesses, O good student.

LH14.la: Deī et deae tē culpābunt, quod multās hostiās nōn mactābātis.
LH14.en: The gods and goddesses will blame you because you were not sacrificing many victims.

LH15.la: Quod herī librō magistrum dēlectābam, hodiē magistrum vītō et per silvam errō.
LH15.en: Because yesterday I was delighting the teacher with a book, today I avoid the teacher and wander through the forest.
LH15.note: Librō is an ablative of means. Per silvam means “through the forest.”

LH16.la: In hortō mēcum stābat et dē albīs rosīs rogābat.
LH16.en: He was standing with me in the garden and was asking about the white roses.
LH16.note: Mēcum is cum mē (“with me”), the preposition attached to the pronoun. It shows accompaniment, but the Lab does not mark it.

LI1.la: Decimā hōrā amīcī plūrēs quam prīmā sunt.
LI1.en: At the tenth hour there are more friends than at the first.
LI1.note: From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae 173. Decimā hōrā is an ablative of time when. Prīmā means “at the first [hour]” and is also an ablative of time when.

LI2.la: Siciliae tē mōvit ad ōrās ventus.
LI2.en: The wind moved you to the shores of Sicily.
LI2.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 3.410. Siciliae limits ōrās: “the shores of Sicily.”

LI3.la: Pauca nūntiāte meae puellae, nōn bona verba.
LI3.en: Report a few words to my girl, not good ones.
LI3.note: From Catullus, Carmen 11.15–16. Pauca modifies verba.

LI4.en: Neptune calmed the swollen waters with a word.
LI4.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 1.142. Verbō is an ablative of means.

LI5.la: Impius nōn potest plācāre dōnīs īram deōrum.
LI5.en: An impious person cannot appease the anger of the gods with gifts.
LI5.note: From Cicero, de Lege Agraria 2.9.22. Dōnīs is an ablative of means.

LI6.la: Multās hōrās in casā manēbam quod fera mē terrēbat.
LI6.en: For many hours I stayed in the cottage because a wild animal was frightening me.
LI6.note: Multās hōrās is an accusative of duration of time (“for many hours”). The Lab does not mark it.

LI7.la: Mārcum dē ferīs monuī, sed quod ad silvās properābat, verbīs meīs nōn respondit.
LI7.en: I warned Marcus about the wild animals, but because he was hurrying to the woods, he did not respond to my words.
LI7.note: Respondeō takes the dative: verbīs meīs is an indirect object (“to my words”).

LI8.en: The Greek land gives grain to the farmer.

LI9.la: Ventus aquās agitāverat, sed nautae fīdī nōn timuērunt.
LI9.en: The wind had stirred up the waters, but the faithful sailors did not fear.

LI10.la: Cōpiās dē perīculō Rōmānus monuit et castra mōvit.
LI10.en: The Roman warned the troops about the danger and broke camp.

LI11.la: Epistula ad oppidum Graecum ā nōtō fīliō meō portābātur.
LI11.en: The letter was being carried to the Greek town by my famous son.

LI12.la: In Graeciā decem annōs labōrābat, sed Ītalia patria est.
LI12.en: He worked in Greece for ten years, but Italy is (his) homeland.
LI12.note: Decem annōs is an accusative of duration of time.

LI13.la: Ubi albus equus natat in aquīs Galliae?
LI13.en: Where does the white horse swim in the waters of Gaul?

LI14.la: Ad ōram decimā hōrā nautae properāvērunt.
LI14.en: The sailors hurried to the shore at the tenth hour.
LI14.note: Decimā hōrā is an ablative of time when.

LI15.la: Fīdus amīcus tuus multīs hostiīs deōs plācābit.
LI15.en: Your faithful friend will appease the gods with many sacrificial victims.
LI15.note: Multīs hostiīs is an ablative of means.

LJ1.la: Saepe ventīs agitāta est magna pīnus.
LJ1.en: A great pine tree has often been tossed by the winds.
LJ1.note: From Horace, Odes 2.10.9–10. Agitāta est is one verb, a perfect passive: mark both words. The participle agrees with pīnus (nom. fem. sing.). Ventīs is an ablative of means.

agitāta: perf. pass. participle, nom. fem. sing.

LJ2.la: Nōn sumus omnīnō sine cūrā novī annī.
LJ2.en: We are not altogether without care about the new year.
LJ2.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Quintum fratrem 3.4.4. Sine cūrā means “without care.” Novī annī limits cūrā.

LJ3.la: Dī patriae turbā servōrum expugnātī erant.
LJ3.en: The gods of the fatherland had been stormed by a crowd of slaves.
LJ3.note: From Cicero, in Verrem 2.4.94. The gods here are their statues. Turbā servōrum is a collective, so it is an ablative of means rather than an agent.

LJ4.la: Saepe meae clāmāvī ‘discēde!’ puellae, tamen sēdit puella mēcum.
LJ4.en: Often I shouted “Depart!” to my girl; nevertheless the girl sat with me.
LJ4.note: From Ovid, Amores 2.18.5–6. There are three verbs: clāmāvī, discēde (in the quotation), and sēdit. Mēcum is cum mē, “with me,” accompaniment; the Lab does not mark it.

LJ5.la: Ante decimam hōram Germānōs Gallī in proeliō superāvērunt.
LJ5.en: Before the tenth hour the Gauls defeated the Germans in battle.
LJ5.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 6.35.4. Ante takes the accusative.

LJ6.la: Taurī in campō sacrō ā sociīs Germānīs necābuntur.
LJ6.en: The bulls will be killed in the sacred field by the German allies.

LJ7.la: Ā nautā dē lūdō nostrō rogātus eram.
LJ7.en: I had been asked by a sailor about our school.
LJ7.note: Rogātus eram is one verb, a pluperfect passive. The subject is in the verb (“I”).

LJ8.la: Pecūnia nōbīs nōn est quod cum cūrā nōn labōrābāmus.
LJ8.en: We do not have money because we were not working with care.
LJ8.note: Nōbīs … est is a dative of possessor. Cum cūrā is an ablative of manner.

LJ9.la: Fēmina, saxa ante iānuam ex hortō movē!
LJ9.en: Woman, move the stones in front of the door out of the garden!

LJ10.la: Rēgīnae nūntius cum equō trāns viam ambulat.
LJ10.en: The queen’s messenger walks with a horse across the road.

LJ11.la: Cōpiae nostrae cōnsiliō vestrō in campō superātae sunt.
LJ11.en: Our troops were defeated in the field by your plan.
LJ11.note: Cōnsiliō vestrō has no preposition and is a thing, so it is an ablative of means.

LJ12.la: Librī pulchrī poētae ā rēgīnā dēmōnstrātī sunt.
LJ12.en: The beautiful books were shown to the poet by the queen.

LJ13.la: Ā cōpiīs Rōmānīs castra post cēnam oppugnābuntur.
LJ13.en: The camp will be attacked by the Roman troops after dinner.

LJ14.la: Nūntiī ē silvīs properābant et ad casam ambulābant.
LJ14.en: The messengers were hurrying out of the woods and walking to the cottage.

LJ15.la: Ego fīlium tuum terreō sed tū mē nōn timēs.
LJ15.en: I frighten your son, but you do not fear me.
LJ15.note: Terreō (“I frighten”) and timeō (“I fear”) are different verbs.

LJ16.la: Oppidum ante decimam hōram expugnātum est et Germānī ā nostrīs vulnerātī sunt.
LJ16.en: The town was captured before the tenth hour, and the Germans were wounded by our men.

LJ17.la: Erat in mēnsā nihil, quod cibus ā puerō post iānuam cēlātus erat.
LJ17.en: There was nothing on the table, because the food had been hidden behind the door by the boy.

LK1.la: Istī librī nōn semper eandem appellant ‘sapientiam’.
LK1.en: Those books of yours do not always call the same thing “wisdom.”
LK1.note: From Cicero, de Finibus 5.12. Appellō takes two accusatives: eandem (the thing named) and sapientiam (what it is called).

LK2.la: Malus magister tē ista docuit, nōn ego.
LK2.en: A bad teacher taught you those things, not I.
LK2.note: From Plautus, Bacchides 163. Doceō takes two accusatives. Docuit is understood after nōn ego.

LK3.la: Simul atque vīderant hoc templum oculīs eōrum, flēbant et multī cum gaudiō clāmābant.
LK3.en: As soon as they had seen this temple with their eyes, they were weeping and many were shouting with joy.
LK3.note: From Ezra 3.12. Oculīs eōrum is an ablative of means.

LK4.la: Ō rēx, magnum gaudium nōbīs erat, ubi tē ipsum dī monuēre optāre pācem.
LK4.en: O king, we had great joy when the gods themselves advised you to long for peace.
LK4.note: From Sallust, Jugurtha 102. Nōbīs … erat is a dative of possessor. Monuēre is monuērunt. Optāre is an infinitive that follows monuēre.

LK5.la: Ad portās castrōrum cōpiae clāmāvērunt in victōriā.
LK5.en: At the gates of the camp the troops shouted in victory.

LK6.la: Spēluncam Dīdō et Aenēās eandem dēvenient.
LK6.en: Dido and Aeneas will come to the same cave.
LK6.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 4.165–166. Dēvenient takes an accusative. Eandem agrees with spēluncam.

LK7.la: Postquam haec castra vīdit, ipse ad lēgātum properāvit.
LK7.en: After he saw this camp, he himself hurried to the lieutenant.

LK8.la: Ubi ille puer parvus in aquā frīgidā sēdit, nōn probāvit servus.
LK8.en: When that small boy sat in the cold water, the slave did not approve.

LK9.la: Simul atque oppidum expugnātum est, cum gaudiō sociī clāmāvērunt.
LK9.en: As soon as the town was captured, the allies shouted with joy.

LK10.la: Quamquam validus est, dēfessōs amīcōs numquam iuvat.
LK10.en: Although he is strong, he never helps his tired friends.

LK11.la: Cotīdiē turbam dē hīs perīculīs monēbam.
LK11.en: Every day I used to warn the crowd about these dangers.

LK12.la: Illae cōpiae hoc templum dēlēvērunt neque fortūnam auxērunt.
LK12.en: Those troops destroyed this temple and did not increase their fortune.

LK13.la: Virī stultī dē taurō eōdem ab agricolā saepe monēbantur.
LK13.en: Foolish men were often warned by the farmer about the same bull.

LK14.la: Ubi aeger erās, cūra bona tibi nōn erat.
LK14.en: When you were sick, you did not have good care.
LK14.note: Tibi … nōn erat is a dative of possessor. Aeger is a predicate adjective.

LK15.la: Quamquam longīs gladiīs cum Graecīs pugnābimus, eōs numquam superābimus.
LK15.en: Although we will fight with the Greeks with long swords, we will never defeat them.
LK15.note: Longīs gladiīs is an ablative of means; cum Graecīs is accompaniment.

LK16.la: Mihi praemium dedit dominus meus quod istam feram gladiō necāveram.
LK16.en: My master gave me a reward because I had killed that wild animal with a sword.
LK16.note: Gladiō is an ablative of means.

LL1.la: Fugātī erant prīmō impetū et clāmōre hostēs; oppidum expugnātum est.
LL1.en: The enemy were routed by the first attack and by the shouting; the town was captured.
LL1.note: From Livy 1.11.2. Prīmō impetū and clāmōre are both ablatives of means.

Fugātī: perf. pass. participle, nom. masc. pl.
Fugātī erant is a pluperfect passive.

LL2.la: Salvē, dux hominum et pater deōrum.
LL2.en: Hail, leader of men and father of the gods.

LL3.la: Tibi mē virtūs tua fēcit amīcum.
LL3.en: Your courage has made me a friend to you.
LL3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Sermones 2.5.33. Mē and amīcum are both accusatives: “made me a friend.” Fēcit is perfect active.

LL4.la: Nam simul atque tē, Lesbia, spectāvī, nihil manet mihi, Lesbia, vōcis.
LL4.en: For as soon as I looked at you, Lesbia, nothing of my voice remains to me, Lesbia.
LL4.note: From Catullus, Carmen 51.6–8. Vōcis is a partitive genitive: “nothing of voice.”

LL5.en: The dissension of the citizens is the enemy’s opportunity.
LL5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae 621. Hostium is genitive plural.

LL6.la: Populus stultus honōrēs saepe dat indignīs.
LL6.en: A foolish people often gives honors to the unworthy.

LL7.la: Ubi lēgātus imperātōrī victōriam mīlitum nūntiāvit, erant in castrīs magnī clāmōrēs.
LL7.en: When the lieutenant announced the victory of the soldiers to the general, there were great shouts in the camp.

LL8.la: Nam frāter imperātōris magnum virtūtis amōrem habēbat.
LL8.en: For the brother of the general had a great love of courage.
LL8.note: Virtūtis is an objective genitive: someone loves courage.

LL9.la: Aut huius populī rēx nōtus eris aut lingua ista fāmam tuam dēlēbit.
LL9.en: Either you will be a famous king of this people or that tongue of yours will destroy your reputation.
LL9.note: The subject of eris is in the verb: “you.”

LL10.la: Tū et magister et dux discipulōrum es.
LL10.en: You are both teacher and leader of the students.

LL11.la: Ubi pānis populō Rōmānō datus est, magnum erat gaudium.
LL11.en: When bread was given to the Roman people, there was great joy.

LL12.la: Vīnī amor perīculum cīvibus urbis saepe est.
LL12.en: The love of wine is often a danger to the citizens of the city.

LL13.la: Ō magister bone, virōs ad studium virtūtis incitā.
LL13.en: O good teacher, rouse the men to the pursuit of courage.

LL14.la: Altō in monte urbis pulchrae castra imperātor aedificat.
LL14.en: On a high mountain of a beautiful city the general builds a camp.

LL15.la: Postquam arx urbis ignibus dēlēta est, cīvēs mortem timēbant.
LL15.en: After the citadel of the city was destroyed by fire, the citizens feared death.
LL15.note: Ignibus is an ablative of means. Postquam takes the perfect indicative.

LL16.la: Vōx mātris nostrae mē et frātrem meum semper terrēbat.
LL16.en: The voice of our mother always used to frighten me and my brother.
LL16.note: Mātris nostrae is a subjective genitive: the mother speaks.

LM1.la: Decem annōs Trōia oppugnāta est ob ūnam fēminam.
LM1.en: Troy was besieged for ten years because of one woman.
LM1.note: From Livy 5.4.11. Decem annōs is an accusative of duration. Ob ūnam fēminam shows cause.

LM2.la: Hoc templum aeternum est, hoc fīnem nōn habet.
LM2.en: This temple is eternal; it has no end.

LM3.la: Nihil igitur mors est nōbīs, quod nātūra animī mortālis habētur.
LM3.en: Death is therefore nothing to us, since the nature of the mind is considered mortal.
LM3.note: From Lucretius 3.380–381. Nōbīs is a dative of reference: “to us.”

LM4.en: For philosophy is the art of life.
LM4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Finibus 3.4.

LM5.en: With mutual spirits they love and are loved.

LM6.la: Et vocāvit Deus āridam ‘terram’, et congregātiōnēs aquārum appellāvit ‘maria’.
LM6.en: And God called the dry land “earth,” and he called the gatherings of the waters “seas.”
LM6.note: From Genesis 1.10. Vocō and appellō take two accusatives.

LM7.la: Hunc nēmō vī potuit superāre nec aurō.
LM7.en: No one was able to conquer this man by force or by gold.

LM8.la: Hanc hiemem cum patre et frātre in Ītaliā manēbō, et artēs generum ēgregiōrum populī vidēbō.
LM8.en: This winter I will remain in Italy with my father and brother, and I will see the arts of the distinguished races of the people.
LM8.note: Hanc hiemem is an accusative of duration: “(during) this winter.”

LM9.la: Graecī magnā mentis celeritāte nūntī illīus servātī sunt.
LM9.en: The Greeks were saved by the great swiftness of that messenger’s mind.
LM9.note: The ablative group magnā mentis celeritāte nūntī illīus is an ablative of means.

LM10.la: Postquam rēx populum Rōmānum dē perīculīs hiemis longae et frīgidae monuit, magnō cum studiō cōpiae et animālium et cibī statim auctae sunt.
LM10.en: After the king warned the Roman people about the dangers of the long and cold winter, supplies of both animals and food were immediately increased with great eagerness.

LM11.la: Nam magnum mūneris amōrem prīnceps semper habēbat.
LM11.en: For the chief always had a great love of gifts.

LM12.la: Quamquam in Eurōpā multa flūmina vīdī, trāns ea numquam natāvī.
LM12.en: Although I have seen many rivers in Europe, I have never swum across them.

LM13.la: Eādem hieme castra ārsērunt, et imperātor multīs vulneribus necātus est.
LM13.en: In the same winter the camp burned, and the general was killed by many wounds.
LM13.note: Multīs vulneribus is an ablative of cause (or means).

LM14.la: Propter maris perīcula mīlitēs in castrīs multum tempus manēbant.
LM14.en: Because of the dangers of the sea the soldiers remained in the camp for a long time.
LM14.note: Multum tempus is an accusative of duration.

LM15.la: Dux ā cīvibus dē vulneribus in corporibus mīlitum rogātus est.
LM15.en: The leader was asked by the citizens about the wounds on the soldiers’ bodies.

LM16.la: Ob hiemēs frīgidās multōrum animālium corpora in fīnībus Germānōrum habent magnās vīrēs.
LM16.en: Because of the cold winters the bodies of many animals in the territory of the Germans have great strength.

LM17.la: Simul atque trāns pontem angustum ambulāvī, amīcus meus trāns flūmen natāvit.
LM17.en: As soon as I walked across the narrow bridge, my friend swam across the river.

LM18.la: Ob parvam cōpiam frūmentī rēx cīvibus pānem statim nōn dedit.
LM18.en: Because of the small supply of grain the king did not immediately give the citizens bread.

LM19.la: Eōrum cōpiae vīribus et virtūte hostium statim fugātae sunt.
LM19.en: Their troops were immediately routed by the strength and courage of the enemy.

LN1.la: Rēx Graecōrum multās cōpiās dūxit ad Trōiam.
LN1.en: The king of the Greeks led many troops to Troy.

LN2.la: Ventī vīs verberat mare, et magnās dēlet nāvīs.
LN2.en: The force of the wind whips the sea and destroys large ships.
LN2.note: From Lucretius 1.271–272. The subject of dēlet is understood: vīs.

LN3.la: Ille ōrātor cum dīligentiā potest et dīcere et scrībere.
LN3.en: That orator can both speak and write with care.
LN3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Brutus 24.93.

LN4.la: Haec ego nōn multīs scrībō, sed tibi.
LN4.en: I write these things not to many, but to you.

LN5.la: ‘Decimō annō urbs Trōiae cadet,’ dīcit Calchās.
LN5.en: “In the tenth year the city of Troy will fall,” says Calchas.

LN6.la: Bellum magnum geret in Ītaliā, populōs ferōcēs contundet, et cīvibus mūrōs pōnet.
LN6.en: He will wage a great war in Italy, crush fierce peoples, and place walls for the citizens.
LN6.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 1.263–264. The subject is understood: “he.”

LN7.la: Caesar mīlitēs dūcit et prope oppidum Uticam castra pōnit.
LN7.en: Caesar leads the soldiers and pitches camp near the town of Utica.
LN7.note: From Caesar, de Bello Civili 2.26.2. Uticam is in apposition to oppidum.

LN8.la: Quamquam longam epistulam ad tē scrīpsī, eam nōn mīsī.
LN8.en: Although I wrote a long letter to you, I did not send it.

LN9.la: Illō tempore annī Mārcus albās vaccās trāns campōs ad montēs dūcēbat.
LN9.en: At that time of year Marcus was leading white cows across the plains to the mountains.

LN10.en: The nation was grieving at the death of the famous general.
LN10.note: Morte is an ablative of cause.

LN11.la: Per viās angustās ad arcem et turrīs urbis currimus.
LN11.en: We run through narrow streets to the citadel and the towers of the city.

LN12.la: Dux gentis ad fīnēs Britannōrum castra posuerat.
LN12.en: The leader of the nation had pitched camp at the territory of the Britons.

LN13.la: Māter et sorōrēs meae in urbe cotīdiē vīnum bibunt.
LN13.en: My mother and sisters drink wine in the city every day.

LN14.la: Hieme stellae sunt clārae in Britanniā.
LN14.en: In winter the stars are bright in Britain.

LN15.la: Ad tē cōpiās decem hōrīs mittam. Statim castra pōne!
LN15.en: I will send troops to you in ten hours. Pitch camp at once!
LN15.note: The two sentences are separate: the first is future, the second an imperative.

LN16.la: Multās hōrās nāvis ārsit quod mīles prīncipī ignem nōn nūntiāverat.
LN16.en: The ship burned for many hours because the soldier had not reported the fire to the chief.
LN16.note: Multās hōrās is an accusative of duration. Ārdeō is intransitive.

LN17.la: Illā nocte lūna in mare nōn cecidit.
LN17.en: On that night the moon did not fall into the sea.

LN18.la: In Galliā propter magna animālia gladiōs longōs semper gerēbāmus.
LN18.en: In Gaul, because of the large animals, we always carried long swords.

LN19.la: Prīnceps, quod mūnera vītae numquam vītāvit, gentem multōs annōs regēbat.
LN19.en: The chief, because he never avoided the duties of life, ruled the nation for many years.

LN20.la: Caesarī in Britanniā erunt multae cōpiae.
LN20.en: Caesar will have many troops in Britain.
LN20.note: Caesarī … erunt … cōpiae is a dative of possessor.

LO1.la: Amor pānis mihi magnum corpus dedit.
LO1.en: The love of bread gave me a large body.

LO2.la: Hōc tempore annī in campō dux et cōpiae manēbunt.
LO2.en: At this time of year the leader and the troops will remain in the field.

LO3.la: Ubi rēx mortem imperātōris nūntiāvit, hae fēminae flēvērunt.
LO3.en: When the king announced the death of the general, these women wept.

LO4.la: Ante templum album in forō illa taberna semper patet.
LO4.en: In front of the white temple in the forum that shop is always open.

LO5.la: Ipsa nōn est laeta quamquam et frātrem et sorōrem habet.
LO5.en: She herself is not happy although she has both a brother and a sister.

LO6.la: In nigrā spēluncā statim latēbit istud animal dīrum.
LO6.en: That terrible animal of yours will immediately lie hidden in the black cave.
LO6.note: The book prints istum animal; the app corrects it to istud, the neuter nominative.

LO7.la: In lūdō magister ēgregius discipulōs pigrōs vocāvit, sed cūram nōn habuērunt.
LO7.en: In school the distinguished teacher called the lazy students, but they did not have care.
LO7.note: The subject of habuērunt is understood: the students.

LO8.la: Propter hiemem aqua frīgida flūminis Graecōs terrēbat.
LO8.en: Because of the winter the cold water of the river frightened the Greeks.

LO9.la: Pater noster, quod aeger est, hiemem nōn labōrābit.
LO9.en: Our father, because he is sick, will not work during the winter.
LO9.note: Hiemem is an accusative of duration.

LO10.la: Ducis fīlia flēbat ob taurī magnī vōcem.
LO10.en: The leader’s daughter was weeping because of the voice of the large bull.

LO11.la: Eō tempore sine frūmentō erāmus sed est nōbīs in forō magna cōpia.
LO11.en: At that time we were without grain, but we have a large supply in the forum.
LO11.note: Est nōbīs … cōpia is a dative of possessor.

LO12.la: Rōmānī nāvēs Germānās oppugnāvērunt sed ventō et marī superātī sunt.
LO12.en: The Romans attacked the German ships but were overcome by the wind and the sea.
LO12.note: The book prints Germanās; the app corrects it to Germānās.

LO13.la: Ante proelium deī mūneribus sacrīs imperātōris plācātī erant.
LO13.en: Before the battle the gods had been appeased by the sacred gifts of the general.

LO14.la: Soror et frāter animal vidēbant; illa statim clāmāvit, sed hīc in campō sēdit.
LO14.en: The sister and brother were watching an animal; she immediately shouted, but he sat in the field.
LO14.note: Illa is “she” and hīc is “this one,” “he.”

LP1.la: Platōn agit Sōcratī grātiās, quod ab illō doctus est.
LP1.en: Plato gives thanks to Socrates because he was taught by him.

LP2.en: Danger is never conquered without danger.
LP2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus 244.

LP3.la: Eādem enim virtūte et mala fortūna vincitur et regitur bona.
LP3.en: For by the same virtue bad fortune is conquered and good fortune is ruled.

LP4.la: Invītus, rēgīna, tuā dē ōrā discessī.
LP4.en: Unwilling, queen, I departed from your shore.
LP4.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 6.460. Dē ōrā shows separation.

LP5.la: Simul ac magnās cōpiās fīliō trādidit, ille Mithridātēn ēgit in aedem Gorneam.
LP5.en: As soon as he handed over large forces to his son, that man drove Mithridates into the Gornean temple.

LP6.la: Marī et terrā eārum regiōnum Caesarem prohibēbat.
LP6.en: He kept Caesar from the sea and land of those regions.
LP6.note: From Caesar, de Bello Civili 3.15.1. Marī et terrā is an ablative of separation.

LP7.la: Rēctē vērō tē, Cȳre, beātum appellant, quod virtūtī tuae fortūna iūncta est!
LP7.en: They rightly call you, Cyrus, blessed, because fortune has been joined to your virtue!

LP8.la: Cīvēs Rōmānī quī negōtiantur in Siciliā nōn dēfendunt, nōn dīligunt, eum salvēre nōn optant.
LP8.en: The Roman citizens who do business in Sicily neither defend him nor esteem him, nor do they wish him well.
LP8.note: From Cicero, in Verrem 2.2.15. Quī is a relative pronoun, which you will study in Lesson XXI.

LP9.la: Ē turrī turba ā rēgīnā salūtāta est.
LP9.en: The crowd was greeted by the queen from the tower.

LP10.la: Equus virī, quamquam ad aquam ductus est, nōn bibit.
LP10.en: The man’s horse, although it was led to the water, does not drink.

LP11.la: Propter cibī amōrem magnā cēnā numquam carēbat.
LP11.en: Because of his love of food he never lacked a large dinner.
LP11.note: Magnā cēnā is an ablative of separation after carēbat.

LP12.la: Iste mīles dē equō cecidit et vītam āmīsit.
LP12.en: That soldier of yours fell from his horse and lost his life.

LP13.la: Diū et bene ā rēge dēfendēbātur clāde urbs.
LP13.en: For a long time and well the city was defended from destruction by the king.
LP13.note: Clāde is an ablative of separation without a preposition.

LP14.la: Hodiē trādēris prīncipī hostium; post decem annōs patriae tuae reddēris.
LP14.en: Today you will be handed over to the chief of the enemy; after ten years you will be returned to your country.
LP14.note: Both verbs are future passive: note the long ē.

LP15.la: Eius vīrēs corporis et virtūtem et studium superant.
LP15.en: The powers of his body surpass both his virtue and his zeal.

LP16.la: Ubi nāvis ob ventōs magnōs āmissa est, nautārum corpora deō maris trādita sunt.
LP16.en: When the ship was lost because of the great winds, the bodies of the sailors were handed over to the god of the sea.

LP17.la: Parva aedēs meae vīllae iūncta est.
LP17.en: A small house is joined to my farmhouse.
LP17.note: Aedēs in the singular means “temple”; in the plural it can mean “house.” Here the book translates it as house.

LP18.la: Virtūte et vīribus lībertātem nostram dux dēfendet.
LP18.en: The leader will defend our freedom with courage and strength.

LP20.en: The citizens were frightened by the destruction of the temple.
LP20.note: Clāde is an ablative of cause.

LQ1.la: Ibi potest valēre populus, ubi lēgēs valent.
LQ1.en: There the people can be strong where the laws are strong.
LQ1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus 291.

LQ2.la: In prīncipiō erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum et Deus erat Verbum.
LQ2.en: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.
LQ2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From John 1.1.

LQ3.en: Desire is the root of all evils.
LQ3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From 1 Timothy 6.10.

LQ4.la: Lēx videt īrātum; īrātus lēgem nōn videt.
LQ4.en: The law sees an angry man; an angry man does not see the law.
LQ4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus 324.

LQ5.la: Apud Graecōs dīcitur, ‘amīcōrum sunt commūnia omnia’.
LQ5.en: Among the Greeks it is said, “all things belong in common to friends.”
LQ5.note: From Cicero, de Officiis 1.51. Amīcōrum is a genitive of possession.

LQ6.la: Ille mihi pār esse deō vidētur, ille, sī fās est, superāre deōs.
LQ6.en: That man seems to me to be equal to a god, that man, if it is right, to surpass the gods.
LQ6.note: From Catullus 51.1–2. Pār takes the dative deō.

LQ7.la: Dīximus artis poēticae est nōn omnia dīcere.
LQ7.en: We have said that it is the mark of poetic art not to say everything.
LQ7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Servius. Artis poēticae est means “it belongs to poetic art.”

LQ8.la: Urbs antīqua fuit, Carthāgō, dīves cōpiārum et studiīs ācris bellī.
LQ8.en: There was an ancient city, Carthage, rich in resources and fierce in the pursuits of war.

LQ9.la: Rēx omnibus cīvibus iūra paria nōn dederat.
LQ9.en: The king had not given equal rights to all the citizens.

LQ10.la: Ācrī amōre aurī hospitem dīvitem Mārcus necāvit.
LQ10.en: Because of a keen love of gold, Marcus killed the rich guest.
LQ10.note: Ācrī amōre aurī is an ablative of cause.

LQ11.la: Puer piger patrī similis, mātrī dissimilis erat.
LQ11.en: The lazy boy was like his father and unlike his mother.
LQ11.note: Similis and dissimilis take the dative.

LQ12.la: Ego et is animālia ā rēgīnae hortō semper prohibēmus.
LQ12.en: He and I always keep the animals away from the queen’s garden.

LQ13.la: In castrīs habitat, nam in urbe huic sunt inimīcī multī et ācrēs.
LQ13.en: He lives in the camp, for in the city he has many fierce enemies.
LQ13.note: Huic sunt inimīcī is a dative of possessor.

LQ14.la: Mīles fortis omnēs fēminās et līberōs perīculō ignis līberāvit.
LQ14.en: The brave soldier freed all the women and children from the danger of fire.
LQ14.note: Perīculō ignis is an ablative of separation.

LQ15.la: In bellō omnia cāra mihi āmīsī.
LQ15.en: In war I lost everything dear to me.

LQ16.la: Apud amīcum meum magnō cum gaudiō hospitēs per noctem bibēbant.
LQ16.en: At the house of my friend the guests drank with great joy throughout the night.

LQ17.la: Ā Gallīs et Germānīs castra simul oppugnāta sunt; post proelium longum hī prīncipem imperātōrī nostrō trādidērunt, illī ad fīnīs discessērunt.
LQ17.en: The camp was attacked at the same time by the Gauls and Germans; after the long battle the latter handed over their chief to our general, and the former departed to their territory.
LQ17.note: Hī, “these,” refers to the nearer group (the Germans); illī, “those,” to the first (the Gauls).

LQ18.en: The old guest lacked all strength.
LQ18.note: Omnibus vīribus is an ablative of separation.

LR1.la: Urbem Rōmam ā prīncipiō rēgēs habuēre; lībertātem et cōnsulātum L. Brūtus īnstituit.
LR1.en: Kings held the city of Rome from the beginning; L. Brutus established liberty and the consulship.
LR1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Tacitus, Annales 1.11. Habuēre is habuērunt.

LR2.la: Rēctum iter, quod iam cognōvī et dēfessus errandō, aliīs dēmōnstrō.
LR2.en: I point out to others the right road, which I have already learned, though weary from wandering.
LR2.note: From Seneca, Epistulae Morales 8.3. Quod is a relative pronoun; its antecedent is iter. Errandō is a gerund, “by wandering.”

LR3.la: Fīlia mea, salvē. ego is sum quī tē prōdūxī, pater.
LR3.en: My daughter, hello. I am the one who brought you forth, your father.
LR3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Plautus, Rudens 1173. Is … quī is “the one who.”

LR4.la: Hic portās frangit, sed ille iānuās.
LR4.en: This man breaks the gates, but that man the doors.
LR4.note: From Ovid, Amores 1.9.20. Frangit is understood after ille.

LR5.la: Ōtium sine litterīs mors est et ad vītam hominis sepultūra.
LR5.en: Leisure without literature is death and a burial for the life of a man.
LR5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca, Epistulae Morales 82.3.

LR6.la: Cui deus ‘at quoniam coniūnx mea nōn potes esse, arbor eris certē’ dīxit ‘mea’.
LR6.en: To her the god said, “But since you cannot be my wife, you will certainly be my tree.”
LR6.note: From Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.556–557. Cui at the start is a connective relative: “to whom,” best translated “to her.”

LR7.la: Dionȳsius, dē quō ante dīxī, nāvigābat ventō secundō Syrācūsās, postquam aedem Proserpinae in Graeciā expīlāverat.
LR7.en: Dionysius, about whom I spoke before, was sailing to Syracuse with a favorable wind, after he had plundered the temple of Proserpina in Greece.
LR7.note: From Cicero, de Natura Deorum 3.83. Syrācūsās is an accusative of place to which without a preposition.

LR8.la: Bone amīce, salvē, cui commendāvī fīlium meum.
LR8.en: Good friend, hello, to whom I have entrusted my son.

LR9.la: Ad captīvōs quōrum salūs ā rēge vetere dēfenditur auxilium hāc aestāte mittam.
LR9.en: I will send aid this summer to the captives whose safety is being defended by the old king.
LR9.note: The book prints auxīlium; the app corrects it to auxilium.

LR10.la: Illam vīllam quae est propīnqua urbī vendidit.
LR10.en: He sold that farmhouse which is near the city.
LR10.note: Urbī depends on propīnqua (dative with an adjective).

LR11.la: Tum librōs quōs lēgī līberīs reddō.
LR11.en: Then I return to the children the books that I have read.

LR12.la: Quī tibi amīcī sunt tē saepe laudant.
LR12.en: Those who are friends to you often praise you.
LR12.note: Quī is the subject of sunt; the antecedent is understood: “those.”

LR13.la: Ubi dē itineribus mīles mē rogāvit, eī nihil respondī.
LR13.en: When the soldier asked me about the routes, I answered him nothing.

LR14.la: Virum cui rēx praemium dedit brevī tempore salūtābimus.
LR14.en: We will greet in a short time the man to whom the king gave a reward.

LR15.la: Paucī istōs amīcōs dīvitēs probant quibuscum semper bibis et edis.
LR15.en: Few approve of those rich friends with whom you always drink and eat.
LR15.note: Quibuscum is quibus + cum, “with whom.” The antecedent is amīcōs.

LR16.la: Castra quae in hōc monte posuī ab hostibus nōn expugnābuntur.
LR16.en: The camp which I pitched on this mountain will not be taken by storm by the enemy.

LR17.la: Imperātor cuius pater illum librum scrīpsit ēgregius est.
LR17.en: The general whose father wrote that book is distinguished.
LR17.note: Cuius is genitive: it shows possession.

LR18.la: Quod ā validō mīlite Germānō est frāctus gladius, frāter meus ā proeliō discessit.
LR18.en: Because his sword was broken by a strong German soldier, my brother left the battle.
LR18.note: Pitfall: this quod is a conjunction (“because”), not a relative pronoun. It has no antecedent.

LR19.la: Puellam pulchram quācum ad lūdum ambulās iam vīdī.
LR19.en: I have already seen the beautiful girl with whom you walk to school.
LR19.note: Quācum is quā + cum. The antecedent is puellam.

LR20.en: In summer many ships plow the seas.

LS1.la: Vir bonus est quis? Quī cōnsulta patrum, quī lēgēs iūraque servat.
LS1.en: Who is a good man? He who preserves the decrees of the fathers, who preserves the laws and rights.
LS1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Epistulae 1.16.40–41. Quis is the interrogative pronoun; the second and third quī are relative pronouns with “he” understood.

LS2.la: Per mē quod eritque fuitque estque patet.
LS2.en: Through me lies open what will be, what was, and what is.
LS2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.517–518. Quod is a relative pronoun without an expressed antecedent: “what.”

LS3.la: Aenēās condidit urbem, trādūxitque deōs in Latium, genus unde Latīnum, Albānīque patrēs, atque altī mūrī Rōmae sunt.
LS3.en: Aeneas founded a city and brought his gods into Latium, whence came the Latin race, the Alban fathers, and the high walls of Rome.
LS3.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 1.5–7. Unde here is “from where.” The -que on trādūxitque and Albānīque means “and.”

LS4.la: Cūr nōn mittō meōs tibi, Pontīliāne, librōs? Nē mihi tū mittās, Pontīliāne, tuōs.
LS4.en: Why do I not send you my books, Pontilianus? So that you do not send me yours.
LS4.note: From Martial, Epigramma 7.3. Nē … mittās is a negative purpose clause.

LS5.la: Ō dī immortālēs! Ubi gentium sumus? Quam patriam habēmus? In quā urbe habitāmus?
LS5.en: O immortal gods! Where in the world are we? What country do we have? In what city do we live?
LS5.note: From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.9. Gentium is a partitive genitive: “of nations.” Quam and quā are interrogative adjectives.

LS6.la: Quae nātūrā aut fortūnā data sunt hominibus?
LS6.en: What things were given to people by nature or fortune?
LS6.note: From Cicero, de Oratore 2.45. Quae is an interrogative pronoun here (“what things”), the subject of data sunt; nātūrā and fortūnā are ablatives of means.

LS7.la: Nōn vīribus aut celeritāte corporum rēs magnae geruntur, sed cōnsiliō, auctōritāte, sententiā, quibus vīta senis augētur.
LS7.en: Great things are accomplished not by the strength or speed of bodies, but by planning, authority, and judgment, by which the life of an old man is increased.
LS7.note: From Cicero, de Senectute 17. Quibus is a relative pronoun whose antecedent is cōnsiliō, auctōritāte, sententiā.

LS8.la: Rogās, Lesbia, ‘Quot mihi bāsiātiōnēs tuae sunt satis?’
LS8.en: You ask, Lesbia, “How many kisses of yours are enough for me?”
LS8.note: From Catullus, Carmen 7.1–2. Quot is an indeclinable interrogative adjective.

LS9.en: What will I report to you about the crowd?

LS10.la: Quod bellum sine auxiliō deōrum Rōmānī gessērunt?
LS10.en: Which war did the Romans wage without the help of the gods?

LS11.la: Cuius equī taurīque illī sunt, et quō eōs servī agunt? Sunt eius quī in urbe habitat, et ex ignī ad salūtem dūcuntur.
LS11.en: Whose horses and bulls are those, and where are the slaves driving them? They belong to the one who lives in the city, and they are being led out of the fire to safety.
LS11.note: Quō is the adverb “to where.” Eius quī … means “(the one) of him who ….”

LS12.en: How is the mind joined to the body?
LS12.note: Quō modō is an idiom: “in what way.”

LS13.la: Quam diū in Graeciā hāc hieme manēbitis? Paucōs mēnsīs.
LS13.en: How long will you remain in Greece this winter? A few months.
LS13.note: Quam diū is “how long.” Paucōs mēnsīs is an accusative of duration, the answer.

LS14.la: Nōnne dolent, quod dē magistrī morte lēgērunt, līberī?
LS14.en: Don’t the children grieve because they have read about the death of the teacher?

LS15.la: Ubi istum ānulum vendidistī? Apud Lūcium.
LS15.en: Where did you sell that ring of yours? At Lucius’s house.

LS16.en: When will people be without hatred of enemies?
LS16.note: Odiō … carēbunt is an ablative of separation.

LS17.la: Patriam līberōsque is cui magna virtūs est semper dēfendet.
LS17.en: He who has great courage will always defend his country and children.
LS17.note: Cui … est is a dative of possessor: “to whom there is” means “who has.”

LS18.la: Quī dominus avārus ā servīs ancillīsque amātur?
LS18.en: Which greedy master is loved by slaves and slave-girls?

LS19.la: Propter longam hiemem mīles in castrīs multōs mēnsēs manēbat.
LS19.en: Because of the long winter the soldier remained in camp for many months.
LS19.note: The book prints longum hiemem; the app corrects it to longam, since hiems is feminine.

LS20.la: Num iste equus magna onera portāre poterat?
LS20.en: Surely that horse of yours could not carry great burdens, could it?

LT1.la: Ūnum mēnsem in nāvī fuī, ubi simul ob tempestātem semper mortem exspectābam miser.
LT1.en: I was on a ship for one month, where at the same time because of the storm I was always awaiting death, wretched.
LT1.note: From Terence, Hecyra 422–424. Ūnum mēnsem is an accusative of duration. Miser describes the speaker.

LT2.la: Homō stultus: postquam dīves esse coepit, pervēnit ad mortem!
LT2.en: Foolish man: after he began to be rich, he arrived at death!
LT2.note: From Cicero, de Oratore 2.274. Coepit takes an infinitive: “began to be.”

LT3.la: Ubi id tempus quod cōnstituerat vēnit, lēgātī ad Caesarem revertērunt.
LT3.en: When the time that he had set came, the ambassadors returned to Caesar.
LT3.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 1.8.3. Quod is a relative pronoun; its antecedent is tempus.

LT4.la: Dūxitque cohortīs ad Rubicōnem flūmen, quī prōvinciae eius fīnis erat.
LT4.en: And he led the cohorts to the Rubicon river, which was the boundary of his province.
LT4.note: From Suetonius, Divus Iulius 1.31.2. The Rubicon was the boundary of Caesar’s province.

LT5.la: Omnīs terrās fortibus virīs nātūra aperuit.
LT5.en: Nature has opened all lands to brave men.
LT5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Tacitus, Historiae 4.64. Omnīs is an alternate accusative plural ending.

LT6.la: Quid agam? Quem mihi amīcum inveniam misera? Aut quō cōnsilia haec nūntiābō? Aut unde mihi auxilium petam?
LT6.en: What am I to do? What friend am I to find for myself, wretched woman? Or to where shall I report these plans? Or from where shall I seek help for myself?
LT6.note: From Terence, Phormio 728–729. These are deliberative questions: agam and petam look like futures, and you will learn later that they are subjunctives.

LT7.la: Alpibus Ītaliam mūnierat anteā nātūra nōn sine aliquō dīvīnō nūmine
LT7.en: Previously nature had fortified Italy with the Alps, not without some divine providence.
LT7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Provinciis Consularibus 34.

LT8.la: Naucratem, quem convenīre voluī, in nāvī nōn erat, neque domī neque in urbe inveniō.
LT8.en: Naucrates, whom I wished to meet, was not on the ship, and I find him neither at home nor in the city.
LT8.note: From Plautus, Amphitruo 1009–1010. Naucratem is the object of inveniō; “in nāvī nōn erat” is a parenthesis.

LT9.en: Life is short, art is long.

LT10.la: Homō malus, quamquam dīves est, sēdem et grātiam post mortem dē deīs emere nōn potest.
LT10.en: A wicked man, although he is rich, cannot buy a seat and favor from the gods after death.

LT11.la: Cūr bonōs pūnīre et malōs laudāre tibi dēbēmus?
LT11.en: Why should we punish the good and praise the bad, for you?
LT11.note: Tibi is a dative of reference: “for you,” “in your view.”

LT12.la: Ubi lībertās cecidit, multīs hominibus in idem tēctum convenīre nōn potest.
LT12.en: When liberty has fallen, it is not possible for many men to assemble under the same roof.
LT12.note: The infinitive convenīre is the subject of potest: “to assemble is not possible.”

LT13.la: Tum prīnceps, quod cohors arcem mūnīverat, cīvēs servāre vīsus erat.
LT13.en: Then the leader, because the cohort had fortified the citadel, had seemed to save the citizens.

LT14.la: Celeritās illīus equī est similis tempestātī quae ventō validō ācta est.
LT14.en: The speed of that horse is like a storm which has been driven by a strong wind.
LT14.note: The book prints tempestāte after similis; similis more often takes the genitive or dative.

LT15.la: Ducis in cōnsiliō posita est virtūs decimae cohortīs.
LT15.en: The courage of the tenth cohort rested on the plan of the leader.
LT15.note: Positus est in + ablative: “is placed in,” hence “rests on.”

LT16.la: Fenestram aperiēbam ubi clāmōrēs turbae audīvī.
LT16.en: I was opening the window when I heard the shouts of the crowd.
LT16.note: Ubi is “when.” The imperfect and perfect contrast: a continuing action interrupted.

LT17.en: How long will the children sleep today?

LT18.la: Illōs puerōs pūnīre mē iussit, quod hanc arborem cecīdērunt.
LT18.en: He ordered me to punish those boys, because they cut down this tree.
LT18.note: The book prints cecidērunt (from cadō, “fall”); the app corrects it to cecīdērunt (from caedō, “cut”), since the verb has an object.

LU1.la: Caesar dē lībertāte populī Rōmānī bellum gerēbat cum Antōniō.
LU1.en: Caesar was waging war with Antony for the liberty of the Roman people.
LU1.note: From Cicero, Philippicae 7.11. Here “Caesar” is Octavian, Caesar’s heir.

LU2.la: Omnia animālia quae hospitēs nostrī neque invenīre neque coercēre possunt in hīs terrīs habitant.
LU2.en: All the animals which our guests can neither find nor catch live in these lands.
LU2.note: Quae is the object of both infinitives.

LU3.en: Surely Julia is like you, isn’t she?

LU4.la: Ex captīvīs nostrae cohortēs hostis cōnsilia reperīre coepērunt.
LU4.en: Our cohorts began to find out the enemy’s plans from the captives.
LU4.note: Hostis is a genitive singular here, not a nominative.

LU5.la: Quantum auxilium mittētur ad imperātōrem fortem, quī in Britanniā victus est?
LU5.en: How much help will be sent to the brave general who was defeated in Britain?

LU6.la: Ignī quī ad nāvēs nostrās brevī tempore perveniet viam ventus aperuit.
LU6.en: The wind opened a way for the fire which will reach our ships in a short time.
LU6.note: Ignī is dative: the wind opened a way “for” the fire.

LU7.la: Tempestātēs gravēs hominēs ab forō ōtiōque diū prohibuēre.
LU7.en: Severe storms kept men from the forum and from leisure for a long time.

LU8.note: Dative of possessor: “to the gods are.”

LU9.la: Eōs pūnīre mīlitēs quī mūnera relīquērunt iubēmus.
LU9.en: We order them to punish the soldiers who abandoned their duties.
LU9.note: The book prints Ēos; the app corrects it to Eōs.

LU10.la: Quantā in grātiā tē apud eum posuī?
LU10.en: In how great favor have I placed you with him?
LU10.note: Apud eum: “at his house,” and so “with him.”

LU11.la: Animal mihi redditum est quod multōs mēnsēs āmissum erat.
LU11.en: The animal which had been lost for many months was returned to me.
LU11.note: Quod is a relative pronoun whose antecedent is animal. Multōs mēnsēs is an accusative of duration.

LU12.la: Dīvitibus multī sunt fīdī quod auctōritātem habet pecūnia.
LU12.en: Many are faithful to the rich because money has authority.

LU13.la: Paucī et iūs et lēgēs dēfendunt, ubi perīculum est.
LU13.en: Few defend both justice and laws when there is danger.

LU14.la: Quō modō vir dē turrī cecidit? Quis eum iuvābat?
LU14.en: How did the man fall from the tower? Who was helping him?

LU15.la: In tabernā amīcī ānulum et librum mātrī emam.
LU15.en: In my friend’s shop I will buy a ring and a book for my mother.

LU16.la: Ubi aedēs incendēre illā nocte, magnā cum celeritāte ad salūtem cucurrimus.
LU16.en: When they burned the house that night, we ran to safety with great speed.

LU17.la: Postquam nāvēs hostis vī ventī frāctae erant, āram victōriae in līmine aedis posuimus.
LU17.en: After the enemy’s ships had been broken by the force of the wind, we placed an altar of victory on the threshold of the temple.

LU18.en: From where has a nature suited to us come together?
LU18.note: Conveniō with the dative means “be suited for.” The sentence is open to more than one reading; please see the audit.

LU19.la: Vīdistīne vaccam pulchram quae in līmine vīllae veteris sedēbat?
LU19.en: Did you see the beautiful cow which was sitting on the threshold of the old villa?

LV1.la: Quid ego ēgī? In quod mē coniēcī malum?
LV1.en: What have I done? Into what evil have I thrown myself?
LV1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Terence, Hecyra 132.

LV2.la: Multōs annōs Nerō sine cūrā deōrum imperium et scelera continuāvit.
LV2.en: For many years Nero continued his rule and his crimes without care for the gods.
LV2.note: From Tacitus, Annales 14.12. Multōs annōs is an accusative of duration.

LV3.la: Terra ‘mātrem’ appellātur, quod genus ipsa fēcit hūmānum.
LV3.en: The Earth is called “mother” because she herself made the human race.
LV3.note: From Lucretius, de Rerum Natura 5.820–823. Quod is a conjunction: “because.”

LV4.la: Nihil enim contrā mē fēcit odiō meī.
LV4.en: For he did nothing against me out of hatred of me.
LV4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Haruspicum Responso 5. Odiō meī is an ablative of cause.

LV5.la: Ubi domesticum bellum manet, intus īnsidiae sunt, intus perīculum est, intus est hostis.
LV5.en: Where domestic war remains, within there is treachery, within there is danger, within is the enemy.

LV6.la: Nihil enim est factum opere et manū quod nōn cōnficiet et cōnsūmet tempus
LV6.en: For nothing has been made by work and hand which time will not finish and consume.
LV6.note: From Cicero, pro Marcello 11. Quod is a relative pronoun; its subject is tempus.

LV7.la: Fraus est accipere, quod nōn potes reddere.
LV7.en: It is fraud to accept what you cannot return.
LV7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae 168. Quod is a relative pronoun without an expressed antecedent.

LV8.la: Sed fugit intereā, fugit inreparābile tempus.
LV8.en: But meanwhile it flees, irretrievable time flees.
LV8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Georgics 3.284.

LV9.en: How many people does the earth sustain?
LV9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Plautus, Poenulus 90. Hominum is a partitive genitive.

LV10.la: Omnēs hominēs, quī perīcula bellī vītāvērunt, deīs grātiās agere iussī sunt.
LV10.en: All men who avoided the dangers of war were ordered to give thanks to the gods.
LV10.note: The book prints grātīās; the app corrects it to grātiās.

LV11.la: Quī omnia cupiunt, illīs deī nihil saepe dant.
LV11.en: The gods often give nothing to those who desire everything.

LV12.la: Nōnne Mārcus et amīcī eius contrā lēgēs pecūniam capere coāctī erant?
LV12.en: Surely Marcus and his friends had been compelled to take money against the laws, hadn’t they?

LV13.la: Quae nōbīs pulchra videntur iste imperātor dēlēverit.
LV13.en: That commander of yours will have destroyed the things that seem beautiful to us.
LV13.note: The antecedent of quae (“the things”) is understood. Dēlēverit is future perfect.

LV14.la: Quem deum invocābunt ducēs cohortium ante proelium?
LV14.en: Which god will the leaders of the cohorts call upon before the battle?

LV15.la: Poēta ē fenestrā in aquam vīnum coniēcerat.
LV15.en: The poet had thrown wine from the window into the water.

LV16.la: Imperātor ille ad imperium populī Rōmānī multās gentēs in Āsiā adiūnxit.
LV16.en: That general added many tribes in Asia to the empire of the Roman people.

LV17.la: Caede animalium mentēs deōrum in altās sēdēs plācāvērunt.
LV17.en: By the slaughter of animals they appeased the minds of the gods in their high abodes.
LV17.note: In + accusative usually means “into”; please see the audit for a query on in altās sēdēs.

LV18.la: Post caedem dīram nihil in urbe relīquērunt.
LV18.en: After the dreadful slaughter they left nothing in the city.
LV18.note: The book prints diram and reliquerunt; the app marks the long vowels.

LY1.la: Quid dīcam dē Sōcrate, cuius mortem semper fleō, Platōnem legēns?
LY1.en: What should I say about Socrates, whose death I always weep for, while reading Plato?
LY1.note: From Cicero, de Natura Deorum 3.82. Legēns is a present active participle: “while reading.”

LY2.la: Surgēns accēpit puerum et mātrem eius et vēnit in terram Isrāhēl.
LY2.en: Rising, he took the boy and his mother and came into the land of Israel.
LY2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Matthew 2.21. Isrāhēl is indeclinable and stands in apposition to terram.

LY3.la: Cōnscientia bene āctae vītae nōs dēlectat.
LY3.en: The knowledge of a life well lived delights us.
LY3.note: From Cicero, de Senectute 9. Āctae is a perfect passive participle: “having been lived.”

LY4.la: Pompēius pecūniam mīlitibus ex praedā ante prehēnsā dare et bellum cum Mithridāte cōnficere poterat.
LY4.en: Pompey was able to give money to the soldiers from the booty previously seized and to finish the war with Mithridates.
LY4.note: From Cicero, de Provinciis Consularibus 28. Prehēnsā modifies praedā; ante is an adverb here.

LY5.la: Saepe tacēns vōcem verbaque vultus habet.
LY5.en: Often even a silent face has a voice and words.
LY5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Ovid, Ars Amatoria 1.574. Tacēns modifies vultus.

LY6.la: Oppressōs vōs tenēbō ab mīlitibus Caesaris.
LY6.en: I will hold you back, overwhelmed, from the soldiers of Caesar.

LY7.la: Caesar iubet L. Plancum hōs comprehēnsōs ad sē mittere.
LY7.en: Caesar orders L. Plancus to send these men, having been seized, to him.
LY7.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 5.25.4. Sē is a reflexive pronoun referring to Caesar.

LY8.la: Quotiēns fugās et caedēs iussit prīnceps?
LY8.en: How many times has the emperor ordered flights and slaughters?
LY8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Tacitus, Annales 14.64.

LY9.la: Dīvīsa praeda est, et maria properantēs petunt.
LY9.en: The booty has been divided, and hastening they seek the seas.
LY9.note: From Seneca, Agamemnon 422. Properantēs is the subject of petunt, “those hastening.”

LY10.la: Fēminae ex forō venientēs tempestāte oppressae sunt.
LY10.en: Women coming from the forum were overwhelmed by the storm.

LY11.en: Happy, I bought the beloved horse.
LY11.note: Fēlīx modifies the subject understood in ēmī.

LY12.en: Why did they lose Marcus after he had been seized?
LY12.note: Comprehēnsum is a perfect passive participle: “having been seized.”

LY13.la: Cicerō omnia dē Catilīnae īnsidiīs comperta dīxit.
LY13.en: Cicero told everything discovered about Catiline’s ambush.

LY14.la: Onera imperiī et vim hostium sustinēre caput populī Rōmānī nōn dubitāvit.
LY14.en: The head of the Roman people did not hesitate to sustain the burdens of empire and the force of the enemy.

LY15.la: Aurum in oppidō captō inventum mīlitēs dīvidēbant.
LY15.en: The soldiers were dividing the gold found in the captured town.

LY16.la: Brūtus cum virīs in Āsiam missus ingentī cum praedā iter faciet.
LY16.en: Brutus, sent into Asia with his men, will march with huge booty.

LY17.la: Senem pecūniam dextrā tenentem istīus miserī comprehendērunt et eum in fugam coēgērunt.
LY17.en: They seized the old man of that wretch, holding money in his right hand, and drove him to flight.
LY17.note: Dextrā is an ablative of means. In fugam coēgērunt is “put to flight.”

LY18.la: Onere cūrārum pressus uxōrī dīxit dē mūneribus bellī.
LY18.en: Weighed down by the burden of his cares, he spoke to his wife about the duties of war.

LY19.la: Per tacentēs mortium sēdēs Aenēās cum patre veniēbat.
LY19.en: Aeneas was coming with his father through the silent abodes of the dead.
LY19.note: From Seneca, Agamemnon 422 (adapted). Please see the audit on mortium.

LY20.note: Mē is the object of the participle reprehendēns.

LY21.la: Nōn opere ipsō sed pondere aurī dēlectābantur.
LY21.en: They were pleased not by the workmanship itself but by the weight of the gold.

LY22.la: Caesar in operibus dē Galliā dīvīsā scrībit.
LY22.en: Caesar writes in his works about Gaul as divided.
LY22.note: A reference to the famous opening of the Gallic War.

LZ1.en: He lived well, while he lived.
LZ1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Terence, Hecyra 462. Dum is a conjunction: “while.”

LZ2.la: Vīvēs, et vīvēs ita ut nunc vīvis, multīs meīs et fortibus praesidiīs oppressus.
LZ2.en: You will live, and you will live as you now live, hemmed in by my many strong guards.
LZ2.note: From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.6. Praesidiīs is from praesidium, “guard.”

LZ3.la: Vērus amīcus numquam reperiētur: est enim is quī est tandem alter īdem.
LZ3.en: A true friend will never be found: for he is one who is, in the end, another self.
LZ3.note: From Cicero, de Amicitia 80. Alter īdem means “another self.”

LZ4.la: Age ergō, sōlus servāre hunc potes.
LZ4.en: Come, then, you alone can save this man.
LZ4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Terence, Phormio 540. Age ergō: “Come, then.”

LZ5.la: Quotiēnscumque dīcō, totiēns mihi videor in iūdicium venīre nōn ingenī sōlum sed etiam virtūtis.
LZ5.en: As many times as I speak, so many times I seem to myself to come into a judgment not only of my talent but also of my courage.
LZ5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Cluentio 51. Nōn … sōlum sed etiam: “not only … but also.”

LZ6.la: Tōtīus ferē Galliae lēgātī, prīncipēs cīvitātum, ad Caesarem grātulātum convēnērunt.
LZ6.en: Ambassadors of nearly all Gaul, the leaders of the states, came together to Caesar to congratulate him.
LZ6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 1.30.1. Grātulātum, “(in order) to congratulate,” expresses purpose.

LZ7.la: Nōs lēgem bonam ā malā nūllā aliā nisi nātūrae normā dīvidere possumus.
LZ7.en: We can distinguish a good law from a bad one by no other standard except the norm of nature.
LZ7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Legibus 1.16.44. The book prints mālā; the app corrects it to malā.

LZ8.la: Tandem lūx aperuit bellum ducemque bellī. Servōs ad lībertātem Appius Herdonius ex Capitōliō vocābat.
LZ8.en: At last the light revealed the war and the leader of the war. Appius Herdonius was calling the slaves to freedom from the Capitoline.
LZ8.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 3.15.8–9. Appius Herdonius led a failed slave revolt in 460 B.C.

LZ9.la: Neque praeter tē in oppidō ūllus servus istō nōmine est.
LZ9.en: And besides you, there is no slave in the town by that name.
LZ9.note: From Plautus, Captivi 590. Praeter tē: “except you.”

LZ10.la: Neuter imperātor ūllum mīlitem magnā virtūte pugnantem reperīre poterat.
LZ10.en: Neither commander could find any soldier fighting with great courage.
LZ10.note: Magnā virtūte is an ablative of description.

LZ11.la: Aliī aliam in terram fūgērunt. Tandem omnēs captī ab imperātōre pūnītī sunt.
LZ11.en: Some fled into one land, some into another. At last all were captured and punished by the general.

LZ12.la: Cīvis bonārum artium imperiī pondus sustinēbit.
LZ12.en: A citizen of honorable principles will sustain the weight of empire.
LZ12.note: Bonārum artium is a genitive of description: “honorable principles.”

LZ13.la: Postquam dux proeliō interfectus est, mīlitēs dēfessī altōs per montīs et praeter oppida inimīca iter fēcērunt.
LZ13.en: After the leader was killed in battle, the weary soldiers marched through the high mountains and past hostile towns.

LZ14.la: Uter servus fuit dominō relictō fīdus?
LZ14.en: Which slave was faithful to his abandoned master?
LZ14.note: Fīdus takes the dative: dominō relictō.

LZ15.la: Homō semper aliud, Fortūna aliud cupit.
LZ15.en: Man always wants one thing, Fortune another.

LZ16.la: Imperātor cōpiās currentēs mittere in castra lēgātum iussit.
LZ16.en: The general ordered the lieutenant to send the running troops into the camp.
LZ16.note: Lēgātum is the object of iussit; cōpiās currentēs is the object of mittere.

LZ17.la: Propter vulnus grave pater meus diū nōn vīxit.
LZ17.en: Because of a serious wound my father did not live long.

LZ18.la: Quamquam sōlus saxa nūlla iēcerat, tamen ā magistrō pūnītus est.
LZ18.en: Although he alone had thrown no stones, nevertheless he was punished by the teacher.

LZ19.la: In tōtā Ītaliā ūnus est sōlus inventus quī Gallōs vincēre potuit.
LZ19.en: In all of Italy one man alone was found who could conquer the Gauls.
LZ19.note: Quī … potuit is a relative clause modifying ūnus.

LZ20.la: Nōn sōlum tēcta in urbe oppugnāvit, sed etiam omne templum et āram dēlēvit.
LZ20.en: Not only did he attack the buildings in the city, but he also destroyed every temple and altar.
LZ20.note: Nōn sōlum … sed etiam: “not only … but also.”

LAB1.en: We often wished to see this day.
LAB1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Terence, Hecyra 652. Diēs is a masculine fifth-declension noun.

LAB2.la: Noctēs atque diēs patet ātrī iānua Dītis.
LAB2.en: Night and day the door of dark Dis stands open.
LAB2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Aeneid 6.127. Noctēs atque diēs is an accusative of duration. Dīs is another name for Pluto, god of the Underworld.

LAB3.la: Cicerōnī in omnibus eius perīculīs singulārem fidem Atticus dēdit.
LAB3.en: Atticus gave Cicero singular loyalty in all his dangers.
LAB3.note: From Cornelius Nepos, Vita Attici 4.4. Atticus was a close friend of Cicero who helped him escape from Rome in 49 B.C.

LAB4.la: Nostrī mīlitēs, simul in āridō cōnstitūtī sunt, in hostēs impetum fēcērunt atque eōs in fugam dedērunt.
LAB4.en: Our soldiers, as soon as they had been stationed on dry land, made an attack on the enemy and put them to flight.
LAB4.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 4.26.5. Impetum faciō with in + accusative: “attack.” In fugam dō: “put to flight.”

LAB5.la: In tē mihi omnis spēs est.
LAB5.en: In you is all my hope.
LAB5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 6.7.5. Mihi is a dative of possessor.

LAB6.la: Fuit, fuit ista quondam in hāc rē pūblicā virtūs.
LAB6.en: There was, there was once that courage in this republic.
LAB6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.3.

LAB7.la: Dīc bonā fide: nōnne tū id aurum cēpistī?
LAB7.en: Speak in good faith: surely you took that gold, didn’t you?

LAB8.la: Cui posteā ‘Scaevolae’ ob clādem dextrae manūs cognōmen datum est.
LAB8.en: Afterwards the cognomen “Scaevola” was given to him because of the loss of his right hand.
