LAB8.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 2.13.1. A cognōmen was an honorific title placed at the end of a Roman’s name.

LAB9.la: Fēcerisne quod in hāc rē pūblicā nōn modo factum anteā numquam est, sed in omnī memoriā est omnīnō inaudītum?
LAB9.en: Have you done what has never before been done in this republic, but is altogether unheard of in all memory?
LAB9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Vatinium 33. Inaudītum = nōn audītum.

LAB10.la: Ipsa, tenēns dextrā vīnum, pulcher Dīdō albae vaccae inter cornua fundit.
LAB10.en: She herself, beautiful Dido, holding the wine in her right hand, pours it between the horns of a white cow.
LAB10.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 4.60–61. Vīnum is understood with fundit.

LAB11.la: Vīvēns vītam longam, nōs ūsum rērum multārum docuit.
LAB11.en: Living a long life, he taught us the use of many things.
LAB11.note: The book prints Vivens; the app corrects it to Vīvēns.

LAB12.la: Rēs dīrae neque vī neque spē vincentur sed cōnsiliō.
LAB12.en: Dreadful situations will be conquered neither by force nor by hope but by planning.

LAB13.la: Alteram ille amat sorōrem, ego alteram.
LAB13.en: He loves one sister, I the other.

LAB14.la: Huius domūs dominus fidem in illīs servīs positūrus nōn dubitāvit.
LAB14.en: The master of this house, about to place his trust in those slaves, did not hesitate.
LAB14.note: Positūrus is a future active participle: “about to place.”

LAB15.la: Hannibal in Ītaliā pugnāns, utrīusque imperātōris exercitum ūnō proeliō fugāvit.
LAB15.en: Hannibal, fighting in Italy, routed the army of each commander in one battle.
LAB15.note: Utrīusque is the genitive of uterque.

LAB16.la: Ubi in Galliam pervēnit, nūllus dux contrā eum in campō castra posuit.
LAB16.en: When he arrived in Gaul, no leader pitched camp against him on the plain.

LAB17.la: Exercitus circum montīs iter mox faciet, omnia paene perīcula vītāns.
LAB17.en: The army will soon march around the mountains, avoiding almost all dangers.

LAB18.la: Quis ex ōtiō multum frūctum nōn cēpit?
LAB18.en: Who did not take much profit from leisure?

LAB19.la: Post mortem illōrum hostium reī pūblicae Cicerō populō Rōmānō dīxit, ‘Vīxērunt’.
LAB19.en: After the death of those enemies of the republic, Cicero said to the Roman people, “They have lived.”
LAB19.note: Vīxērunt, “they have lived,” was a Roman way of announcing that someone had died.

LAB20.la: Malum cōnsilium factūrae, istae fēminae virōs miserōs superābunt.
LAB20.en: Those women, about to make a wicked plan, will overcome the wretched men.
LAB20.note: Factūrae is a future active participle agreeing with fēminae.

LAC1.la: Sīc pulsō Tarquiniō, populī Rōmānī nōmen rēgis audīre nōn poterant.
LAC1.en: Thus, Tarquin having been driven out, the Roman peoples could not bear to hear the name of king.
LAC1.note: From Cicero, de Republica 2.52. Pulsō Tarquiniō is an ablative absolute: noun + perfect participle.

LAC2.en: Spring, therefore, opens the seas to those sailing.
LAC2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 2.52. Nāvigantibus is a present participle used as a noun.

LAC3.la: Adultā nocte, lūna surgēns ostendēbat aciēs.
LAC3.en: The night having advanced, the rising moon was showing the battle lines.
LAC3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Tacitus, Historiae 3.23. Adultā is a perfect passive participle: “having come of age.”

LAC4.la: Iam maria lātē tenente Pompēiō, repente lēgātus eius, Octāvius Libō, magnīs cōpiīs nāvium hostem circumvēnit.
LAC4.en: With Pompey holding the seas far and wide, suddenly his lieutenant, Octavius Libo, surrounded the enemy with a large force of ships.
LAC4.note: From Florus, Epitome 2.13.2.31. Maria … tenente Pompēiō is an ablative absolute; maria is the object of the participle.

LAC5.en: Jupiter shortened the seasons of the old spring.
LAC5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.116. Veteris modifies vēris.

LAC6.la: Cornūque coactō, iam Lūna tōtō frātrem ‘Sōlem’ reddēbat orbe.
LAC6.en: The horn having been brought together, the Moon now was giving back her brother “Sun” with her whole disk.
LAC6.note: From Lucan, Pharsalia 1.537–538. Cornū here is the horn (tip) of the crescent moon.

LAC7.la: Prīmō impetū factō ab dextrō cornū, hostēs pelluntur atque in fugam coniciuntur.
LAC7.en: The first attack having been made from the right wing, the enemy are driven off and thrown into flight.

LAC8.la: Erat victrīx rēs pūblica, caesīs Antōnī cōpiīs et ipsō expulsō.
LAC8.en: The republic was victorious, Antony’s forces having been cut down and he himself driven out.
LAC8.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Brutum 1.10.2. There are two ablative absolutes joined by et.

LAC9.en: This speech having been delivered, Ambiorix departs.
LAC9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 5.27.11.

LAC10.la: Eurōpa, trāns mare ab simulātō taurō vecta, virgineā tenuit cornua vāra manū.
LAC10.en: Europa, carried across the sea by a simulated bull, held the bent horns with a maidenly hand.
LAC10.note: From Ovid, Amores 1.3.23–24. Vecta is a perfect passive participle modifying Eurōpa.

LAC11.la: Cūnctī gladiōs, Caesare duce, sine morā sūmpsērunt.
LAC11.en: All took up their swords without delay, Caesar being leader.
LAC11.note: Caesare duce is an ablative absolute of the noun + noun type.

LAC12.en: The house began to burn while the boy was sleeping.

LAC13.la: Ad mūrōs urbis appropinquantēs arcem Rōmānam vidēre poterant.
LAC13.en: Approaching the walls of the city, they could see the Roman citadel.
LAC13.note: Appropinquantēs is not an ablative absolute: it agrees with the subject, understood.

LAC14.la: Hīs interfectīs, cēterī incolae impetibus crēbrīs territī sunt.
LAC14.en: With these men killed, the rest of the inhabitants were terrified by frequent attacks.
LAC14.note: The book printed the genitive plural impetuum crēbrōrum; Dr. Lake confirmed the ablative impetibus crēbrīs (means).

LAC15.la: Caesarī, imperiō acceptō, omnia facientī semper erat fortūna.
LAC15.en: Caesar, having received power and doing everything, always had good fortune.
LAC15.note: Caesarī … facientī: dative of possession, “to Caesar there was fortune.” Imperiō acceptō is an ablative absolute.

LAC16.la: Iussīs ad campōs mīlitibus, Caesar in monte cōnstitit.
LAC16.en: The soldiers having been ordered to the plains, Caesar halted on the mountain.

LAC17.la: Bellō cōnfectō, imperātor ipse in Ītaliam pervēnit et per urbem Rōmam magnō gaudiō cīvium vectus est.
LAC17.en: The war having been finished, the general himself arrived in Italy and was carried through the city of Rome to the great joy of the citizens.
LAC17.note: Vectus est is the perfect passive of vehō.

LAC18.la: Tandem fugit ad mē pulsus ā Graeciā, cupiēns amīcōs.
LAC18.en: At last he fled to me, driven from Greece, desiring friends.

LAC19.la: Vēre appropinquante, ad Graeciam nāvī vehēmur.
LAC19.en: Spring approaching, we will sail to Greece by ship.
LAC19.note: Vehēmur is the future passive of vehō, “we will be carried” = “we will sail.”

LAC20.la: Rēge crūdēlī cīvitātem regente, quid potest esse fēlīx?
LAC20.en: With a cruel king ruling the state, what can be happy?
LAC20.note: Rēge … regente is an ablative absolute whose participle has an object.

LAD1.la: Aqua Appia in urbem inducta est ab Appiō Claudiō Crassō cēnsōre
LAD1.en: The Appian Aqueduct was brought into the city by Appius Claudius Crassus the censor.
LAD1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Frontinus, de Aquīs Urbis Rōmae 5.1.2. Inducta est is in + dūcō: “was led into.”

LAD2.la: Tūne eum, quem esse hostem comperistī, discēdere sustinēbis?
LAD2.en: Will you allow that man to depart, whom you have discovered to be an enemy?
LAD2.note: From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.27. -ne introduces the question. Sustinēbis takes the infinitive: “bear to, allow.”

LAD3.la: Quae verba, Rōmānī, iam in hāc rē pūblicā nōn sōlum tenebrīs vetustātis sed etiam lūce lībertātis oppressa sunt.
LAD3.en: Which words, Romans, have now in this republic been overwhelmed not only by the gloom of antiquity but also by the light of liberty.
LAD3.note: From Cicero, pro Rabirio Perduellionis Reo 13. Tenebrīs vetustātis: “by the gloom of antiquity.”

LAD4.la: Nūllus cāsus odiō inter amīcōs est; nūllus cāsus fideī inter inimīcōs est.
LAD4.en: There is no occasion for hatred among friends; there is no occasion for faith among enemies.
LAD4.note: The book prints fidē in the second clause; the app corrects it to fideī, a dative parallel to odiō.

LAD5.la: Sine ūllā auctōritāte populī bellum gerere et sociōs cīvēsque in proeliō coercēre nūllī iūs est.
LAD5.en: No one has the right to wage war without any authority of the people and to restrain allies and citizens in battle.
LAD5.note: Nūllī iūs est is a dative of possessor: “to no one is there a right.”

LAD6.la: Cibus īdem multa nōmina per Asiam habet.
LAD6.en: The same food has many names throughout Asia.

LAD7.la: Adventū hostis compertō, Caesar dextrō cornū ad campum sine morā appropinquāre coepit.
LAD7.en: The arrival of the enemy having been learned, Caesar began to approach the plain with his right wing without delay.
LAD7.note: The book prints appropinquēre; the app corrects it to appropinquāre.

LAD8.la: Illam clāram trādēmus fīliīs lēgem quam ā patribus accēpimus.
LAD8.en: We will hand down to our sons that famous law which we received from our fathers.

LAD9.la: Auxiliīs in fugam pulsīs, cūnctī rem pūblicam servāre cōnstituērunt.
LAD9.en: The auxiliaries having been put to flight, all decided to save the republic.

LAD10.la: Illum mūrum dēlēre mīlitēs iussit ubi hostēs victūrī cōnsistēbant.
LAD10.en: He ordered the soldiers to destroy that wall where the enemy, about to conquer, were making a stand.
LAD10.note: The book prints vīctūrī (from vīvō); the app corrects it to victūrī (from vincō, “about to conquer”).

LAD11.la: Alter puer ē vītā prehēnsus est, alter vīvēns senex.
LAD11.en: One boy was seized from life, the other lived on to be an old man.

LAD12.la: Tandem ingenium tōtīus exercitūs imperātōrī clārum esse vidētur, bellō cōnfectō.
LAD12.en: At last, the war having been finished, the talent of the whole army seems famous to the general.
LAD12.note: Bellō cōnfectō is an ablative absolute.

LAD13.la: Compertīs īnsidiīs, nāvem solvit sine ūllā glōriae spē.
LAD13.en: The ambush having been discovered, he set sail without any hope of glory.

LAD14.la: Quiēs est praemium mentibus cūrā solūtīs.
LAD14.en: Rest is a reward for minds freed from care.
LAD14.note: Cūrā is an ablative of separation with solūtīs.

LAD15.la: Uter discipulus ad lūdum sine ūllīs lībrīs vēnit?
LAD15.en: Which student came to school without any books?

LAE1.la: Flēns miserābilis fuit propter recentem memoriam clārissimī patris.
LAE1.en: Weeping, he was pitiable because of the recent memory of his most famous father.
LAE1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Brutus 23.90. Clārissimī is a superlative: “most famous.”

LAE2.la: Nihil est fortius quam virī bonī mōribus similēs familiāritāte iūnctī.
LAE2.en: Nothing is stronger than good men, similar in character, joined by close friendship.
LAE2.note: From Cicero, de Officiis 1.55. After quam, virī is in the nominative, like nihil.

LAE3.la: In caelōque deum sēdēs et templa locārunt.
LAE3.en: And in the sky they placed the abodes and temples of the gods.
LAE3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Lucretius, de Rerum Natura 5.1188. Locārunt is locāvērunt.

LAE4.en: Of wild animals none is wiser than the elephant.
LAE4.note: From Cicero, de Natura Deorum 1.97. Elephantō is an ablative of comparison.

LAE5.la: Quid dīcis tū, ō fēmina audācissima? Quotiēns tē vetuī ad eius fīlium appropinquāre?
LAE5.en: What do you say, you most bold woman? How many times have I forbidden you to approach his son?

LAE6.la: Tē, quae nōbīs nostrā vītā dulcior es, vidēbimus.
LAE6.en: We will see you, who are sweeter to us than our life.
LAE6.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 14.7.1. Nostrā vītā is an ablative of comparison.

LAE7.la: Nāvis spectāre īnfernō summum dē gurgite caelum vidētur.
LAE7.en: The ship seems to look up at the highest sky from the low whirlpool.
LAE7.note: From Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.504–506. Summum caelum: “the top of the sky.”

LAE8.la: Ille vir, cui patriae salūs dulcior quam cōnspectus fuit, est comprehēnsus.
LAE8.en: That man, to whom the safety of the fatherland was sweeter than sight, was seized.
LAE8.note: From Cicero, pro Balbo 11. Cōnspectus, -ūs: “the ability to see.”

LAE9.la: Ubi ea via invenītur quae in caelum dūcit et in illam sēdem eōrum quī iam vīxērunt et corpore līberātī sunt?
LAE9.en: Where is found that road which leads into the sky and to the abode of those who have already lived and have been freed from the body?

LAE10.la: Patria mea quam cārissima mihi semper fuit.
LAE10.en: My country has always been as dear as possible to me.
LAE10.note: Quam with a superlative: “as … as possible.”

LAE11.la: Tē in caelum ipsa ferē sustulit virtūs.
LAE11.en: Virtue itself almost raised you to the sky.

LAE12.en: Which of the two victims will be more pleasing to the gods?

LAE13.la: Opere inceptō, lūdōs vidēre magister discipulōs vetuit.
LAE13.en: With the work begun, the teacher forbade the students to watch the games.
LAE13.note: Opere incepto is an ablative absolute.

LAE14.la: Tibi quam mihi sunt etiam lātiōrēs et longiōrēs pedēs.
LAE14.en: You have even wider and longer feet than I.
LAE14.note: Quam mihi: the second element is dative, like the first (tibi).

LAE15.la: Quandō ad reī pūblicae cūram ā turpī hostium timōre animōs revocābimus?
LAE15.en: When will we call our minds back to the care of the republic from the shameful fear of the enemy?

LAE16.la: Nihil mentem animumque meum etiam dēlectāre potest, falsus ā meō amīcō, virō fidēlissimō.
LAE16.en: Nothing can even delight my mind and spirit, deceived by my friend, a most faithful man.
LAE16.note: Falsus is the perfect passive participle of fallō.

LAE17.la: Ille cum virtūte vīvit, falsūrus etiam in morte nūllum.
LAE17.en: He lives with virtue, about to deceive no one even in death.
LAE17.note: Falsūrus is a future active participle: “about to deceive.”

LAE18.la: Hieme appropinquante, summa salūs reī pūblicae et spēs victōriae in virtūte exercitūs pōnuntur.
LAE18.en: With winter approaching, the highest safety of the republic and the hope of victory are placed in the courage of the army.
LAE18.note: Hieme appropinquante is an ablative absolute.

LAE19.la: Quid dulcius frūctū bonārum artium est?
LAE19.en: What is sweeter than the fruit of the good arts?
LAE19.note: Frūctū is an ablative of comparison.

LAE20.la: Cūr hunc mōrem turpem servāvistis? Iste mōs nōn vetitus est, sed nōbīs ā patribus trāditus est.
LAE20.en: Why have you kept this shameful custom? That custom has not been forbidden, but has been handed down to us by our fathers.

LAE21.la: Quam miser sum quod medicus mē vīnum bibere vetuit.
LAE21.en: How wretched I am because the doctor has forbidden me to drink wine.

LAE22.la: Victus ab multīs hostibus, ille imperātor auctōritāte apud mīlitēs carēre vidētur.
LAE22.en: Conquered by many enemies, that general seems to lack authority among the soldiers.

LAF1.en: I have learned a worthy and most useful thing.

LAF2.en: Nothing is nobler than a humble cottage.
LAF2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 1.6.4.8. Humilī casā is an ablative of comparison.

LAF3.la: Numquam māiōre in perīculō cīvitās fuit; numquam improbī cīvēs habuērunt parātiōrem ducem.
LAF3.en: The state was never in greater danger; never did wicked citizens have a more prepared leader.
LAF3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 16.11.3. The book prints maiōre; the app adds the macron on the first a (māiōre). Improbus: “wicked”; parātus: “prepared.”

LAF4.la: Timor mortis ad humilius opus nōbilēs manūs mittit.
LAF4.en: The fear of death sends noble hands to rather humble work.
LAF4.note: From Quintilian, Declamationes Maiores 12.15.16. Humilius: “rather humble.”

LAF5.la: Postquam tantam rem Marius sine ūllō incommodō cōnfēcit, magnus et clārus anteā, māior atque clārior esse coepit.
LAF5.en: After Marius accomplished so great a matter without any trouble, he, great and famous before, began to be greater and more famous.
LAF5.note: From Sallust, Bellum Iugurthinum 92. Incommodum: “trouble”; anteā: “previously.”

LAF6.la: Nātālī diē mihi dulcior haec lūx est.
LAF6.en: This day is sweeter to me than my birthday.
LAF6.note: From Juvenal, Saturae 12.1. Nātālī diē is an ablative of comparison.

LAF7.la: Propter ignis inventiōnem in ūnum locum plūrēs conveniēbant, habentēs ab nātūrā praemium praeter reliqua animālia.
LAF7.en: Because of the discovery of fire, more (people) came together into one place, having from nature a reward beyond the rest of the animals.

LAF8.la: Tū loca, quae nimium grāta fuēre, cavē.
LAF8.en: You, beware of the places which were too pleasing.
LAF8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Ovid, Remedia Amoris 738. Fuēre is fuērunt.

LAF9.la: Nam et eīs fidem habēmus, quōs plūs intellegere quam nōs crēdimus.
LAF9.en: For we also have faith in those whom we believe to understand more than we do.
LAF9.note: From Cicero, de Officiis 2.33.3. Plūs is a neuter noun: “more.”

LAF10.la: Caesarī nihil vērā glōriā dulcius est, quam ob rem ab eō nōn sōlum nihil timēre sed etiam māiōra et meliōra exspectāre dēbētis.
LAF10.en: Nothing is sweeter to Caesar than true glory; for which reason you ought to fear nothing from him but even to expect greater and better things.
LAF10.note: From Cicero, Philippica 5.51. Quam ob rem: “for which reason.”

LAF11.la: ‘Frātrī similior quam patrī es.’ Hīs aliīsque ambitiōnem iuvenis incitat.
LAF11.en: “You are more like your brother than your father.” With these and other (words) he stirs up the young man’s ambition.
LAF11.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 1.47.6. After quam, patrī is in the dative, like frātrī.

LAF12.la: Lūce sunt clāriōra nōbīs tua cōnsilia omnia.
LAF12.en: All your plans are clearer to us than light.
LAF12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.6.12. Lūce is an ablative of comparison.

LAF13.en: I see and approve the better things, I do the worse.

LAF14.la: Malum omne quod latet est gravius quam quod patet.
LAF14.en: Every evil that lies hidden is heavier than one that is in plain view.

LAF15.la: Ūtilissimum semper erit mōrēs māiōrum nostrōrum discere.
LAF15.en: It will always be most useful to learn the customs of our ancestors.

LAF16.la: Cavē peiōra cōnsilia. Morbus animī pēior est quam corporis.
LAF16.en: Beware of worse plans. A disease of the mind is worse than (a disease) of the body.

LAF17.la: Sumus sapientiōrēs quam illī quod rēs nostrās auximus.
LAF17.en: We are wiser than they because we have increased our resources.

LAF18.la: Iste audācissimus homō aurum argentumque ex aede sustulit.
LAF18.en: That very bold man removed gold and silver from the temple.

LAF19.la: Duce īnsidiārum pūnītō, cīvium caedēs in summō monte fuerat maxima.
LAF19.en: The leader of the ambush having been punished, the slaughter of the citizens on the top of the mountain had been the greatest.
LAF19.note: Duce … pūnītō is an ablative absolute.

LAF20.la: Hic est liber optimus quem umquam lēgī.
LAF20.en: This is the best book that I have ever read.

LAG1.la: Nēmō potest dē eā rē turpissimē dīcere.
LAG1.en: No one can speak most shamefully about that matter.

LAG2.la: Clāde Icēnōrum, plūrimī quī dē bellō multum dubitābant, nōn diūtius pācem dēlēgērunt.
LAG2.en: After the defeat of the Iceni, most of those who were very much in doubt about the war no longer chose peace.
LAG2.note: From Tacitus, Annales 12.32. The Iceni were a tribe of Britons at the time of Claudius’ conquest in A.D. 43.

LAG3.la: Cōnscientia bene āctae vītae multōrumque bene factōrum memoria dulcissima est.
LAG3.en: The awareness of a life well lived and the memory of many deeds well done is sweetest.
LAG3.note: From Cicero, Cato Maior de Senectute 9.7. The book prints actae; the app adds the macron (āctae).

LAG4.la: Fuit, fuit ista quondam in hāc rē pūblicā virtūs, et virī dūriōribus suppliciīs cīvem malum quam acerbissimum hostem coercēre fortiter dēligēbant.
LAG4.en: There was, there was once that courage in this republic, and men chose to restrain a wicked citizen bravely with harsher punishments than the most bitter enemy.

LAG5.la: Cicerō bellissimus tibi salūtem plūrimam optat. Etiam atque etiam valē.
LAG5.en: Cicero, very charming, wishes you very much health. Farewell again and again.
LAG5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 14.7.3.

LAG6.la: Philippus in aciē tūtior quam in theātrō fuit: hostium manūs saepe vītāvit, suōrum effugere nōn valuit.
LAG6.en: Philip was safer in battle than in the theater: he often avoided the hands of the enemy, but was not able to escape those of his own (family).
LAG6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 9.6.25.1.

LAG7.la: Camillus currū equīs albīs iūnctō ad urbem vectus, triumphus ob eam ūnam maximē rem clārior quam grātior fuit.
LAG7.en: Camillus, carried to the city in a chariot yoked with white horses: the triumph was more famous than pleasing on account of that one thing especially.
LAG7.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 5.23.6.3. Currus, -ūs: “chariot.”

LAG8.la: Et enim patria mihi vītā meā multō est cārior.
LAG8.en: For my country is also much dearer to me than my life.
LAG8.note: From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.27.8. Multō is an ablative of degree of difference.

LAG9.la: In omnī genere ac varietāte artium, etiam illārum quae sine summō ōtiō nōn facile discuntur, Cn. Pompēius excellit.
LAG9.en: In every kind and variety of arts, even of those which are not easily learned without the greatest leisure, Gnaeus Pompey excels.

LAG10.la: Quantum memoriā repetere praeterita possum, nēmō est mihi tē amīcus vetustior.
LAG10.en: As far as I can recall the past by memory, no one is a friend older to me than you.

LAG11.en: Which of us two was more worthy of the cross?
LAG11.note: From Horace, Sermones 2.7.45. Dignus takes the ablative.

LAG12.la: Aenēās Ītaliam reget, genus altō ā sanguine Teucrī prōdet, ac tōtum sub lēgēs mittet orbem.
LAG12.en: Aeneas will rule Italy, will bring forth a race from the noble blood of Teucer, and will send the whole world under (its) laws.
LAG12.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 4.230–231. Teucer was the legendary founder of the Trojan race.

LAG13.la: Illa clādēs omnibus quae huic urbī accidērunt gravior et māior erat.
LAG13.en: That disaster was graver and greater than all (the disasters) that happened to this city.
LAG13.note: Omnibus is an ablative of comparison.

LAG14.la: Multōs senēs et stultōs saepe vīdī, sed stultiōrem quam Mārcum vīdī nēminem.
LAG14.en: I have often seen many old and foolish men, but I have seen no one more foolish than Marcus.

LAG15.la: Perīculō vītātō, mihi vīsus est et monēre tē sapienter et culpāre amīcissimē.
LAG15.en: With the danger avoided, he seemed to me both to advise you wisely and to blame you most kindly.

LAG16.la: Quod in plūribus simul locīs hostēs in legiōnēs impetum fēcērunt, incendere castra eōs prohibēre nōn poterāmus.
LAG16.en: Because the enemy made an attack on the legions in several places at once, we could not stop them from burning the camp.

LAG17.la: Hominēs saepius spē quam dolōre carent.
LAG17.en: People lack hope more often than grief.

LAG18.la: Quid iste mīles stultius facere potuit quam imperātōrem dē officiīs monēre?
LAG18.en: What more foolish thing could that soldier have done than to warn the general about his duties?

LAG19.la: Et multō facilior et tūtior est vīta eōrum quī pācem et ōtium dēlēgērunt.
LAG19.en: And the life of those who have chosen peace and leisure is much easier and safer.

LAG20.la: Habentibus sapientiam, virtūs et lībertās vītā ipsā cārior esse dēbent.
LAG20.en: For those having wisdom, virtue and liberty ought to be dearer than life itself.
LAG20.note: Habentibus is a participle used as a noun.

LAG21.la: Age deīs grātiās! Maximum gaudium ex tuīs epistulīs cēpī, nam quod cupīveram atque optāveram mihi dīxistī.
LAG21.en: Give thanks to the gods! I took the greatest joy from your letters, for you told me what I had wished and hoped for.

LAG22.la: Nēmō contrā patriam dūcere potest exercitum.
LAG22.en: No one can lead an army against his country.

LAH1.la: Ācerrimum tertiae septimaeque legiōnum proelium erat.
LAH1.en: The battle of the third and seventh legions was the fiercest.

LAH2.en: With winter approaching, the first snow fell.
LAH2.note: From Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 18.132.4.

LAH3.la: Tertiō diē, Caesar ad Pompēium pervēnit, iuxtāque eum castra posuit.
LAH3.en: On the third day, Caesar came to Pompey and pitched camp next to him.
LAH3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Civili 3.41.1. Iuxtā + accusative: “next to.”

LAH4.la: Ab dextrō cornū, ubi septima legiō cōnstiterat, hostēs pelluntur atque in fugam coniciuntur.
LAH4.en: From the right wing, where the seventh legion had halted, the enemy are driven off and thrown into flight.
LAH4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 7.62.3.

LAH5.la: Ab sinistrō cornū, quem locum duodecima legiō tenēbat, prīmī ōrdinēs hostium trānsfīxī pilīs ceciderant, sed ācerrimē reliquī resistēbant.
LAH5.en: From the left wing, a place which the twelfth legion was holding, the first ranks of the enemy had fallen, pierced through by spears, but the rest resisted most fiercely.
LAH5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 7.62.1. Ōrdō, -dinis: “rank”; trānsfīxī: “pierced through”; pīlum: “spear.”

LAH6.la: Equus trīgintā mēnsibus prīmum dentēs mediōs dīcitur āmittere.
LAH6.en: A horse is said to lose its middle teeth first at thirty months.
LAH6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Marcus Terentius Varro, Res Rusticae 2.7.2.3.

LAH7.la: Caesar quoque in proximō colle castra pōnit.
LAH7.en: Caesar also pitches camp on the nearest hill.
LAH7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Civili 1.65.5.

LAH8.la: Sīc M. Cicerō dēcessit, vir nātus ad reī pūblicae salūtem. Vīxit sexāgintā et trēs annōs.
LAH8.en: Thus M. Cicero died, a man born for the safety of the republic. He lived sixty-three years.

LAH9.la: Decimā hōrā amīcōs plūrēs quam prīmā repperiēs.
LAH9.en: At the tenth hour you will find more friends than at the first.
LAH9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae D28.

LAH10.la: Quandō pater ā patriā discessit? Tunc dentēs mihi cadēbant prīmī.
LAH10.en: When did my father leave his country? At that time my first teeth were falling out.

LAH11.la: Magister Gorgiās centum et septem vīxit annōs, neque umquam ā studiō atque opere discessit.
LAH11.en: The teacher Gorgias lived one hundred and seven years, and never departed from study and work.
LAH11.note: From Cicero, Cato Maior de Senectute 13.13.

LAH12.la: Nōn vīribus aut celeritāte corporis rēs magnae geruntur, sed cōnsiliō et auctōritāte.
LAH12.en: Great things are accomplished not by strength or speed of body, but by planning and authority.
LAH12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Cato Maior de Senectute 17.8.

LAH13.la: Flūmine surgentī, septima legiō pontēs meliōrēs celerius quam tertia aedificāre potest.
LAH13.en: With the river rising, the seventh legion can build better bridges more quickly than the third.

LAH14.la: Magister sapiēns ā tribus discipulīs nōn facile falsus est.
LAH14.en: The wise teacher was not easily deceived by three students.

LAH15.la: Dentēs meī dolēbant quod medicum vītāveram.
LAH15.en: My teeth were hurting because I had avoided the doctor.

LAH16.la: Sphinx Oedipum rogāvit: ‘Quid prīmā lūce habet quattuor pedēs, merīdiē duōs, nocte trēs?’
LAH16.en: The Sphinx asked Oedipus: “What has four feet at dawn, two at noon, three at night?”

LAH17.la: Officia mea multō graviōra sunt quam tua.
LAH17.en: My duties are much heavier than yours.
LAH17.note: Multō is an ablative of degree of difference.

LAH18.la: Adventū trium nūntiōrum Cincinnātus agrōs arātūrus cōnsistēbat.
LAH18.en: At the arrival of three messengers, Cincinnatus, about to plow the fields, stopped.
LAH18.note: Arātūrus is a future active participle.

LAH19.la: Prīmō annō duo cōnsulēs ā cīvibus dēligentur.
LAH19.en: In the first year two consuls are chosen by the citizens.

LAH20.la: Illā nocte nix in montem cecidit.
LAH20.en: On that night snow fell on the mountain.

LAI1.en: And a large part of me will avoid Libitina (death).
LAI1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Odes 3.30.6–7. Libitīnam = mortem. Meī is a genitive of the whole.

LAI2.la: Est enim ēloquentia ūna quaedam dē summīs virtūtibus.
LAI2.en: For eloquence is one of the greatest virtues.
LAI2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Oratore 3.55.2. Quaedam dē: “a certain one of.”

LAI3.la: Exceptā sapientiā, nihil melius hominī est ā dīs immortālibus datum.
LAI3.en: With the exception of wisdom, nothing better has been given to man by the immortal gods.
LAI3.note: From Cicero, de Amicitia 20.8. Exceptā = ex + capiō.

LAI4.la: Hominēs in hāc urbe vīderītis in duās partēs esse dīvīsōs.
LAI4.en: You will have seen men in this city divided into two parts.

LAI5.la: Intereā Caesar eā legiōne mīlia passuum XVIIII mūrum in altitūdinem pedum sēdecim perdūcit.
LAI5.en: Meanwhile Caesar with that legion draws out a wall nineteen miles long to a height of sixteen feet.
LAI5.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 1.8.1. Perdūcit = per + dūcō.

LAI6.la: Ipse dē tōtō exercitū cīvium sociōrumque sex mīlia peditum, mīlle equitēs dēlēgit.
LAI6.en: He himself chose, from the whole army of citizens and allies, six thousand infantry and a thousand cavalry.

LAI7.la: Caesar mīlia passuum septem ab eō locō vectus, in apertō ac lātō lītore nāvēs cōnstituit.
LAI7.en: Caesar, having been carried seven miles from that place, stationed the ships on an open and wide shore.

LAI8.la: Ariovistī cōpiae ā nostrīs mīlia passuum quattuor et vīgintī absunt.
LAI8.en: The forces of Ariovistus are twenty-four miles away from our men.
LAI8.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 1.41.5. Ariovistī is the genitive of a proper name.

LAI9.la: Fāta viam invenient, aderitque vocātus Apollō.
LAI9.en: The Fates will find a way, and Apollo, when summoned, will be present.
LAI9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Aeneid 3.395. Fāta: “the Fates.”

LAI10.la: Sed in istō iuvene, quamquam animī satis, auctōritātis parum est.
LAI10.en: But in that young man, although there is enough spirit, there is little authority.
LAI10.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum 16.14.2. Satis and parum are nouns here, followed by the genitive.

LAI11.la: Ex ingentibus saxīs sex pedum mūrum mūnīverant Gallī.
LAI11.en: The Gauls had built a six-foot wall of huge stones.
LAI11.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 7.46.1. Sex pedum is a genitive of measurement.

LAI12.la: Maior est populus, cui miscēmur, hoc perīculī plūs est.
LAI12.en: The greater the crowd with which we mingle, the more danger there is.
LAI12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca, Epistulae Morales 7.2.4. Populus: “mob.” Hoc is an ablative of degree of difference.

LAI13.la: Vōs virtūtem ōdistis? Nihil novī facitis.
LAI13.en: Do you hate virtue? You are doing nothing new.
LAI13.note: From Seneca, Dialogi 7.20.6. The book prints ōdisti; the app adds the macron (ōdistis).

LAI14.la: Quantum numerum esse difficilius scrībam, nam auctōrēs discrepant. Exercitum Pūnicum alius decem, alius septem, alius haud plūs quam duōrum mīlium esse scrībit.
LAI14.en: I will write with more difficulty how large the number was, for the authors disagree. One writes that the Punic army was ten (thousand), another seven, another not more than two thousand.
LAI14.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 26.49.2. Discrepō: “disagree.”

LAI15.la: Quīdam dē mīlitibus sōlus pontem dēlēre hostēs audācter prohibuit.
LAI15.en: One of the soldiers alone boldly prevented the enemy from destroying the bridge.

LAI16.la: Post impetum erat relictum nihil in oppidō praeter duo templa.
LAI16.en: After the attack nothing was left in the town except two temples.

LAI17.la: Illa urbs ab legiōne dēlēta ā lītore septendecim mīlia passuum abest.
LAI17.en: That city, destroyed by a legion, is seventeen miles from the shore.

LAI18.la: Quid cibī canibus ēsūrīs hodiē dabis?
LAI18.en: What food will you give to the dogs about to eat today?
LAI18.note: Ēsūrīs: future active participle of edō.

LAI19.la: Quod ad castra equitēs ad tempus nōn pervēnerant, imperātor peditēs in aciem dūcere dubitāvit.
LAI19.en: Because the cavalry had not arrived at the camp on time, the general hesitated to lead the infantry into battle.

LAI20.la: Magister meus satis ingenī sed parum industriae habet.
LAI20.en: My teacher has enough talent but little industry.

LAI21.la: Miserrimus senex et patrī similis ante oculōs meōs adesse vīsus est.
LAI21.en: A most wretched old man, similar to my father, seemed to be present before my eyes.

LAI22.la: Magistrīs bene docentibus, nihil bonī carēs praeter magnitūdinem animī.
LAI22.en: With the teachers teaching well, you lack nothing good except greatness of spirit.

LAI23.la: Māior pars hominum ōtium amat sed industriam ōdit.
LAI23.en: The greater part of people loves leisure but hates industry.

LAI24.la: Gladiō inventō, ūnus ē servīs nōbīs locum ubi dominus interfectus erat dēmōnstrāvit.
LAI24.en: With the sword found, one of the slaves showed us the place where the master had been killed.

LAJ1.la: Omnis dē corpore fūgit dolor, omnis stetit in vulnere sanguis.
LAJ1.en: All pain fled from his body, all the blood stood in the wound.

LAJ2.la: Ā Mānliō exercitū acceptō, duo et vīgintī mīlia peditum, mīlle ducentōs equitēs cōnfēcit.
LAJ2.en: With the army received from Manlius, he gathered twenty-two thousand infantry and twelve hundred cavalry.
LAJ2.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 23.40.2. Cōnfēcit here means “he secured, gathered.”

LAJ3.la: P. Scīpiō nōnāgintā mīlia peditum, duodecim mīlia equitum in Hispāniam trādūxit.
LAJ3.en: Publius Scipio led ninety thousand infantry and twelve thousand cavalry across into Spain.

LAJ4.la: Virtūs autem nōn potest maior aut minor esse.
LAJ4.en: Virtue, however, cannot be greater or less.
LAJ4.note: From Seneca, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 71.8.6.

LAJ5.la: Nam et illam meam clādem vōs et omnēs bonī maximum esse reī pūblicae vulnus iūdicāstis.
LAJ5.en: For both you and all good men judged that disaster of mine to be the greatest wound of the republic.
LAJ5.note: From Cicero, Pro Sestio 31.10–11. Iūdicāstis = iūdicāvistis.

LAJ6.la: Numquam hominem stultiōrem vīdī nec vidēbō!
LAJ6.en: I have never seen a more foolish man, nor will I!

LAJ7.la: Ille nōn est mihi pār virtūtibus nec officiīs, sed habuit suam Venerem.
LAJ7.en: He is not equal to me in virtues or duties, but he had his own charm.
LAJ7.note: From Seneca, de Beneficiis 2.28.2. Suam Venerem: “his own charm.”

LAJ8.la: Nihil melius ā deīs hominī datum est quam amor patriae.
LAJ8.en: Nothing better has been given to man by the gods than love of country.

LAJ9.la: Lūcem diēī ē terrā tollere videntur ei, quī lībertātem ē vītā tollunt, quā nihil ā deīs melius, nihil cārius habēmus.
LAJ9.en: They seem to take the light of day from the earth, who take liberty from life, than which we have nothing better from the gods, nothing dearer.
LAJ9.note: Quā is an ablative of comparison.

LAJ10.la: Adventū inimīcō dūrō, animus senis maximō dolōre victus est.
LAJ10.en: With the arrival of a harsh enemy, the old man’s spirit was overcome by very great grief.

LAJ11.la: Ob ingenium atque cōnsilia audācia cōnsul noster summam spem cīvium superāvit.
LAJ11.en: On account of (his) talent and bold plans, our consul surpassed the highest hope of the citizens.

LAJ12.la: Vēre adfutūrō, plūrimae avēs in summīs arboribus saepe videntur.
LAJ12.en: With spring about to arrive, very many birds are often seen in the tops of the trees.
LAJ12.note: Adfutūrō: future active participle of adsum.

LAJ13.la: Aestās mē maximē dēlectat quod diēs longiōrēs ac noctēs breviōrēs sunt quam hieme.
LAJ13.en: Summer delights me most because the days are longer and the nights shorter than in winter.
LAJ13.note: Hieme is an ablative of comparison (or time) after quam.

LAJ14.la: Aptissima praemia nōbilium animōrum semper fuērunt et erunt eadem, fortūna et fāma.
LAJ14.en: The most fitting rewards of noble spirits have always been and will be the same: fortune and fame.

LAJ15.la: Quid est deīs grātius quam sanguis hostiārum?
LAJ15.en: What is more pleasing to the gods than the blood of victims?

LAJ16.la: Nēmō praeter senem inter meliōra atque pēiōra sapienter dēligere potest.
LAJ16.en: No one except an old man can choose wisely between better and worse things.

LAJ17.la: Nōngentīs Gallīs impetum facientibus, sexta legiō diū et ācriter pugnābat.
LAJ17.en: With nine hundred Gauls making an attack, the sixth legion fought for a long time and fiercely.

LAJ18.la: Quamquam quīndecim līberī trāns collīs altiōrēs ambulāre coepērunt, novem sōlī iter difficillimum cōnfēcērunt.
LAJ18.en: Although fifteen children began to walk across higher hills, only nine completed the most difficult journey.

LAJ19.la: Mē ipsum satis iste fefellit ubi et cīvis mihi bonus et amīcus fidēlis vidēbātur.
LAJ19.en: That man deceived even me enough when he seemed to me both a good citizen and a faithful friend.

LAJ20.la: Nōn suae sōlum patriae maximus dux erat, sed etiam omnium gentium rēgibus et imperātōribus pār.
LAJ20.en: He was not only the greatest leader of his own country, but also equal to the kings and generals of all nations.

LAK1.la: Propter amōrem omne opus iterum perdis?
LAK1.en: Because of love, are you wasting all (your) work again?

LAK2.la: Vix populum patria sustinet illa suum.
LAK2.en: That country scarcely supports its own people.
LAK2.note: From Ovid, Epistulae (Heroides) 16.183–184. Suum refers back to patria.

LAK3.la: In tē ipse sēcēde, cum esse cōgeris in turbā.
LAK3.en: Withdraw into yourself, when you are forced to be in a crowd.
LAK3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 25.6.8. Ipse is an intensive pronoun agreeing with the understood “you.”

LAK4.la: Simul atque sē ex fugā recēpērunt, statim ad Caesarem lēgātōs dē pāce mīsērunt.
LAK4.en: As soon as they had withdrawn from flight, they at once sent envoys to Caesar about peace.
LAK4.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 4.27.1. Sē recēpērunt: “withdrew.”

LAK5.la: Magna pars eōrum prō cīvibus Rōmānīs sē gerēbat.
LAK5.en: A large part of them behaved like Roman citizens.
LAK5.note: From Asconius, pro Cornelio 60.4. Prō here means “in the manner of.”

LAK6.la: Cohortēs in flūmine pontēs fēcerat duōs distantēs inter sē mīlia passuum IV.
LAK6.en: The cohorts had made two bridges over the river, four miles apart from each other.

LAK7.la: Nihil audācter ipsī per sē sine P. Sullā facere potuerant.
LAK7.en: They had not been able to do anything boldly, by themselves, without P. Sulla.

LAK8.la: Corpus enim multīs eget rēbus, ac animus ex sē auget, sē ipse alit, sē exercet.
LAK8.en: For the body needs many things, but the mind grows from itself, nourishes itself, exercises itself.
LAK8.note: From Seneca, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 80.3.7. Egeō takes the ablative.

LAK9.la: Homō doctus in sē semper dīvitiās habet.
LAK9.en: A learned man always has riches in himself.
LAK9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Phaedrus, Fabulae 4.23.1.

LAK10.la: Cassivellaunus, vastātīs fīnibus, maximē etiam permōtus dēfectiōne cīvitātum, lēgātōs dē pāce ad Caesarem mittit.
LAK10.en: Cassivellaunus, his territory laid waste and especially disturbed by the desertion of the states, sends envoys to Caesar about peace.

LAK11.la: In verbum ‘populus’, omnis pars cīvitātis omnēsque eius ōrdinēs continentur.
LAK11.en: In the word “populus,” every part of the state and all its ranks are contained.

LAK12.la: Quid dulcius hominum generī ab nātūrā datum est quam suī līberī?
LAK12.en: What has been given by nature to the human race that is sweeter than its own children?
LAK12.note: From Cicero, post Reditum ad Populum 2.6.

LAK13.la: Neque enim potest exercitum is continēre imperātor quī sē ipse nōn continet.
LAK13.en: For that general cannot restrain an army who does not restrain himself.
LAK13.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Lege Manilia 38.

LAK14.la: Nihil enim cupiō quam mē mihi similem esse.
LAK14.en: For I want nothing except to be like myself.
LAK14.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum 9.16.2. Mihi similem: similis takes the dative.

LAK15.la: Hostibus fugātīs, deinde Caesar omnēs equitēs ante sē praemīsit.
LAK15.en: The enemy having been routed, Caesar then sent all the cavalry ahead of himself.

LAK16.la: Eī quī ā timōre mortis sē vix continēre possunt virtūte carent.
LAK16.en: Those who can hardly restrain themselves from the fear of death lack virtue.

LAK17.la: Hostēs deīs multās hostiās frūstrā mactāvērunt, septem enim hōrīs Caesar nūllō negōtiō vastāre agrōs eōrum oppidaque incendere poterat.
LAK17.en: The enemy slaughtered many victims to the gods in vain, for in seven hours Caesar could ravage their fields and burn their towns without any trouble.
LAK17.note: Septem hōrīs: ablative of time within which.

LAK18.la: Ubi fīlius suus ē vītā excessit, pater dolōre victus omnēs frūctūs industriae et fortūnae suae ferē perdidit.
LAK18.en: When his own son departed from life, the father, overcome by grief, almost lost all the fruits of his industry and fortune.

LAK19.la: In maximīs rēbus avus tuus sē turpissimē semper gerēbat.
LAK19.en: In the greatest matters your grandfather always behaved most shamefully.

LAK20.la: Hostēs ante mediam noctem cum manū magnā in campum apertum vēnērunt et ad merīdiem mānsērunt.
LAK20.en: The enemy came before midnight with a large band into the open plain and remained until noon.

LAK21.la: Quis istum cōnsulem pēius quam suōs inimīcōs nōn ōderat?
LAK21.en: Who did not hate that consul more than his own enemies?
LAK21.note: Ōderat: ōdī has present meanings; its pluperfect translates as an imperfect.

LAK22.la: Captīvus enim reprehendendus tibi omnia sua praeter vītam trādidit.
LAK22.en: For the captive, who deserved blame, handed over to you all his belongings except his life.
LAK22.note: Reprehendendus: a gerundive, “deserving to be blamed” (cf. Lesson LV).

LAL1.la: Homērus semper in mediās rēs audītōrem rapit.
LAL1.en: Homer always snatches the listener into the middle of things.
LAL1.note: From Horace, Ars Poetica 148–149. In mediās rēs: “into the midst of things.”

LAL2.la: Contrā hostem aut fortem oportet esse aut supplicem.
LAL2.en: Against an enemy one ought to be either brave or humble.
LAL2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae C39.

LAL3.la: Caesar enim cōpiās habēbat in Galliā proelium committere.
LAL3.en: For Caesar had the forces in Gaul to begin battle.

LAL4.la: Nōn nōs aut ferrō Libycās vastāre terrās vēnimus, aut raptās ad lītora vertere praedās.
LAL4.en: We have not come either to ravage the Libyan lands with the sword, or to turn seized plunder toward the shores.

LAL5.la: Cūr dēnique hīs esse līberōs nōn licet? Nam hominēs sunt tōtā ex Āsiā sānctissimī.
LAL5.en: Why, at last, is it not permitted for them to be free? For they are the most blessed men from all of Asia.

LAL6.en: There is nothing new under the sun.
LAL6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Ecclesiastes 1.10.

LAL7.la: Egnātius, quod candidōs habet dentēs, usque renīdet.
LAL7.en: Egnatius, because he has shining white teeth, keeps smiling.

LAL8.la: Necesse est enim sōlem aut ipsum per sē movērī, aut cum mundō vertī ūnō locō manentem.
LAL8.en: For it is necessary that the sun either be moved by itself, or turn with the universe while remaining in one place.
LAL8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Hyginus, Astronomica 4.13.2.

LAL9.la: Arma gravī numerō violentaque bella parābam scrībere, sed Cupīdō, iste fūr, dīcitur rīsisse atque ūnum surripuisse pedem.
LAL9.en: I was preparing to write of arms and violent wars in a weighty meter, but Cupid, that thief, is said to have laughed and stolen one foot.
LAL9.note: From Ovid, Amores 1.1.1–4. Gravī numerō: in weighty meter.

LAL10.la: Maiōrēs eōrum omnia quae licēbat illīs relīquēre: dīvitiās, imāginēs, memoriam suī clāram; virtūtem nōn relīquēre.
LAL10.en: Their ancestors left them everything which was permitted: riches, statues, a famous memory of themselves; they did not leave virtue.
LAL10.note: From Sallust, Bellum Iugurthinum 85.38. Relīquēre is relīquērunt.

LAL11.la: Magna pars plēbis Appium nōn minus reum timēbat quam cōnsulem.
LAL11.en: A large part of the people feared Appius no less as a defendant than as a consul.
LAL11.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 2.61.6. Reum is in apposition to Appium.

LAL12.en: He wisely kept the province entrusted to him.

LAL13.la: Ad tē cui sum amīcissimus, tōtumque mē vertisse dēbuī. Sed haec plūribus etiam fortasse verbīs, quam necesse fuit, scrīpsī.
LAL13.en: I ought to have turned wholly to you, to whom I am most friendly. But I have written these things, perhaps, with more words than was necessary.

LAL14.la: Quō modō sine ferrīs animālia caedī possunt?
LAL14.en: How can animals be killed without iron?

LAL15.la: Numquam facilius culpa quam in turbā latet.
LAL15.en: Blame never hides more easily than in a crowd.

LAL16.la: Ubi dē sententiīs nostrīs rogāris, tē paucīs verbīs respondēre oportet.
LAL16.en: When you are asked about our opinions, you ought to reply in a few words.

LAL17.la: Aut nōbīs cōpiās cibī augēre necesse erit aut in castrīs longam hiemem manēre nōn poterimus.
LAL17.en: Either we will have to increase our supplies of food, or we will not be able to remain in camp for the long winter.

LAL18.la: Ex meā sententiā, quōs timēmus, ōdimus.
LAL18.en: In my opinion, those whom we fear, we hate.

LAL19.la: Posteā omnia quae patuērunt neque in templō fuērunt rapī rēx iussit.
LAL19.en: Afterward the king ordered everything that was open and not in the temple to be seized.

LAL20.la: Quem fīnem onerum vītae ad nōs deī mittent? Ōtiumne habēre nōbīs umquam licēbit?
LAL20.en: What end of life’s burdens will the gods send to us? Will we ever be allowed to have leisure?

LAL21.en: At night we are allowed to kill a thief.

LAL22.la: Quamquam paucī in prōvinciam proelium commīserant, cīvium studium ab imperātōre nōn incitārī poterat.
LAL22.en: Although a few had begun battle in the province, the enthusiasm of the citizens could not be stirred up by the general.

LAM1.la: Nam omnēs īdem sentiunt, sed quod nōn est omnibus stantibus necesse dīcere, ā mē id dictūrum īrī intellegō.
LAM1.en: For all feel the same, but because it is not necessary for all standing to speak, I understand that it will be said by me.
LAM1.note: From Cicero, pro Marcello 33. Dictūrum īrī: future passive infinitive (supine + īrī).

LAM2.la: Suscipis onus officī quod tē putās sustinēre posse?
LAM2.en: Are you undertaking the burden of a duty which you think you can bear?
LAM2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Sexto Roscio Amerino 112.

LAM3.la: Factum hic esse id nōn negat.
LAM3.en: He does not deny that it was done here.
LAM3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Terence, Heauton Timorumenos 15.

LAM4.la: Mē tacitūrum esse maximīs dē rēbus exīstimāvistis?
LAM4.en: Did you think that I would be silent about the greatest matters?

LAM5.la: Crēdō esse amōris maculam huic hominī in pectore.
LAM5.en: I believe that this man has a stain of love in his heart.
LAM5.note: From Plautus, Poenulus 198. Huic hominī is a dative of possessor with esse.

LAM6.la: Nūlla spēs est factūrum tē quod optō et quod oportet.
LAM6.en: There is no hope that you will do what I wish and what is fitting.
LAM6.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Brutum 1.13.2. Factūrum (esse) is the future infinitive with esse omitted.

LAM7.la: Iuvenem nostrum nōn possum nōn amāre sed ab eō nōs nōn amārī plānē intellegō.
LAM7.en: I cannot not love our young man, but I clearly understand that we are not loved by him.
LAM7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum 10.10.6.

LAM8.la: Quis spērābat post Carthāginem secundam in Āfricā bellum inceptūrum esse?
LAM8.en: Who hoped that, after the second Carthage, a war would begin in Africa?
LAM8.note: From Lucius Annaeus Florus, Epitome Rerum Romanorum 1.36.1.

LAM9.la: Fēminīs raptīs, ipse Rōmulus fēminās docēbat id superbiā patrum factum esse quī cōnūbium fīnitimīs negāverat.
LAM9.en: With the women seized, Romulus himself taught the women that this had been done through the pride of the fathers, who had denied marriage to the neighbors.

LAM10.la: Cognōvī enim ex multōrum amīcōrum epistulīs ad arma rem spectāre.
LAM10.en: For I have learned from the letters of many friends that the matter is heading toward arms.

LAM11.la: Cognōscit arcem captam esse nūntiōsque missōs ad eōs, quī sē ex fugā in fīnitimās cīvitātēs recēpisse dīcēbantur.
LAM11.en: He learns that the citadel has been captured and that messengers have been sent to those who were said to have withdrawn from the flight into the neighboring states.

LAM12.la: Crēdō eī cui tū scīs iam minimē crēdere mē dēbēre.
LAM12.en: I trust the man to whom you know I ought no longer trust at all.

LAM13.la: Tē mihi fidēlem esse aequē atque ego sum mihi sciēbam.
LAM13.en: I knew that you were as faithful to me as I am to myself.

LAM14.la: Exīstimō illum virum sapientem mē docuisse linguam ūtilissimam et facillimam.
LAM14.en: I think that that wise man taught me a most useful and very easy language.

LAM15.la: Cōnsule dē īnsidiīs tacente, nihil malī accidisse Caesarī putō.
LAM15.en: With the consul silent about the plot, I think that nothing bad happened to Caesar.

LAM16.la: Rōmānī crēdidērunt sponte suā stēllās sē movēre, praeter terram nihil stāre.
LAM16.en: The Romans believed that the stars move of their own accord, and that nothing stands still except the earth.

LAM17.la: Avum meum semper fuisse et futūrum esse fidēlem cīvitātī sciō.
LAM17.en: I know that my grandfather has always been and will always be faithful to the state.

LAM18.la: Omnēs scīmus initia maximōrum esse minima.
LAM18.en: We all know that the beginnings of the greatest things are the smallest.

LAM19.la: Cicerōnem intellegimus librum optimum et amplissimum dē amīcitiā scrīpsisse.
LAM19.en: We understand that Cicero wrote a very good and very great book about friendship.

LAM20.la: Cūr mihi nōn dīxistī tē ad mē ab patre tuō missum esse?
LAM20.en: Why did you not tell me that you had been sent to me by your father?

LAM21.la: Ūnus ex cōnsulibus putāvit equitēs ad aciem frūstrā praemissōs esse.
LAM21.en: One of the consuls thought that the cavalry had been sent ahead to the battle line in vain.

LAM22.la: Fugiēns urbis ā mūrīs, quāsdam dē nāvibus ab hostibus audācibus incendī invēnī.
LAM22.en: Fleeing from the walls of the city, I found that some of the ships were being burned by the bold enemy.

LAN1.la: Hinc septem vidēre collīs et tōtam licet aestimāre Rōmam.
LAN1.en: From here it is possible to see the seven hills and to judge the whole of Rome.

LAN2.la: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs ad Ītaliam vēnit.
LAN2.en: I sing of arms and the man who first came from the shores of Troy to Italy.

LAN3.la: Atque animum nunc hūc celerem, nunc dīvidit illūc.
LAN3.en: And now here, now there, he divides his swift mind.
LAN3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Aeneid 4.285.

LAN4.la: Māgō, frāter Hannibalis, Carthāginem init, unde duodecim mīlia peditum et mīlle quīngentōs equitēs, et vīgintī elephantōs in Ītaliam trānsmissūrus erat.
LAN4.en: Mago, brother of Hannibal, enters Carthage, from where he was going to send across into Italy twelve thousand infantry, fifteen hundred cavalry, and twenty elephants.

LAN5.la: P. Clōdium, crēdō tē audīsse cum veste fēminae prehēnsum domī Caesaris.
LAN5.en: I believe you have heard that Publius Clodius was caught in a woman’s dress at Caesar’s house.

LAN6.la: Quid nunc? Ea domī est? Cūr eam exīre hinc vīdī domō?
LAN6.en: What now? Is she at home? Why did I see her go out of the house from here?

LAN7.la: Recipe mē aeternā domō nōn exitūrum!
LAN7.en: Take me back into my eternal home, never to leave!

LAN8.en: They said that he would not return to Rome.
LAN8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Milone 62.

LAN9.la: Q. Fulvius Flaccus ex Hispāniā rediit Rōmam cum magnā fāmā gestārum rērum.
LAN9.en: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus returned from Spain to Rome with great fame for his deeds.
LAN9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 40.43.4.

LAN10.la: Inde Iāsōn ipse cum Mēdēā Corinthum adiit.
LAN10.en: From there Jason himself went to Corinth with Medea.

LAN11.en: Run here to the temple of Venus!

LAN12.la: Īte, nūntiāte rēgī vestrō et, quae āmīsit, et, quae adhūc habet, praemia esse bellī.
LAN12.en: Go, tell your king that both what he has lost and what he still has are the rewards of war.
LAN12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 4.11.21.

LAN13.la: Flūmen in eandem partem unde vēnit redit.
LAN13.en: The river returns to the same part from which it came.

LAN14.la: Quōsdam ex līberīs hīc mānsūrōs esse crēdō.
LAN14.en: I believe that some of the children will stay here.

LAN15.la: Incipit rēs melius īre quam putāveram.
LAN15.en: Things begin to go better than I had thought.

LAN16.la: Silvā ab equitibus vastātā, rūs adeunt neque hūc iterum redībunt.
LAN16.en: With the forest laid waste by the cavalry, they go to the country and will not return here again.

LAN17.la: Scīmus Catōnem apud patrēs nostrōs appellātum esse sapientem.
LAN17.en: We know that Cato was called wise among our fathers.

LAN18.la: Domum rediī simul atque audīvī tē eō pervēnisse.
LAN18.en: I returned home as soon as I heard that you had arrived there.

LAN19.la: Fīlius meus mēcum Rōmae adest, sed fīlia mea cum virō manēns Athēnīs habitat.
LAN19.en: My son is here in Rome with me, but my daughter, staying with her husband, lives in Athens.

LAN20.la: Prīmā lūce exī domō et Delphōs properā!
LAN20.en: At dawn go out of the house and hurry to Delphi!

LAN21.la: Ductī ad Hispāniam, inde hostēs flūmen lātum ponte trānsiērunt.
LAN21.en: Led to Spain, from there the enemy crossed the wide river by a bridge.

LAN22.la: Sed sentīre dēbēs omnium oculōs nunc in tē esse coniectōs; ūnum tē sapientem et appellant et exīstimant.
LAN22.en: But you must realize that the eyes of all are now cast upon you; they both call you and consider you uniquely wise.

LAO1.la: Est modus in rēbus, sunt certī dēnique fīnēs.
LAO1.en: There is a limit in things; there are, finally, fixed boundaries.
LAO1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Sermones 1.1.106.

LAO2.la: Mitte lūcem tuam et vēritātem tuam; ipsae dūcent mē.
LAO2.en: Send out your light and your truth; they themselves will lead me.
LAO2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Psalms 43:3.

LAO3.la: Nōn quī iussus aliquid facit, miser est, sed quī invītus facit.
LAO3.en: The wretched man is not he who does something when ordered, but he who does it unwillingly.
LAO3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca, ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales 61.3.

LAO4.la: Neque audiēs virum bonum quemquam neque vidēbis!
LAO4.en: You will neither hear nor see any good man!
LAO4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Catilinam 1.26.

LAO5.en: Each person is the architect of his own fortune.
LAO5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Pseudo-Sallust, Epistulae ad Caesarem 2.1, quoting Appius Claudius Caecus.

LAO6.la: Itaque beneficium ipsum est: nihil dē reditū cōgitāre.
LAO6.en: And so the favor itself is: to think nothing about a return.

LAO7.la: Delphī igitur nunc in minōre glōriā sunt, quia minus ōrāculōrum vēritās excellit.
LAO7.en: Delphi, therefore, is now held in less glory, because the truth of the oracles excels less.

LAO8.la: Arcum meum pōnam in nūbibus et erit signum foederis inter mē et inter terram.
LAO8.en: I will place my bow in the clouds and it will be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
LAO8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Genesis 9:13.

LAO9.la: Numquam enim nisi nāvī plēnā tollō vectōrem.
LAO9.en: For I never take on a passenger unless the ship is full.
LAO9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.5.9, attributed to Julia, daughter of Augustus.

LAO10.la: Nec enim cuīquam bonō malī quicquam ēvenīre potest nec vīvō nec mortuō, nec umquam eius rēs ā dīs inmortālibus neglegentur.
LAO10.en: For nothing evil can happen to any good man, either living or dead, nor will his affairs ever be neglected by the immortal gods.
LAO10.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Tusculanae Disputationes 1.99.

LAO11.la: Haec imitāminī, per deōs immortālīs, quī dignitātem, quī laudem, quī glōriam quaeritis! haec ampla sunt, haec dīvīna, haec immortālia.
LAO11.en: Imitate these things, by the immortal gods, you who seek merit, you who seek praise, you who seek glory! These things are great, these divine, these immortal.
LAO11.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Sestio 102.1.

LAO12.la: Nōn īdem omnibus virīs nātūra tribuit ingenium: alius dūrior est, alius clēmentior.
LAO12.en: Nature has not granted the same ability to all men: one is harder, another more lenient.

LAO13.la: Lēx est haec: honestē vīvere, aliquem nōn laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
LAO13.en: This is the law: to live honorably, to harm no one, to give to each his own.
LAO13.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Justinian, Institutiones 1.1.3–4.

LAO14.la: Posteā Caesar intellēxit mātrem dīvīnam sibi tribuisse amplās glōriae altitūdinēs.
LAO14.en: Afterward Caesar understood that his divine mother had granted him great heights of glory.

LAO15.la: Nec mortem fugere quisquam nec amōrem potest.
LAO15.en: No one can flee either death or love.

LAO16.la: Sed mihi nihil pulchrum vidētur in quō est aliquid turpe.
LAO16.en: But nothing seems beautiful to me in which there is something shameful.

LAO17.la: Populī est servus quīcumque patriae est ūtilis.
LAO17.en: Whoever is useful to his country is a servant of the people.

LAO18.la: Negant enim quemquam virum bonum esse nisi sapientem.
LAO18.en: For they say that no man is good unless he is wise.

LAO19.la: Sī quam auctōritātem cupimus, virtūtī cūram dare nōs oportet, sine quā nec auctōritātem neque ūllam rem bonam habēre possumus.
LAO19.en: If we desire any influence, we must give attention to virtue, without which we can have neither influence nor any good thing.

LAO20.la: Quidquid facis, cum virtūte facis cum glōriā.
LAO20.en: Whatever you do, do with virtue, with glory.

LAO21.la: Aliī dīcunt Sōcratem sapientiā atque virtūte omnēs superāvisse; aliī negant eum fuisse sapientissimum aut summum virtūte.
LAO21.en: Some say that Socrates surpassed everyone in wisdom and virtue; others deny that he was the wisest or the greatest in virtue.

LAO22.la: Dīxit animōs hominum esse dīvīnōs, reditum in caelum patēre optimōque et iūstissimō cuique facillimum.
LAO22.en: He said that the souls of men are divine, that the return to heaven lies open, and is easiest for each best and most just man.

LAP1.en: I think that nothing evil has happened to Scipio.
LAP1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Amicitia 10.

LAP2.la: Salvē, puer tibi et reī pūblicae tuae fēlīx erit.
LAP2.en: Hail, boy! You will be fortunate for yourself and for your state.
LAP2.note: From Pseudo-Aurelius Victor, de Viris Illustribus Urbis Romae 75.1; the words are said to the nurse of the baby Sulla.

LAP3.la: Nihil magis amat cupiditās, quam quod nōn licet.
LAP3.en: Desire loves nothing more than what is not allowed.

LAP4.la: Iamque serpentēs campum tenēbant, ārdentīsque oculōs suffectī sanguine et ignī sībila lambēbant linguīs vibrantibus ōra.
LAP4.en: And now the serpents were holding the plain, and, their burning eyes suffused with blood and fire, they licked their hissing mouths with quivering tongues.

LAP5.la: Semper equidem magnō cum metū incipiō dīcere.
LAP5.en: Indeed I always begin to speak with great fear.
LAP5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Cluentio 51.

LAP6.la: Nōn sustineō illum relinquere, cui dedī vītam, quem ē perīculō ēripuī.
LAP6.en: I cannot bear to abandon the man to whom I gave life, whom I snatched from danger.
LAP6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca, de Beneficiis 4.15.3.2.

LAP7.la: Semper honōs nōmenque tuum laudēsque manēbunt.
LAP7.en: Your honor and name and praises will always remain.
LAP7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Aeneid 1.609.

LAP8.la: In nūllō avārus bonus est, in sē pessimus.
LAP8.en: A greedy man is good toward no one, and worst toward himself.
LAP8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae 246.

LAP9.la: Nūlla est igitur haec amīcitia, sī alter vēritātem audīre nōn cupit, alter fallere nōn dubitat.
LAP9.en: There is therefore no friendship, if one does not wish to hear the truth, and the other does not hesitate to deceive.

LAP10.la: Mārcus, magnā virtūte vir, magnā industriā, magnā grātiā, imperium tōtīus cīvitātis accēperat.
LAP10.en: Marcus, a man of great virtue, of great industry, of great influence, had received command of the whole state.

LAP11.la: Nōnne mihi cum virīs summā auctōritāte fuisse amīcitiam scīvistī?
LAP11.en: Did you not know that I had friendship with men of the highest authority?

LAP12.la: Hominēs eiusdem ōrdinis nōn semper sunt paris sapientiae.
LAP12.en: Men of the same rank are not always of equal wisdom.

LAP13.la: Illum mūrum dēlērī oportuit ubi signa nostra capta sunt.
LAP13.en: That wall, where our standards were captured, ought to have been destroyed.

LAP14.la: Sī Hispānī mīlitēs prōvinciam vastābunt, nostrī ōrdinēs sē recipient.
LAP14.en: If the Spanish soldiers ravage the province, our ranks will withdraw.

LAP15.la: Tē bellum ōdisse et arma audīmus.
LAP15.en: We hear that you hate war and arms.

LAP16.la: Ille iam pūnītus quod vetitum est id bibere nōn dēbuit.
LAP16.en: That man, already punished, ought not to have drunk what was forbidden.

LAP17.la: Imperātor hostium nihil eōrum quae nūntiābantur laetō animō audīvit.
LAP17.en: The enemy’s general did not hear any of what was being reported with a cheerful mind.

LAP18.en: From where did the thief enter, in the middle of the night?

LAP19.la: Plēbs cōgitat aliquem ferra armaque Hispānōrum ēreptūrum esse.
LAP19.en: The people think that someone will snatch away the iron and arms of the Spaniards.

LAP20.la: Ex captīvīs enim cognōvit cōnsulem Rōmānum cum sex mīlibus peditum, quattuor equitum eō ipsō diē pervēnisse.
LAP20.en: For he learned from the captives that the Roman consul had arrived with six thousand infantry and four thousand cavalry on that very day.

LAP21.la: Caesar intellēxit lēgātōs in Āfricā adesse et sē ipsum exspectāre.
LAP21.en: Caesar understood that the envoys were in Africa and were waiting for him himself.

LAP22.la: Nōn putō eum duōs mēnsēs vīctūrum esse.
LAP22.en: I do not think that he will live two months.

LAP23.la: Eram in magnā spē tē amīcum meum in fidem tuam receptūrum esse.
LAP23.en: I was in great hope that you would take my friend under your protection.

LAP24.la: Ipsī dīvitiās habentēs hāc in prōvinciā agere multa cōguntur quae eīs grāta nōn videntur.
LAP24.en: They themselves, though possessing riches, are forced to do many things in this province which do not seem pleasing to them.

LAQ1.en: You do not know how many evils I am enduring.

LAQ2.la: Quid agam, iūdicēs? Quō mē vertam?
LAQ2.en: What should I do, judges? Where should I turn?
LAQ2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Verrem 2.5.

LAQ3.la: Celeriter sex cohortēs secundā vigiliā iubet discēdere, parī equitēs numerō.
LAQ3.en: He orders six cohorts to depart quickly in the second watch, and an equal number of cavalry.

LAQ4.la: Quam sīs audāx, hinc omnēs intellegere potuērunt.
LAQ4.en: Everyone could understand from this how bold you are.
LAQ4.note: From Cicero, pro Sexto Roscio Amerino 87.

LAQ5.la: Q. Ligārius omnī culpā caret; domō exit nōn modo nūllum ad bellum sed nē ad minimam quidem suspīciōnem bellī.
LAQ5.en: Quintus Ligarius is free of all blame; he leaves home not only for no war, but not even for the least suspicion of war.

LAQ6.la: Quis enim cēlāre ignem possit, lūce quī semper prōditur ipse suā?
LAQ6.en: For who could hide a fire, which is always betrayed by its own light?

LAQ7.la: Periī, quid agam? quō mē vertam? quid virō meō respondēbō?
LAQ7.en: I am ruined! What should I do? Where should I turn? What will I say to my husband?
LAQ7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Terence, Hecyra 516.

LAQ8.la: Ex vinculīs pars solvent canēs, pars pressa sequuntur signa pedum, cupiuntque suum reperīre perīculum.
LAQ8.en: Some release the dogs from their chains, others follow the pressed tracks of feet, and desire to find their own danger.

LAQ9.la: Sī venēnum mortis causā datum est, nōn quaeritur quālis sit, sed quid faciat.
LAQ9.en: If poison was given for the sake of death, it is not asked what kind it is, but what it does.

LAQ10.la: Nec quisquam satis certum habet quid aut spēret aut timeat.
LAQ10.en: Nor does anyone have enough certainty about what he should either hope or fear.
LAQ10.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 22.7.10.

LAQ11.la: Catulō audiente et Caesare, videor dēbēre nōn tam pugnāre tēcum quam quid ipse sentiam dīcere.
LAQ11.en: With Catulus and Caesar listening, it seems best to me not so much to fight with you as to say what I myself think.
LAQ11.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Oratore 2.40.7.

LAQ12.la: “Tū tamen intereā calidō mihi sanguine poenās solvēs” inquit.
LAQ12.en: “Meanwhile, you will pay the penalty to me with your warm blood,” he says.

LAQ13.la: Nōn enim videō cūr, quid ipse sentiam dē morte, nōn audeam vōbīs dīcere.
LAQ13.en: For I do not see why I should not dare to tell you what I myself think about death.
LAQ13.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Cato Maior de Senectute 77.1.

LAQ14.en: And so I do not know where I should turn.
LAQ14.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Ligario 1.

LAQ15.la: Itaque refectīs cibō somnōque peditibus imperātor secundā vigiliā surgit.
LAQ15.en: And so, with the infantry refreshed by food and sleep, the general rises at the second watch.
LAQ15.note: From Quintus Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 5.4.23.

LAQ16.la: Ex tuā epistulā cognōvī quot cōpiās in Āsiā habeās.
LAQ16.en: From your letter I learned how many troops you have in Asia.

LAQ17.la: Putāvistīne mē dē pācis condiciōnibus tacitūrum esse?
LAQ17.en: Did you think that I would be silent about the terms of peace?

LAQ18.la: Venēnum unde venīret et quō modō parārētur nēmō scīvit.
LAQ18.en: No one knew where the poison came from and in what way it was prepared.

LAQ19.la: Hōs servōs ad poenam iam mōre maiōrum trāditōs ex mediā morte ēripere ac līberāre nōn dēbēs.
LAQ19.en: You ought not to snatch from the middle of death and free these slaves, already handed over to punishment by the custom of the ancestors.

LAQ20.la: Nōn comperērunt quō modō captīvī ē vinculīs ēriperentur.
LAQ20.en: They did not find out in what way the captives were being snatched from their chains.

LAQ21.la: Cognitīs virī armīs, uxor statim sēnsit eum interfectum esse neque sē rūrsus eum vīsūram esse.
LAQ21.en: The weapons of her husband having been recognized, the wife at once realized that he had been killed and that she would not see him again.

LAQ22.la: Omnis magister quālis poena sit adulēscentī idōnea scit.
LAQ22.en: Every teacher knows what kind of punishment is suitable for a youth.

LAQ23.la: Ubi Gȳgēs rēx ānulum dīvīnum ad sē vertit, ā nūllō vidēbātur, ipse autem omnia vidēbat; īdem rūrsus vidēbātur ubi in locum ānulum vertit.
LAQ23.en: When King Gyges turned the divine ring toward himself, he was seen by no one, but he himself saw everything; he was seen again when he turned the ring back into place.

LAQ24.la: Quantās poenās daret mox sciēbās etiam mē tacente.
LAQ24.en: You soon knew what penalties he would pay, even with me silent.

LAR1.la: Eādem nocte accidit ut esset lūna plēna.
LAR1.en: On the same night it happened that the moon was full.
LAR1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 4.29.

LAR2.la: Magister bonus ita docuit nōs per apostolum suum nōs rēctē vīvere et rēctē facere, ut laudēmur ab hominibus.
LAR2.en: A good teacher has thus taught us, through his apostle, to live rightly and to act rightly, so that we may be praised by men.

LAR3.la: Erit autem nārrātiō ab ōrātōre aperta ac dīlūcida ut iūdex quae dicentur quam facillimē accipiat.
LAR3.en: The narration by the orator will be open and clear so that the judge may understand as easily as possible what will be said.

LAR4.la: Itaque monēbō vōs, iūdicēs, ut hominēs, quōrum cognita virtūs, industria, fortūna in rē mīlitārī sit ā vōbīs retineātis. Fuit enim maior tālium virōrum in hāc rē pūblicā cōpia.
LAR4.en: And so I will advise you, judges, that you preserve men whose virtue, industry, and fortune in military affairs are known to you. For there was a greater supply of such men in this republic.

LAR5.la: Istae quidem artēs valent, quō puerī facilius possint maiōra discere.
LAR5.en: Indeed these arts are valuable, so that boys may more easily learn greater things.

LAR6.la: Rēs operis ab exiguīs initiīs eō crēvit ut iam magnitūdine labōret suā.
LAR6.en: The matter of the work has grown from slight beginnings to such an extent that it is already struggling under its own size.

LAR7.la: Superbia rēgis fēcerat ut lībertās esset laetior.
LAR7.en: The arrogance of the king had brought it about that liberty was more welcome.

LAR8.la: Tot urbēs līberāvērunt ut ab omnibus laudentur.
LAR8.en: They freed so many cities that they are praised by everyone.

LAR9.la: Senātor ad senātum properat ut Caesarem salūtet.
LAR9.en: The senator hurries to the senate to greet Caesar.

LAR10.la: Ab eō quaesīvī cūr sinistram tenēret.
LAR10.en: I asked him why he was holding his left hand.

LAR11.la: Tempestās tanta erat ut multa tēcta dēlērentur.
LAR11.en: The storm was so great that many roofs were destroyed.

LAR12.la: Ita ē montibus Gallī fugātī erant ut in campō prō castrīs nostrīs contendere cōgerentur.
LAR12.en: The Gauls had been routed from the mountains in such a way that they were forced to fight on the plain in front of our camp.

LAR13.la: Adeō rīsit ut in aquam caderet.
LAR13.en: He laughed so much that he fell into the water.

LAR14.la: Audāciam eius mē terrēre sed virtūtem mē dēlectāre dīxī.
LAR14.en: I said that his boldness frightened me but that his courage delighted me.

LAR15.la: Venēnum est tam ācre ut captīvus diū nōn vīctūrus sit.
LAR15.en: The poison is so strong that the captive will not live long.

LAR16.la: Nūntium mīsimus quī condiciōnēs pācis nūntiāret.
LAR16.en: We sent a messenger to announce the terms of peace.

LAR17.en: Soon they will come to see us.

LAR18.la: Ille ōrātor sīc ōrātiōnēs habet ut omnēs eum intellegant.
LAR18.en: That orator delivers speeches in such a way that everyone understands him.

LAR19.en: I was drinking wine to sleep better.

LAR20.la: Tantus erat timor noster īnsidiārum ut cūnctum aurum in aede dēpōnerēmus.
LAR20.en: So great was our fear of the plot that we placed all the gold in the temple.

LAR21.la: Adulēscēns poenās solvit nē ex suīs sēdibus pellātur.
LAR21.en: The youth pays the penalty so as not to be driven from his home.

LAR22.la: Cōnsul rogāvit quō modō captīvus et dextram et sinistram frangeret.
LAR22.en: The consul asked in what way the captive broke both his right and his left hand.

LAR23.la: Procul hostēs ā potentī exercitū nostrō fugātōs esse vidēre poteram.
LAR23.en: I could see from a distance that the enemy had been routed by our powerful army.

LAR24.la: Mihi vidēris praedam sīc dīvīsisse ut nē pars minima quidem incolīs darētur.
LAR24.en: You seem to me to have divided the booty in such a way that not even the smallest part was given to the inhabitants.

LAS1.la: Dum licet, in rēbus iūcundīs vīve beātus, vīve memor, quam sīs aevī brevis.
LAS1.en: While you may, live happily among pleasant things, live mindful of how short your lifetime is.
LAS1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Sermones 2.6.96–97.

LAS2.la: Magnō mē timōre līberāveris, dummodo inter mē atque tē mūrus sit.
LAS2.en: You will have freed me from great fear, provided there is a wall between me and you.

LAS3.la: Id faciat saepe, dum nē dēfessus sit.
LAS3.en: Let him do it often, provided he is not tired.
LAS3.note: From Marcus Porcius Cato, de Agri Cultura 5.4.7.

LAS4.la: Ille cōnsul profectus in Hispāniam, ut Hannibalī ab Alpibus dēscendentī occurreret, in Ītaliam ex prōvinciā rediit.
LAS4.en: That consul, having set out into Spain to meet Hannibal descending from the Alps, returned from the province to Italy.
LAS4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 28.42.20.

LAS5.la: Nāvem ascendō ut statim eam. Iam sum domī, iam rediī ex exiliō.
LAS5.en: I am boarding the ship to leave at once. Now I am at home, now I have returned from exile.

LAS6.la: Ita Carthāgine profectus nāvibus, Scīpiō exercitum in lītore dūcēbat, parātus contendere quācumque parte hostis occurrisset.
LAS6.en: Having set out in this way from Carthage with ships, Scipio was leading the army along the shore, ready to hasten to whatever part the enemy might meet him.

LAS7.la: Et quoniam hanc ōrātiōnem habeō nec in imperītā multitūdine nec in aliquō conventū agrestium, audācius paulō dē studiīs hūmānitātis dīcam.
LAS7.en: And since I am giving this speech neither among an inexperienced crowd nor in some gathering of uncultivated men, I will speak a little more boldly about the pursuits of civilization.

LAS8.la: Rūrsus ubi almus diēs hebetāverat stēllās, Cerēs nātam ab occāsū sōlis quaerēbat ad ortūs sōlis.
LAS8.en: Again, when the gentle day had weakened the stars, Ceres sought her daughter from the setting of the sun to its rising.

LAS9.la: Senātus intellēxit quō modō Vērus excessisset vītā.
LAS9.en: The senate understood in what way Verus had departed from life.
LAS9.note: From the Scriptores Historiae Augustae, Vita Marci Antonini Philosophi 20.4.2.

LAS10.la: Ingenium adeō mōvit sōla Corinna meum ut meīs tetigerim carminibus Mūsās.
LAS10.en: Corinna alone has so moved my talent that I have touched the Muses with my poems.

LAS11.la: Quid faciam nunc, sī trēs virī mē in carcerem coercuerint?
LAS11.en: What should I do now, if three men have shut me up in prison?

LAS12.la: Reus in carcerem ductus est C. Verrēs, homō vītā atque factīs omnium iam sententiā damnātus
LAS12.en: The defendant was led to prison: C. Verres, a man already condemned by the judgment of all for his life and his deeds.

LAS13.la: Ita cōnstituit ut reus, antequam verbum accūsātōris audīsset, causam dīcere cōgerētur.
LAS13.en: He so arranged it that the defendant was compelled to plead his case before he had heard a word from the accuser.

LAS14.la: Reus nunc vocātur quī causam dīcat.
LAS14.en: Now a defendant is called who will plead his case.

LAS15.la: Aperuī fenestram ut videam sōlis occāsum.
LAS15.en: I opened the window to see the sunset.

LAS16.la: Nunc iūdicēs vidētis esse tālēs ut carcere reum nōn solūtūrī sint.
LAS16.en: Now, judges, you see that they are such men that they will not release the defendant from prison.

LAS17.la: Iānuam clausī nē quis ex vīllā excēderet.
LAS17.en: I closed the door so that no one would leave the house.

LAS18.la: Lēgibus patriae ruptīs, iūdex vetuit reum in carcerem abdūcī.
LAS18.en: With the laws of the country broken, the judge forbade the defendant to be led away into prison.

LAS19.la: Manus parva tot hostēs in summō colle vīdit ut repente cōnstitisset et fūgisset.
LAS19.en: A small band saw so many enemies on the top of the hill that it suddenly stopped and fled.

LAS20.la: Sī quid tetigistī, iūdex tē reprehendet.
LAS20.en: If you have touched anything, the judge will blame you.

LAS21.la: Sī tālis est ille imperātor ut deīs grātiās numquam agat, tum poenās eum solūtūrum esse putō.
LAS21.en: If that general is the kind of man who never gives thanks to the gods, then I think he will pay the penalty.

LAS22.la: Ūnus quisque clāmāre coepit ut adulēscentēs pigrōs incitāret.
LAS22.en: Each and every one began to shout in order to rouse the lazy youths.

LAS23.la: Dīxistī tē contentūrum esse prīmā lūce; cupiō scīre cūr contenderīs sōlis occāsū.
LAS23.en: You said that you would hasten at dawn; I want to know why you hastened at sunset.

LAS24.la: Reus ex carcere excēdet, dummodo portās undique claudās.
LAS24.en: The defendant will leave the prison, provided that you close the gates on all sides.

LAT1.la: Omnia vincit Amor; et nōs cēdāmus Amōrī.
LAT1.en: Love conquers all things; and let us yield to Love.
LAT1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Eclogues 10.69.

LAT2.la: Saepe stilum vertās, iterum quae digna legī sint scrīptūrus.
LAT2.en: You should often turn the stylus, if you are going to write things worth reading again.
LAT2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Sermones 1.10.72–73.

LAT3.en: Let us see whether he can write more.

LAT4.la: Quī imperia libēns accipit, partem acerbissimam servitūtis fugit: facere quod nōlit.
LAT4.en: He who willingly accepts commands avoids the bitterest part of slavery: doing what he does not want.
LAT4.note: From Seneca, ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales 61.3.

LAT5.la: Quī dēdit beneficium, taceat, nārret, quī accēpit.
LAT5.en: Let him who gave a favor be silent; let him who received it tell of it.
