LAT5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca, de Beneficiis 2.11.2.

LAT6.la: Nōlō ego tē, quī dominus es, mihi onus istud sustinēre
LAT6.en: I do not want you, who are the master, to bear this burden for me.
LAT6.note: From Plautus, Asinaria 655. Istud is the neuter adjective agreeing with onus.

LAT7.la: Neque ego rūrsus nōlō eum, quī sit dictūrus, sollicitum surgere.
LAT7.en: And again I do not want the man who is going to speak to get up anxious.

LAT8.la: Quaesīvī ā Catilīnā in conventū apud M. Laecam fuisset necne.
LAT8.en: I asked Catiline whether he had been at the meeting at the house of M. Laeca or not.

LAT9.la: Mox et ipse Nerō aurīgāre atque etiam spectārī saepius voluit.
LAT9.en: Soon Nero himself also wanted to drive a chariot and even to be watched more often.

LAT10.la: Cui plūs licet quam pār est, plūs vult quam licet.
LAT10.en: He who is allowed more than is fair wants more than is allowed.
LAT10.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae C22.

LAT11.la: Quid? Sī volam dēmōnstrāre hominēs quī aut nōn minōris aut etiam plūris ēmerint, nōnne possum? Etenim quī modus est in hīs rēbus cupiditātis?
LAT11.en: What? If I want to show men who have bought at not less or even at more, can I not? For what limit is there to desire in these matters?

LAT12.la: Ubi errat aetās maior, male discit minor.
LAT12.en: When the older age errs, the younger learns badly.

LAT13.la: Fēminae puellaeque ad lūdōs veniunt nōn sōlum ut videant sed etiam ut ipsae videātur.
LAT13.en: Women and girls come to the games not only to see but also to be seen themselves.

LAT14.la: Caeduntur multī ferrōque lapideque aut intrā mūrōs aut extrā praecipe cāsū.
LAT14.en: Many are cut down by iron and stone, either inside the walls or outside, headlong in their fall.

LAT15.la: Vīta senis grātior quam adulēscentis mihi vidētur quod hīc vult diū vīvere, ille diū vīxit.
LAT15.en: The life of an old man seems more pleasant to me than that of a youth, because the latter wants to live long, the former has lived long.

LAT16.la: Nēmō enim est tam senex ut diūtius nōlit vīvere.
LAT16.en: For no one is so old that he is unwilling to live longer.

LAT17.la: Tālis erat nātūra regiōnis ut nēmō sine ingentī difficultāte ibi incoleret.
LAT17.en: The nature of the region was such that no one lived there without great difficulty.

LAT18.la: Pater iter pedibus faciat, nam in equum ascendere nōlēbat.
LAT18.en: Let father make the journey on foot, for he was unwilling to climb onto a horse.

LAT19.la: Nōlī timēre leōnem; tē tangere nōlit; vinculīs autem coercētur.
LAT19.en: Don’t fear the lion; let him not wish to touch you; moreover, he is held in chains.

LAT20.la: Omnēs līberī celeriter discēdant nē ab animālibus laedantur.
LAT20.en: Let all the children depart quickly so that they are not harmed by the animals.

LAT21.la: Contendant hinc quam celerrimē, leō enim nōn longē ā eīs aberit.
LAT21.en: Let them hurry away from here as quickly as possible, for the lion will not be far from them.

LAT22.la: Optimus quisque beneficia aliōrum laudāre quam sua ab aliīs beneficia laudārī māvult.
LAT22.en: Every good person prefers to praise the favors of others than to have his own favors praised by others.

LAT23.la: At ego vōbīs, sī virī esse vultis, viam ostendam quā tanta ista mala fugiātis.
LAT23.en: But I will show you, if you wish to be men, a way by which you may escape those great evils.

LAT24.la: Catō esse quam vidērī bonus mālēbat.
LAT24.en: Cato preferred to be good rather than to seem good.

LAT25.la: Dēpōnat īram; iūdex dē reō supplicium sūmpsit.
LAT25.en: Let him lay aside his anger; the judge has punished the defendant.

LAT26.la: Cōnsul ipse morbō atque aetāte oppressus fīnem vītae adesse sēnsit.
LAT26.en: The consul himself, overcome by illness and age, realized that the end of his life was at hand.

LAU1.la: Quid hōc homine faciās? Quod supplicium dignum libīdinī eius inveniās?
LAU1.en: What would you do with this man? What punishment worthy of his lust would you find?
LAU1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Verrem 2.40.

LAU2.la: Quō nōmine dignus est nēmō, nisi quī tantī honōris onus potest sustinēre.
LAU2.en: No one is worthy of the name, unless he who can bear the burden of so great an honor.
LAU2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Philippica 7.5.

LAU3.la: Postquam Catō adsēdit, cōnsulēs duo itemque senātūs magna pars sententiam eius laudant, et virtūtem animī ad caelum tollunt.
LAU3.en: After Cato sat down, the two consuls and likewise a great part of the senate praise his opinion and raise the courage of his spirit to the sky.

LAU4.la: Prōgeniem sed enim Trōiānō ā sanguine dūcī audierat Tyriās ōlim quae verteret arcēs.
LAU4.en: But indeed she had heard that a lineage was being drawn from Trojan blood that would some day overturn the Tyrian citadels.
LAU4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Aeneid 1.19–20.

LAU5.la: Ego nōn venīrem contrā inimīcum prō amīcō?
LAU5.en: Should I not come against an enemy on behalf of a friend?

LAU6.la: Quid dīcerem, nescīvī, didicī ex tē et scīre nunc coepī.
LAU6.en: What I should say, I did not know; I learned from you and now begin to know.
LAU6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 6.17.4.

LAU7.la: Illa quidem ingēns erat calamitās quam mīlitēs pulsī accēpērunt.
LAU7.en: That was indeed a huge disaster which the routed soldiers received.

LAU8.la: Victus amōre tuī vincula omnia statim rumpat quō dē inimīcīs nostrīs supplicium celerius sūmerem.
LAU8.en: Overcome by love of you, let him at once break all chains, so that I might punish our enemies more quickly.

LAU9.la: Quid enim erat turpius quam reum vīvere beneficiō iūdicis?
LAU9.en: For what was more shameful than for a defendant to live by the favor of the judge?

LAU10.la: Sīc mē deī ōlim iūvērunt ut animum ad frūctum ōtiī nunc advertam.
LAU10.en: The gods once helped me in such a way that I now turn my mind to the fruit of leisure.

LAU11.la: Nonne hominēs omnēs sub sōle vītam vīvere quam sub terram ad sēdem Plūtōnis dēscendere mālunt?
LAU11.en: Do not all people prefer to live their life under the sun than to descend under the earth to the seat of Pluto?

LAU12.la: Adulēscēns nescīvit cūr rēgī poenās tantās sub sanguine prō reō solveret.
LAU12.en: The youth did not know why he was paying such great penalties to the king, under the guise of blood, on behalf of the defendant.

LAU13.la: Contendant domum et servum portam claudere iubeant nē leō vaccās nostrās edat.
LAU13.en: Let them hurry home and order the slave to close the gate so that the lion does not eat our cows.

LAU14.la: Sī causam calamitātis ex mē quaeris, difficultās labōris fuit.
LAU14.en: If you ask me the cause of the disaster, it was the difficulty of the work.

LAU15.la: Hostibus reddī captīvōs negāvit esse ūtile.
LAU15.en: He said that it was not useful for the captives to be returned to the enemy.

LAU16.la: Postquam aurum ēreptum est ex manibus senātōris, auctor factī venēnum mīsit quod illī darētur.
LAU16.en: After the gold was snatched from the hands of the senator, the author of the deed sent poison to be given to him.

LAU17.la: Reperīrī poterant nē duo quidem senātōrēs Rōmānī quī sē illā ipsā nocte ante lūcem mē interfectūrōs esse dīcerent.
LAU17.en: Not even two Roman senators could be found who would say that they were going to kill me on that very night before dawn.

LAU18.la: Propter magnitūdinem dolōris avus meus paucōs dē amīcīs suīs occurrere poterat.
LAU18.en: Because of the greatness of his grief, my grandfather could meet few of his friends.

LAV1.la: Quaesīvit ā tē ut Rōmam statim redīrēs.
LAV1.en: He asked you to return to Rome at once.

LAV2.la: Mārcellus mīlitibus persuādet, ut sē recipiant in castra.
LAV2.en: Marcellus persuades the soldiers to retreat into the camp.
LAV2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From the Bellum Alexandrinum 60.3.

LAV3.la: Quīdam summum bonum dīxērunt voluptātem et omnia ad corpus rettulērunt.
LAV3.en: Some said that pleasure is the highest good and referred everything to the body.
LAV3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 2.6.2.

LAV4.la: Caesar Haeduīs Segūsiāvīsque, quī sunt fīnitimī prōvinciae, decem mīlia peditum imperat.
LAV4.en: Caesar orders ten thousand infantry from the Aedui and the Segusiani, who are neighbors of the province.
LAV4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 7.64.4.

LAV5.la: Quīn ego illī mē invēnisse dīcō hanc praedam, ōrābō igitur ut manū mē solvat?
LAV5.en: Why do I not tell him that I have found this booty, and then ask him to free me from his hand?

LAV6.la: Claudius ōrābat nē populus Claudiās gentēs carcere et vinculīs dignās esse vellet.
LAV6.en: Claudius was begging that the people not wish the Claudian clan to be worthy of prison and chains.

LAV7.la: Fer fortiter summum labōrem: accipiet tē dēfessum dīligēns atque amāns uxor.
LAV7.en: Bear the highest toil bravely: a careful and loving wife will receive you when you are tired.
LAV7.note: From Publius Rutilius Lupus, Schemata Lexeos 1.21.4.

LAV8.la: Lēx omnis aut tribuit aut capit aut pūnit aut iubet aut vetat aut permittit.
LAV8.en: Every law either grants, or takes, or punishes, or orders, or forbids, or permits.

LAV9.la: Paene īnsulārum, Sirmiō, īnsulārumque quās in marī vastō fert Neptūnus, es pulcherrimus.
LAV9.en: Sirmio, you are the loveliest of almost-islands and islands that Neptune bears on the vast sea.

LAV10.la: Duae legiōnēs quae proximē cōnstitūtae erant, praesidiō impedīmentīs erant.
LAV10.en: The two legions that had been most recently established served as a guard for the baggage.

LAV11.la: Caesarem certiōrem faciunt sē nōn facile ab oppidīs vim hostium prohibitūrum esse.
LAV11.en: They inform Caesar that he will not easily keep the force of the enemy from the towns.

LAV12.la: Quis nostrum animō dūrō mortem amīcī ferre potest?
LAV12.en: Which of us can bear a friend’s death with a hard heart?

LAV13.la: Deōs ōrāvimus ut pācem amplam terrīs tribuerent.
LAV13.en: We asked the gods to grant a great peace to the lands.

LAV14.la: Ōrātor nōs monuit nē spem dēpōnerēmus.
LAV14.en: The orator warned us not to give up hope.

LAV15.la: Sēdēs tam frīgida est ut eam tangere nōn possim.
LAV15.en: The seat is so cold that I cannot touch it.

LAV16.la: Certās hōrās mīlitēs praesidiō castrīs sunt.
LAV16.en: The soldiers are a guard for the camp at certain hours.

LAV17.la: Incolae adventum hostium videntēs omnia sua ē domibus in templa contulērunt.
LAV17.en: The inhabitants, seeing the arrival of the enemy, carried all their possessions from their houses into the temples.

LAV18.la: Ēīs persuādēbō ut Delphīs trēs diēs maneant.
LAV18.en: I will persuade them to stay at Delphi for three days.

LAV19.la: Imperātor lēgātō imperāvit ut tertiam aciem sibi subsidiō mitteret.
LAV19.en: The general ordered his lieutenant to send the third line to him as reinforcement.

LAV20.la: Postquam nūntius inīquās rēs pācis nōbīs rettulit, dux nōs iussit ad urbem hostium iterum appropinquāre.
LAV20.en: After the messenger reported the unfavorable terms of peace to us, the leader ordered us to approach the enemy’s city again.

LAV21.la: Nōbīs imperāvit ut arma ā castrīs tollerēmus.
LAV21.en: He ordered us to remove the arms from the camp.

LAV22.la: Vim tempestātis aequō animō audāx nauta fert neque timōre habētur.
LAV22.en: The bold sailor bears the force of the storm with a calm mind and is not held by fear.

LAV23.la: Viīs vastīs, cōpiae nostrae impedīmenta difficillimē tulērunt quīnque diēs.
LAV23.en: With the roads wasted, our forces bore the baggage with great difficulty for five days.

LAV24.la: Cūr hostibus nōn imperant ut sibi obsidēs dent?
LAV24.en: Why do they not order the enemy to give them hostages?

LAW1.la: Ubi lībertās cecidit, audet līberē nēmō loquī.
LAW1.en: When liberty has fallen, no one dares to speak freely.
LAW1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae Turicenses 34.

LAW2.la: Dum loquimur, fūgerit invida aetās: carpe diem!
LAW2.en: While we speak, envious time will have fled: seize the day!
LAW2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Horace, Odes 1.11.7–8.

LAW3.la: Ita fit ut māter omnium bonārum rērum sit sapientia.
LAW3.en: And so it happens that wisdom is the mother of all good things.
LAW3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Legibus 1.58.

LAW4.la: Catilīnam orbem terrae caede atque ignibus vastāre cupientem nōs cōnsulēs patiēmur?
LAW4.en: Shall we consuls tolerate Catiline, who desires to lay waste the world with slaughter and fire?

LAW5.la: Hominēs vetere mōre ut ferae in silvīs et spēluncīs nāscēbantur cibōque agrestī vēscēbantur.
LAW5.en: People used to be born in the old way, like wild animals, in woods and caves, and to feed on wild food.

LAW6.la: Sed mihi ita persuādeō (potest fierī ut fallar) eam rem laudī tibi fore.
LAW6.en: But I am so persuaded (it can happen that I am deceived) that this matter will be to your credit.
LAW6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 13.73.2.

LAW7.la: Ea quae illī in urbe geruntur, nōbīs dīcere nōluit, ut nōs certiōrēs nōn fierēmus.
LAW7.en: He was unwilling to tell us the things that are being done by them in the city, so that we would not be informed.

LAW8.la: Interim Rōma per litterās certior fit prōvinciam Numidiam Mariō datam.
LAW8.en: Meanwhile Rome is informed by letter that the province of Numidia has been given to Marius.
LAW8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Sallust, Bellum Iugurthinum 82.

LAW9.la: Sed postquam tertiō in proeliō lēgitque virum vir: tum vērō et gemitūs morientium et sanguine in altō armaque corporaque et permixtī sunt caede virōrum.
LAW9.en: But after in the third battle man picked out man: then indeed the groans of the dying, and in deep blood both arms and bodies were mixed together in the slaughter of men.
LAW9.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 11.631–634. The book prints this passage without the poem’s line breaks.

LAW10.la: Id optimō cuique Athēnīs accidere solitum est ut in exsilium expulsus esset.
LAW10.en: It has happened to every best man at Athens that he was driven into exile.

LAW11.la: Dīxit Deus: Fīat lūx. Et facta est lūx.
LAW11.en: God said: “Let there be light.” And there was light.

LAW12.la: Opere nōndum cōnfectō, tē ut Rōmae maneās hortāmur.
LAW12.en: With the work not yet finished, we urge you to remain at Rome.

LAW13.la: Sequere mē et portam carceris aperīre cōnēmur.
LAW13.en: Follow me, and we try to open the door of the prison.

LAW14.la: Certiōrem fierī dēsīderō tē dē et factīs et dictīs omnibus ab eō.
LAW14.en: I want you to be informed about everything he has done and said.

LAW15.la: Rūrī nātus auxiliō sorōrī tamen habitāre in urbe mālō.
LAW15.en: Although born in the country, I nevertheless prefer to live in the city as a help to my sister.

LAW16.la: Quis tibi persuādēre cōnātur nē illī senātōrī cōnfīdās?
LAW16.en: Who is trying to persuade you not to trust that senator?

LAW17.la: Rogātus cūr nūllum supplicium cōnstituisset, iūdex respondit sē patrem necāre nēminem ausūrum esse putāvisse.
LAW17.en: Asked why he had imposed no punishment, the judge answered that he had thought that no one would dare to kill his father.

LAW18.la: Quīdam timor mē in senātū loquī prohibuit.
LAW18.en: A certain fear prevented me from speaking in the senate.

LAW19.la: Adeō vīnō fruor ut mē vix continēre possim.
LAW19.en: I enjoy wine so much that I can scarcely restrain myself.

LAW20.la: Quantō maiōrēs nostrī sē melius quam nōs gessērunt quod deōs verēbantur!
LAW20.en: How much better our ancestors behaved than we do, because they feared the gods!

LAW21.la: Dīvitēs potentēsque sīc pecūniam dīvidere dēbent ut omnēs gaudēre possint.
LAW21.en: The rich and powerful ought to divide their money in such a way that everyone can rejoice.

LAW22.en: People die in order to be born again.

LAW23.la: Scīvistīne turpem mortem fortī virō nōn posse accidere?
LAW23.en: Did you know that a shameful death cannot happen to a brave man?

LAW24.la: Ēī persuāsī ut pollicērētur sē iūdicī cōnfīsūrum esse.
LAW24.en: I persuaded him to promise that he would trust the judge.

LAW25.la: Dīcere solitus est rem pūblicam maiōrem glōriam ex ōtiō suō quam ex aliōrum negōtiīs cōnsecūtūram esse.
LAW25.en: He was accustomed to say that the republic would obtain greater glory from its leisure than from the business of others.

LAW26.la: Uxor ā mē postulāvit ut eam rūs sequerer.
LAW26.en: My wife asked me to follow her to the country.

LAX1.la: Igitur cum videāmus stēllās orīrī et occidere, necesse est mundum quoque cum stēllīs vertī.
LAX1.en: Therefore, since we see the stars rise and set, it is necessary that the universe also turn with the stars.

LAX2.la: Ut canis in vacuō leporem cum Gallus agrō vīdit, et hic praedam pedibus petit, ille salūtem.
LAX2.en: As when a Gallic dog has seen a hare in an empty field, and the one seeks his prey with his feet, the other safety.

LAX3.la: Historia est testis temporum, lūx vēritātis, vīta memoriae, magistra vītae, nūntia vetustātis.
LAX3.en: History is the witness of the times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, the messenger of antiquity.

LAX4.la: Cum trādita sint cuiusque artis difficillima, reliqua, quia aut faciliōra aut similia sint, trādī nōn necesse esse.
LAX4.en: Since the most difficult parts of each art have been handed down, it is not necessary for the rest, because they are either easier or similar, to be handed down.
LAX4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Oratore 2.69.

LAX5.la: Fabius, cum Rōmam rediit, et in Senātū et prōductus ad populum medium ōrātiōnem habuit.
LAX5.en: When Fabius returned to Rome, he gave a speech both in the Senate and when presented to the middle of the people.
LAX5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 10.26.1.

LAX6.la: Cum dīcimus: Quī beneficium dedit, oblīvīscātur, hoc dīcimus: memoria eius nōn appāreat nec oriātur.
LAX6.en: When we say, “Let him who gave a favor forget,” we are saying this: “Let the memory of it not appear nor arise.”

LAX7.la: Cui placet oblīvīscitur, cui dolet meminit.
LAX7.en: He who is pleased forgets; he who is pained remembers.
LAX7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Murena 42.7.

LAX8.la: Acceptam iniūriam persequī nōn placet? Immō vehementer placet; sed aliud tempus est petendī, aliud persequendī.
LAX8.en: Does it not please to avenge an injury received? Indeed, very much so; but there is one time for making a claim, another for avenging.
LAX8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Murena 44.1. Petendī and persequendī are gerunds in the genitive.

LAX9.la: Etiamsī tū nōn ōdistī eum quī mihi fēcit iniūriam, ego ōdī eum quī fēcit tibi.
LAX9.en: Even if you do not hate the man who did wrong to me, I hate the man who did wrong to you.
LAX9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 1.1.12.

LAX10.la: Tamen ad Mūsās, cum laeserint, reversus sum apta in alternōs cōgere verba pedēs.
LAX10.en: Still, though they have hurt me, I have returned to the Muses to compel fitting words into alternate feet.

LAX11.la: Mementōte quae fēcerit Dominus Deus vester Marīae in viā cum ēgrederēminī dē Aegyptō.
LAX11.en: Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam on the road when you came out of Egypt.

LAX12.la: Quī numquam ades, nunc, cum adsīs, perīs.
LAX12.en: You who are never here, now, when you are here, you perish.

LAX13.la: Cum ab testibus saepe falsus sit, iūdiciō nēminī cōnfīdat.
LAX13.en: Since he has often been deceived by witnesses, let him trust no one in judgment.

LAX14.la: Iūdex, cum multum negōtium remanēret, rem statim cōnfēcit.
LAX14.en: The judge, although much business remained, finished the matter at once.

LAX15.la: Discipulus ā magistrō quaesīvit quid prō quōque et quid contrā quemque auctōrem dīcerētur.
LAX15.en: The student asked the teacher what was being said for and what against each author.

LAX16.la: Cum oppidum multīs praesidiīs mūnītum esset, imperātor tamen ad impetum cōpiās comparāvit.
LAX16.en: Although the town was fortified with many guards, the general nevertheless prepared his forces for an attack.

LAX17.la: Imperātor Rōmānus viam mūnīvit quā exercitus ūterētur.
LAX17.en: The Roman general built a road for his army to use.

LAX18.la: Cum dux eōrum mortuus erit, tōta gēns illīus numquam oblīvīscētur.
LAX18.en: When their leader has died, the whole nation of that man will never forget.

LAX19.la: Hostibus nōs dēdidimus nē quid iniūriae paterēmur.
LAX19.en: We surrendered to the enemy in order not to suffer any injury.

LAX20.la: Ōrō senātōrem ut multīs cum gentibus compleat urbem.
LAX20.en: I ask the senator to fill the city with many peoples.

LAX21.la: Lēgātī, cum ā mē hās condiciōnēs inīquās tulissent, ad tē vēnērunt et rogāvērunt ut ante mē causam suam dīcerēs.
LAX21.en: The envoys, when they had received these unfair terms from me, came to you and asked that you state your case before me.

LAX22.la: Iūdicēs quī reum audiēbant, cum maximē dēlectārentur, eī permīsērunt ut domum vīvus reverterētur.
LAX22.en: The judges who were listening to the defendant, since they were greatly pleased, allowed him to return home alive.

LAX23.la: Cum rem pūblicam perdere velīs, ēgredī in aliquās terrās et vītam istam fugae et mortī dēdere dēbēs.
LAX23.en: Since you wish to destroy the republic, you must go out into some lands and give up that life of yours to flight and death.

LAX24.la: Cum neque anteā nec posteā cuīquam essent tot testēs, optimus quisque tamen crēdidit eum poenās datūrum esse.
LAX24.en: Although neither before nor after had anyone had so many witnesses, every good man nevertheless believed that he would pay the penalty.

LAY1.la: Vīs habēre honōrem? Dabō tibi magnum imperium: imperā tibi.
LAY1.en: Do you want to have honor? I will give you great power: command yourself.
LAY1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Publilius Syrus, Sententiae 680.

LAY2.la: Dē iūdiciō, Crasse, vereor ut tibi possim favēre.
LAY2.en: About the trial, Crassus, I fear that I cannot favor you.

LAY3.la: Metuō et timeō, nē hoc crīmen tandem prōpalam fīat.
LAY3.en: I am afraid and I fear that this charge may finally become public.

LAY4.la: Mea sententia placuit Q. Catulō, cuius auctōritās semper in hāc rē pūblicā vīvet.
LAY4.en: My opinion pleased Quintus Catulus, whose authority will always live in this republic.

LAY5.la: Timeō nē mala facta antīqua mea sint inventa omnia.
LAY5.en: I fear that all my old misdeeds have been discovered.

LAY6.la: Iūpiter timuit, nē forte sacrum tot ab ignibus caelum ārdēret.
LAY6.en: Jupiter feared that the sacred heaven might by chance burn from so many fires.

LAY7.la: Ignōsce mihi; nōn possum haec ferre nec feram.
LAY7.en: Forgive me; I cannot bear these things, nor will I.
LAY7.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum 7.2.7.

LAY8.la: Timēns nē ā multitūdine equitum cornū dextrō circumvenīrētur, celeriter ex tertiā aciē singulās cohortēs dētrāxit.
LAY8.en: Fearing that he might be surrounded on the right wing by the large number of cavalry, he quickly withdrew single cohorts from the third line.
LAY8.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Caesar, de Bello Civili 3.89.4.

LAY9.la: Memoriam amīcitiae reliquīs virtūtibus omnibus antepōnō.
LAY9.en: I prefer the memory of friendship to all the other virtues.
LAY9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Rabirio Postumo 44.

LAY10.la: Bella terrā et marī cīvīlia externaque tōtō in orbe terrārum saepe gessī, victorque omnibus veniam petentibus cīvibus pepercī.
LAY10.en: I often waged wars, civil and foreign, on land and sea, in the whole world, and as victor I spared all the citizens who asked for pardon.
LAY10.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Augustus, Res Gestae 1.13.

LAY11.la: Num illīs cōnsulibus, quōrum alter exercitum perdidit, alter vēndidit, parcēs?
LAY11.en: Will you spare those consuls, of whom one lost an army, the other sold it?

LAY12.la: Mementōte quī tum fuerint hostēs, quī sōlī in hāc urbe lēgibus pārēre nōn passī sint.
LAY12.en: Remember who were the enemies then, who alone in this city were unwilling to obey the laws.

LAY13.la: Vereor nē ōrātiō mea dissimilis sententiae eius videātur
LAY13.en: I fear that my speech may seem unlike his opinion.

LAY14.la: Huic virtūtī quae est nōn sōlum maxima sed etiam māter virtūtum omnium reliquārum servīre dēbēs.
LAY14.en: You must serve this virtue, which is not only the greatest but also the mother of all the other virtues.

LAY15.la: Nesciō quid dē hāc epistulā eī placeat.
LAY15.en: I do not know what in this letter may please him.

LAY16.la: Iste iūdex tam avārus erat ut semper dīvitibus et potentibus invidēret.
LAY16.en: That judge was so greedy that he always envied the rich and powerful.

LAY17.la: Rōmānī arbitrātī sunt nēminem imperiō suō resistere posse.
LAY17.en: The Romans thought that no one could resist their rule.

LAY18.la: Cōnsul, timēns nē cōpiīs pigrīs praesit, studet Rōmā ēgredī.
LAY18.en: The consul, fearing that he may be in command of lazy troops, is eager to leave Rome.

LAY19.la: Sed ego Lūciō, ēgregiō atque optimō adulēscentī, meō amīcō, ignōscō, cum studuerit Catilīnae hominī audācissimō atque turpissimō.
LAY19.en: But I pardon Lucius, an outstanding and excellent young man, my friend, although he was devoted to Catiline, a most bold and most shameful man.

LAY20.la: Sī voluit tibi minārī et nocēre, inopiae id sapientiae tribuō.
LAY20.en: If he wanted to threaten and harm you, I attribute it to a lack of wisdom.

LAY21.la: Vōs oportuit, iūdicēs, salūtī huius subvenīre.
LAY21.en: You ought, judges, to have come to the aid of his safety.

LAY22.la: Servus dominum adeō verēbātur ut imperiīs sine morā pareret.
LAY22.en: The slave so feared his master that he obeyed his orders without delay.

LAZ1.la: Ā vōbīs petō ut patiāminī mē prō hōc flente reō ōrātiōnem habēre.
LAZ1.en: I ask you to allow me to give a speech on behalf of this weeping defendant.

LAZ2.la: Solōn dīxit sē fierī senem cotīdiē aliquid discentem.
LAZ2.en: Solon said that he was becoming old while learning something every day.

LAZ3.la: Nōlī verērī nōs; tē nōn laedēmus.
LAZ3.en: Do not fear us; we will not harm you.

LAZ4.la: Cum aliae gentēs iniūriās rēgum patī possent, populus Rōmānus exsiliō et mortī lībertātem anteposuit.
LAZ4.en: Although other peoples could endure the injuries of kings, the Roman people preferred liberty to exile and death.

LAZ5.la: Tē ōrāmus ut auctōritāte et potestāte prō nōbīs ūtāris.
LAZ5.en: We ask you to use your authority and power on our behalf.

LAZ6.la: Nātus sum eōdem annō, cum avus meus mortuus est.
LAZ6.en: I was born in the same year in which my grandfather died.

LAZ7.la: Simul atque cōnsul factus est, plēbs postulāvit ab eō ut Āfricā potīrētur.
LAZ7.en: As soon as he was made consul, the plebs demanded from him that he take possession of Africa.

LAZ8.la: Lapidibus ā līmine cum difficultāte remōtīs, ē carcere ēgredī cōnātī sumus.
LAZ8.en: With the stones removed from the threshold with difficulty, we tried to go out of the prison.

LAZ9.en: Do you dare to feed on only black bread?

LAZ10.la: Ōlim dīxit Catō Maior loquēns dē artibus ōrātōris: Rem tenē, verba sequentur.
LAZ10.en: Once Cato the Elder, speaking about the arts of the orator, said: “Hold the subject, the words will follow.”

LAZ11.la: Nūlla vītae pars neque pūblicīs neque prīvātīs neque domesticīs in rēbus sine iūre esse potest.
LAZ11.en: No part of life, neither in public, nor in private, nor in domestic affairs, can be without law.

LAZ12.la: Ego respondēre soleō meīs cōnsiliīs, perīculīs, labōribus patriam esse servātam.
LAZ12.en: I am accustomed to reply that my country has been saved by my counsels, dangers, and labors.
LAZ12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, de Domo Sua 93.

LAZ13.la: Quis sit summī bonī locus quaeris? Animus. Hic nisi pūrus ac sānctus est, deum nōn capit.
LAZ13.en: Do you ask what is the place of the highest good? The mind. Unless it is pure and holy, it does not hold God.
LAZ13.note: From Seneca, Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium 87.21.

LAZ14.la: Dīīs, quibus septem placuēre collēs, dicābō carmen. Id est: quibus Rōma placuit, quae in septem collibus cōnstitūta est.
LAZ14.en: I will dedicate a song to the gods whom seven hills pleased. That is: to whom Rome pleased, which is built on seven hills.
LAZ14.note: From Pomponius Porphyrio, Commentarium in Q. Horatii Flacci Carmen Saeculare 1.7–8.

LAZ15.la: Mōrēs reī pūblicae fīent peiōrēs, dum ad haec tempora quibus nec vitia nostra nec remedia patī possumus perveniāmus.
LAZ15.en: The morals of the republic will become worse, until we arrive at these times at which we can endure neither our vices nor the remedies.

LAZ16.la: Manifēstumque est errāre eōs, quī numquam ōrātōrem dictūrum nisi dē rē dubiā putāvērunt.
LAZ16.en: And it is clear that those err who have thought that an orator would never speak except about a doubtful matter.

LAZ17.la: Prō multitūdine autem hominum et prō glōriā bellī atque fortitūdinis angustōs sē fīnēs habēre arbitrābantur, quī in longitūdinem mīlia passuum ccxl, in lātitūdinem clxxx patēbant.
LAZ17.en: But in proportion to the number of people and to their glory in war and bravery, they thought they had narrow territories, which extended 240 miles in length and 180 in width.

LAZ18.la: Timeō ut sustineās, sed videō in tē esse omnia.
LAZ18.en: I fear that you cannot bear it, but I see that everything is in you.
LAZ18.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 14.2.3.

LBA1.la: Sī tū exercitusque valētis, bene est.
LBA1.en: If you and the army are well, it is well.
LBA1.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 5.2.1.

LBA2.la: Quid mē accūsās, sī faciō officium meum?
LBA2.en: Why do you accuse me, if I am doing my duty?
LBA2.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Plautus, Asinaria 172. Quid = cūr.

LBA3.la: Haec sī tēcum patria loquātur, nōnne efficere dēbeam?
LBA3.en: If the fatherland were to say these things to you, should I not accomplish them?

LBA4.la: Nōn possum istum accūsāre, sī cupiam.
LBA4.en: I cannot accuse him, even if I wished to.

LBA5.la: Sī pereō, hominum manibus periisse iuvābit.
LBA5.en: If I perish, it will be a pleasure to have perished by the hands of men.
LBA5.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Vergil, Aeneid 3.606.

LBA6.la: Sī vincimus, omnia nōbīs tūta erunt; sīn metū cesserimus, eadem illa advorsa fīent
LBA6.en: If we win, all things will be safe for us; but if we yield through fear, those same things will become adverse.
LBA6.note: From Sallust, Catilinae Coniuratio 58.4. Advorsa: neut. nom. pl., “adverse, opposite.”

LBA7.la: Sī quidem eundem Scīpiōnem ducem in Āfricam Rōmānī mittant, brevem Carthāginis esse aetātem spērēmus.
LBA7.en: If indeed the Romans should send the same Scipio as commander into Africa, let us hope that the life of Carthage will be short.

LBA8.la: Quid superest, nisi ut tē pūnīrī oporteat?
LBA8.en: What remains, except that it is necessary for you to be punished?
LBA8.note: From Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 4.4.4. Superest = manet.

LBA9.la: Quid ille dux Leōnidās dīcit? Pergite animō fortī, Lacedaemoniī, hodiē apud īnferōs fortasse cēnābimus.
LBA9.en: What does that leader Leonidas say? “Press on with brave heart, Spartans; today perhaps we will dine among the dead.”
LBA9.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Tusculanae Disputationes 1.101.9. Pergite from pergō, -ere; īnferōs = mortuōs.

LBA10.la: Sī forte in īnsidiās vēnerō, tū servābis mē, sī mē hostēs cēperint?
LBA10.en: If I happen to fall into an ambush, will you save me, if the enemy have captured me?

LBA11.la: Quid accūsās, Catō, quid fers ad iūdicium? Reum ambitūs accūsās? Nōn dēfendō. Mē reprehendis, quod idem dēfendam quod lēge pūnierim? Pūnīvī ambitum, nōn innocentiam; ambitum vērō ipsum tēcum accūsābō, sī volēs.
LBA11.en: Why do you accuse, Cato, what do you bring to trial? Do you accuse a defendant of bribery? I do not defend. Do you blame me because I defend the same thing that I punished by law? I punished bribery, not innocence; but I will accuse bribery itself with you, if you wish.
LBA11.note: From Cicero, pro Murena 67. Innocentiam: “innocence,” acc. sing.

LBA12.la: Sī quis exīstimet mē aut voluntāte esse mūtātā aut dēbilitātā virtūte aut animō frāctō, vehementer erret.
LBA12.en: If anyone should think that I am either with a changed will, or with weakened courage, or with a broken spirit, he would be badly mistaken.
LBA12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, post Reditum ad Populum 19. Voluntāte from voluntās, -tātis “will”; dēbilitātā from dēbilitō (1) “weaken.”

LBA13.la: Sī fīlius tuus prō patriā velit morī, patī dolōrem possīs?
LBA13.en: If your son should wish to die for his country, could you endure the pain?

LBA14.la: Nisi vestem mūtāveris, nōbīs nōn licēbit rēgīnam vidēre.
LBA14.en: Unless you change your clothes, we will not be allowed to see the queen.

LBA15.la: Negāvit sē ambitūs ā multīs testibus esse accūsātum.
LBA15.en: He said that he had not been accused of bribery by many witnesses.

LBA16.la: Quod sī forte sē nescīvit tē fefellisse, quō modō reprehendī potuit?
LBA16.en: But if by chance he did not know that he had deceived you, how could he be blamed?

LBA17.la: Sīn opēs perdideris, perdēs fortasse fāmam quoque tuam et amīcōs.
LBA17.en: But if you lose your wealth, you will perhaps lose your reputation also, and your friends.

LBA18.la: Cum hominem tollentem praedam cōnspexissem, malī factī eum accūsāvī.
LBA18.en: When I had caught sight of a man carrying off booty, I accused him of the evil deed.

LBA19.la: In maximīs rēbus semper cōnsulō amīcissimīs atque fidēlissimīs sociīs quī sunt mihi vītā ipsā multō cāriōrēs.
LBA19.en: In the most important matters I always consult my most friendly and most faithful allies, who are to me much dearer than life itself.

LBA20.la: Quod sī servīre meae glōriae potius quam eius māvīs, mūtā sententiās inimīcās.
LBA20.en: But if you prefer to serve my glory rather than his, change your hostile opinions.

LBA21.la: Fortasse haec omnia meliōrēs habeant exitūs, sī sententiās sapientium sequāmur.
LBA21.en: Perhaps all these things would have better outcomes, if we should follow the opinions of the wise.

LBA22.la: Sī quis forte ignōret lēgēs nostrās et mōrēs, mīrētur cūr reus ambitūs accūsātus sit.
LBA22.en: If anyone should perhaps be ignorant of our laws and customs, he would wonder why the defendant was accused of bribery.

LBB1.la: Nisi tū urbem āmīsissēs, numquam eam recēpissem.
LBB1.en: If you had not lost the city, I would never have recovered it.

LBB2.en: If he were alive, you would hear his words.
LBB2.note: From Cicero, pro Q. Roscio Comoedo 42.9.

LBB3.la: In eō culpa et crīmen haerēbit. Nam illud quidem nōn dīcēs—quod utinam dīcās!
LBB3.en: In him will cling guilt and charge. For you will not say that—if only you would!
LBB3.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, in Verrem 2.3.107.

LBB4.la: Crēdās nōn dē puerō scrīptum sed ā puerō
LBB4.en: You would think it written not about a boy but by a boy.
LBB4.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Pliny the Younger, Epistula 4.7.7.

LBB5.la: Numquam cum Scīpiōne esset profectus, sī cum istīs sē bellum inlātūrōs esse arbitrārētur.
LBB5.en: He would never have set out with Scipio if he had thought that he would be making war with them.

LBB6.la: Pōns iter paene hostibus dedit, nisi ūnus vir fuisset
LBB6.en: The bridge nearly gave the enemy a way, if one man had not been there.
LBB6.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 2.10.

LBB7.la: Litterās ā tē recēpī, quae mē metū paulō solvērunt. Utinam omnīnō līberāvissent! Sed tamen medicus cōnfirmat tē mox valitūrum esse.
LBB7.en: I received a letter from you, which freed me a little from fear. If only it had freed me altogether! But still the doctor says that you will soon be well.
LBB7.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 16.9.2; metū = timōre; omnīnō adv. “altogether.”

LBB8.la: Sī Mārcellus Syrācūsās cēpisset, duo templa sē Rōmae aedificātūrum vōverat.
LBB8.en: If Marcellus took Syracuse, he had vowed to build two temples at Rome.
LBB8.note: From Cicero, in Verrem 2.4.123; vōverat from voveō, -ēre, vōvī, vōtum “vow.”

LBB9.la: Sī litterae virtūte nōn iuvārentur, numquam sē ad eārum studium contulissent.
LBB9.en: If literature were not helped by virtue, they would never have devoted themselves to its study.

LBB10.la: Iam incolumis manērem, nisi gēns crūdēlis ferrō bellum intulisset.
LBB10.en: I would be remaining safe now, if a cruel race had not brought war with the sword.

LBB11.la: Nunc aliquis dīcat mihi quid tū? nūllane habēs vitia?
LBB11.en: Now someone might say to me: “What about you? Do you have no vices?”

LBB12.la: Hortārer vōs quō animō fortiōrēs essētis, nisi vōs fortiōrēs cognōvissem quam quemquam virum.
LBB12.en: I would encourage you in the spirit in which you might be braver, if I had not known you to be braver than any man.
LBB12.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 14.7.2.

LBB13.la: Meum officium faciō; quod errātum ā nōbīs ortum est corrigō.
LBB13.en: I do my duty; I correct whatever mistake has arisen from us.

LBB14.la: Homō sum; hūmānī nīl ā mē aliēnum putō.
LBB14.en: I am a man; I consider nothing human foreign to me.
LBB14.note: From Terence, Heauton Timorumenos 77; nīl = nihil.

LBB15.la: Nēmō umquam prō patriā morerētur nisi magnam spem immortālitātis habēret.
LBB15.en: No one would ever die for his country unless he had great hope of immortality.

LBB16.la: Flūmen ex nivibus adeō crēvit ut multa aedificia iam complēverit.
LBB16.en: The river has grown so much from the snows that it has already filled many buildings.

LBB17.la: In tē omnis culpa haeret. Nē iūdicēs sceleris aliēnī mē condemnent.
LBB17.en: All the blame clings to you. May the judges not condemn me for another’s crime.

LBB18.la: Caesar veniam prīncipī et uxōrī et frātribus tribuisset, sī captīvī nostrī līberātī essent.
LBB18.en: Caesar would have granted pardon to the leader, his wife, and his brothers, if our prisoners had been freed.

LBB19.la: Utinam scīrēmus quid post mortem accidat!
LBB19.en: If only we knew what happens after death!

LBB20.la: Rēgulus Carthāginem redīre cōnstituit neque ignōrāvit sē ad crūdēlissimum hostem et ad ultima supplicia proficīscī.
LBB20.en: Regulus decided to return to Carthage and was not unaware that he was setting out to a most cruel enemy and to the extreme punishments.

LBB21.la: Sī avis sēdem in arbore aedificet super animālia humī latentia, sit incolumis.
LBB21.en: If a bird should build its nest in a tree above the animals lying hidden on the ground, it would be safe.

LBB22.la: Sī mē incolumem servāverīs, aeternum exemplum beneficiī tuī erō.
LBB22.en: If you save me unharmed, I shall be an everlasting example of your kindness.

LBB23.la: Nisi ea, quae sine causā mīrantur aliī, tibi placent, gaudeō tē animō valēre.
LBB23.en: Unless the things which others admire without cause please you, I am glad that you are well in spirit.

LBB24.la: Tantus clāmor ortus est ut hostēs arbitrārēmur ad mūrum pervēnisse.
LBB24.en: Such a great shout arose that we thought the enemy had come to the wall.

LBB25.la: Sī forte in īnsidiās vēnerō, tū servābis mē, sī mē hostēs cēperint?
LBB25.en: If I happen to fall into an ambush, will you save me, if the enemy have captured me?
LBB25.note: Revisit: from Lesson LIII, Exercise A 10 (a future more vivid condition).

LBB26.la: Nisi vestem mūtāveris, nōbīs nōn licēbit rēgīnam vidēre.
LBB26.en: Unless you change your clothes, we will not be allowed to see the queen.
LBB26.note: Revisit: from Lesson LIII, Exercise A 14.

LBB27.la: Sī tū exercitusque valētis, bene est.
LBB27.en: If you and the army are well, it is well.
LBB27.note: Revisit: from Lesson LIII, Exercise A 1 (a simple condition).

LBC1.la: Reliquās parātās ad nāvigandum nāvēs invēnit.
LBC1.en: He found the remaining ships prepared for sailing.

LBC2.la: Quamquam omnia sunt metuenda, nihil magis quam perfidiam timēmus.
LBC2.en: Although everything is to be feared, we fear nothing more than treachery.
LBC2.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Familiares 1.5a.2.5; perfidiam from perfidia, -ae “dishonesty, faithlessness.”

LBC3.la: Sī qua difficiliōra discentī vidēbuntur, ēlabōrandum est.
LBC3.en: If any parts seem rather difficult to the learner, they must be worked out.
LBC3.note: From Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 2.8.8; ēlabōrandum from ex + labōrō “elaborate.”

LBC4.la: Libyae magnās it Fāma per urbēs, virīsque adquīrit eundō.
LBC4.en: Rumor goes through the great cities of Libya, and gains strength by going.
LBC4.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 4.173–175; adquīrit from adquīrō, -ere “acquire.”

LBC5.la: Octāvam legiōnem in magnā glōriā et laude pōnendam putō.
LBC5.en: I think that the Eighth Legion should be placed in great glory and praise.

LBC6.la: Ergō ubi tyrannus est, cōnfitendum est plānē nūllam esse rem pūblicam.
LBC6.en: Therefore, where there is a tyrant, we must confess plainly that there is no republic.
LBC6.note: From Cicero, de Republica 3.43.12; plānē adv. “plainly, clearly.”

LBC7.la: Alter autem et mōribus et ipsō genere dīcendī dūrior est.
LBC7.en: The other is harsher both in his manners and in his very style of speaking.

LBC8.la: Quae spēs tandem, quae facultās recuperandae vestrae lībertātis relinquētur?
LBC8.en: What hope, what opportunity of recovering your liberty, will finally be left?
LBC8.note: From Cicero, de Lege Agraria 2.75.12; recuperandae from recuperō (1) “recover.”

LBC9.la: Complūrēs mortālēs ad iūdicandum satis ingeniī habent.
LBC9.en: Many mortals have enough ability for judging.
LBC9.note: From Ps. Sallust, Ad Caesarem de Re Publica 1.8.9.

LBC10.la: Signōque datō iuvenēs Rōmānī ad rapiendās virginēs currunt.
LBC10.en: And when the signal was given, the Roman youths run to seize the maidens.
LBC10.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 1.9.10; virginēs from virgō, -ginis “maiden.”

LBC11.la: Inde Rōmam ad scrībendum novum exercitum redit.
LBC11.en: From there he returns to Rome to enroll a new army.
LBC11.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 5.19.5; scrībendum here in the sense “enroll, enlist.”

LBC12.la: Fit ut laudandus is sit, quī mortem petat prō rē pūblicā, quod oporteat cāriōrem nōbīs esse patriam quam nōs ipsōs.
LBC12.en: It happens that the man who seeks death for the republic is to be praised, because our country ought to be dearer to us than we ourselves.

LBC13.en: By ruling badly, the highest power is lost.

LBC14.la: Ego enim sīc exīstimō, in summō imperātōre quattuor hās rēs inesse oportēre, scientiam reī mīlitāris, virtūtem, auctōritātem, fēlīcitātem.
LBC14.en: For I judge that in a supreme commander these four things ought to be present: knowledge of military affairs, courage, authority, and good fortune.
LBC14.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Lege Manilia 27; inesse from īnsum “be in, belong.”

LBC15.la: Sīn vēra potius quam falsa dīcenda sunt, cupīdō imperiī animōs ferōcēs duārum gentium ad arma incitāvit.
LBC15.en: But if true things rather than false things must be said, the desire for power roused the fierce minds of two nations to arms.
LBC15.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 1.23.7; falsa “false,” nom. neut. pl.

LBC16.la: Prīmum mihi vidētur dē genere bellī, deinde dē magnitūdine, tum dē imperātōre dēligendō esse dīcendum.
LBC16.en: First it seems to me that we must speak about the kind of war, then about its size, then about choosing a commander.
LBC16.note: Unadapted passage (marked with an asterisk in your book). From Cicero, pro Lege Manilia 6.2.

LBC17.la: Negāvit Caesar sē esse parātum ad tantum bellum incipiendum.
LBC17.en: Caesar said that he was not prepared to begin so great a war.

LBC18.la: Nisi Germānīs esset mūtandae sēdis cupīdō, pāce ōtiōque in Galliā Rōmānī fruerentur.
LBC18.en: If the Germans did not have a desire to change their homeland, the Romans would enjoy peace and quiet in Gaul.

LBC19.la: Hoc est genus bellī quod maximē vestrōs animōs incitāre atque incendere ad persequendārum iniūriārum studium dēbet.
LBC19.en: This is the kind of war which ought especially to rouse and inflame your minds to the pursuit of avenging wrongs.

LBC20.la: Nec Brūtus, quī in līberandā patriā est interfectus, nec Rēgulus quī ad supplicium est profectus, ut fidem hostibus datam cōnservāret, mortem timuit.
LBC20.en: Neither Brutus, who was killed in liberating his country, nor Regulus, who set out to punishment so that he might keep the faith given to the enemy, feared death.

LBC21.la: Utinam nē hominēs rērum mūtandārum cupidī rē pūblicā Rōmānā potītī essent.
LBC21.en: If only revolutionaries had not taken control of the Roman republic!

LBC22.la: Ob scelera sua Catilīna senātuī iūdicandus erit et in exsilium mittendus.
LBC22.en: Because of his crimes, Catiline will have to be judged by the senate and sent into exile.

LBC23.la: Intereā parandum est bellum quō vincās celerius.
LBC23.en: Meanwhile, war must be prepared so that you may win more quickly.

LBC24.la: Hīs verbīs Catō semper fīnem loquendī apud senātōrēs fēcit: 'Carthāgō dēlenda est.'
LBC24.en: With these words Cato always made an end of speaking to the senators: “Carthage must be destroyed.”

LBC25.la: Eī persuāsī intereā nē istum hominem castrīs praeficeret.
LBC25.en: Meanwhile I persuaded him not to put that man in charge of the camp.

LBC26.la: Saepissimē Rōmānus epistulam incipiēbat scrībendō, 'Sī valēs, bene est.'
LBC26.en: Very often a Roman began a letter by writing, “If you are well, it is well.”

LBC27.la: Nisi tū urbem āmīsissēs, numquam eam recēpissem.
LBC27.en: If you had not lost the city, I would never have recovered it.
LBC27.note: Revisit: from Lesson LIV, Exercise A 1 (a past contrary-to-fact condition).

LBC28.la: Timeō nē mala facta antīqua mea sint inventa omnia.
LBC28.en: I fear that all my old misdeeds have been discovered.
LBC28.note: Revisit: from Lesson LI, Exercise A 5 (a fear clause).

LBC29.la: Ōrātor nōs monuit nē spem dēpōnerēmus.
LBC29.en: The orator warned us not to give up hope.
LBC29.note: Revisit: from Lesson XLVIII, Exercise A 14 (an indirect command).

LBD1.la: Hominēs quaerunt quid optimum factū sit.
LBD1.en: People ask what is best to do.
LBD1.note: From Cicero, in Verrem 2.1.68; factū is a supine (ablative of specification).

LBD2.la: Vīxet, cui vītam deus aut sua dextra dedisset.
LBD2.en: He would have lived, to whom a god or his own right hand had given life.

LBD3.la: In ea castra Q. Fabius, P. Volumnius, Ā. Postumius lēgātī ab Rōmā vēnērunt questum iniūriās.
LBD3.en: Into that camp the envoys Q. Fabius, P. Volumnius, and A. Postumius came from Rome to complain of injuries.
LBD3.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 3.25.6; questum is a supine of purpose.

LBD4.la: Ut enim nūlla pars est corporis nostrī quae nōn minōris sit quam nōsmet ipsī sumus, sīc mundum ūniversum plūris esse necesse est quam partem aliquam ūniversī.
LBD4.en: For just as there is no part of our body that is not of less value than we ourselves are, so it is necessary that the whole universe is of more value than any part of the whole.
LBD4.note: From Cicero, de Natura Deorum 2.32.14; nōsmet = nōs; ūniversum = tōtum.

LBD5.la: “Vincite” inquit “sī ita vultis” Sabīnus et id clāriōre vōce, ut magna pars mīlitum exaudīret; “neque is sum” inquit “quī gravissimē ex vōbīs mortis perīculō terrear.”
LBD5.en: “Conquer,” said Sabinus, “if you wish,” and in a louder voice, so that a large part of the soldiers could hear; “and I am not the sort who would be terrified most gravely of you by danger of death.”
LBD5.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 5.30.1–2; exaudīret = audīret.

LBD6.la: Quālis tandem Lacaena? Quae cum fīlium in proelium mīsisset et interfectum audīsset, “idcircō” inquit “genueram, ut esset, quī prō patriā mortī nōn dubitāret occurrere.”
LBD6.en: What sort of Spartan woman, then? When she had sent her son into battle and heard that he had been killed, she said, “For this reason I bore him, that there might be someone who would not hesitate to meet death for his country.”
LBD6.note: From Cicero, Tusculanae Disputationes 1.102; idcircō adv. “for this reason”; genueram from gignō; occurrere takes the dative (mortī), “to meet death.”

LBD7.la: Ab Caesare nōn possunt mīlitēs continērī, quīn spē praedae in urbem rumperent urbemque dēlērent.
LBD7.en: The soldiers cannot be restrained by Caesar from breaking into the city and destroying it in hope of booty.

LBD8.la: Fuēre tamen cīvēs, quī sēque remque pūblicam obstinātīs animīs perditum īrent.
LBD8.en: There were nevertheless citizens who, with obstinate minds, were going to ruin themselves and the republic.
LBD8.note: From Sallust, Catilinae Coniuratio 36.4; perditum is a supine of purpose.

LBD9.la: Sit igitur aliquis, quī nihil malī habeat, nūllum ā fortūnā vulnus accēperit: Metellus ille.
LBD9.en: Let there be someone, then, who has nothing bad and has received no wound from fortune: that Metellus.

LBD10.la: Tum dēmum Liscus ōrātiōne Caesaris adductus, quod anteā tacuerat, prōpōnit: esse nōnnūllōs quōrum auctōritās apud plēbem plūrimum valeat.
LBD10.en: Then at last Liscus, moved by Caesar’s speech, declares what he had previously kept silent: that there are some men whose authority has very great influence with the people.

LBD11.la: Quae enim domus tam stabilis, quae tam firma cīvitās est, quae nōn odiīs et discidiīs funditus possit ēvertī?
LBD11.en: For what house is so stable, what state so firm, that it could not be utterly overturned by hatreds and quarrels?

LBD12.la: Nēmō est eōrum quīn perisse tē cupiat?
LBD12.en: Is there any one of them who does not wish that you had perished?

LBD13.la: Ad haec Q. Marcius respondit, sī quid ab senātū petere vellent, ab armīs discēdant, Rōmam supplicēs proficīscantur.
LBD13.en: To this Q. Marcius replied that if they wished to ask anything of the Senate, they should withdraw from arms and go to Rome as suppliants.
LBD13.note: From Sallust, Catilinae Coniuratio 34.1; supplicēs from supplex “suppliant.”

LBD14.la: Questus est ōrāculum quod ipse cōnsuluisset suōs fīnitimōs fefellisse.
LBD14.en: He complained that the oracle which he himself had consulted had deceived his neighbors.

LBD15.la: Classe subitō dēlētā, nautās ad Caesarem mittunt rogātum auxilium.
LBD15.en: The fleet having suddenly been destroyed, they send sailors to Caesar to ask for aid.
LBD15.note: rogātum is a supine of purpose.

LBD16.la: Sī cupīdō opum saepe addūcit testēs ad pecūniam accipiendam, quō modō iūdicēs cōnstituere possunt quī vēra dīcant?
LBD16.en: If desire for wealth often leads witnesses to accept money, how can jurors decide who are speaking the truth?

LBD17.la: Difficile est dictū quantō sīmus in odiō.
LBD17.en: It is difficult to say how much we are hated.
LBD17.note: dictū is a supine (ablative of specification).

LBD18.la: Numquam meās ratiōnēs tuae salūtī antepōnam.
LBD18.en: I will never put my interests before your safety.

LBD19.la: Ūnus dē magistrīs mihi adulēscentī dīcēbat nātūram speciem fingere sed virtūtem fingere hominem.
LBD19.en: One of the teachers used to say to me as a young man that nature forms appearance but virtue forms the man.

LBD20.la: Exercendae memoriae causā, quid quoque diē dīxerim, audīverim, ēgerim, in memoriam redūcō nocte.
LBD20.en: For the sake of training my memory, I review at night what I have said, heard, and done each day.

LBD21.la: Intereā pollicitī sunt sē fūnctūrōs esse officiīs quae anteā suscēpissent.
LBD21.en: Meanwhile they promised that they would perform the duties which they had previously undertaken.

LBD22.la: Semper ita vīvāmus ut ratiōnem vītae reddendam esse nōbīs arbitrēmur.
LBD22.en: Let us always live so that we think that an account of our life must be rendered by us.

LBD23.la: Inimīcī meī dīcunt ea quae prō salūte omnium gesserim cāsū magis et fortūnā quam virtūte et cōnsiliō ā mē gesta esse.
LBD23.en: My enemies say that the things I have done for the safety of all were done by chance and fortune rather than by courage and judgment.

LBD24.la: Quīdam dē cīvibus hinc Corinthum eunt salūtātum imperātōrem, virum ēgregium.
LBD24.en: Some of the citizens go from here to Corinth to greet the general, an outstanding man.
LBD24.note: salūtātum is a supine of purpose.

LBD25.la: Vīta nōs docet nihil esse minus certum voluntāte hominum, nihil minus clārum ratiōnibus plēbis.
LBD25.en: Life teaches us that nothing is less certain than the will of men, nothing less clear than the reasoning of the people.

LBD26.la: Rēge ex urbe expulsō vīgintī ante annīs, populus adhūc nōmen eius timuit.
LBD26.en: The king having been expelled from the city twenty years before, the people still feared his name.

LBD27.la: Nisi tū urbem āmīsissēs, numquam eam recēpissem.
LBD27.en: If you had not lost the city, I would never have recovered it.
LBD27.note: Revisit: from Lesson LIV, Exercise A 1 (a past contrary-to-fact condition).

LBD28.la: Intereā parandum est bellum quō vincās celerius.
LBD28.en: Meanwhile, war must be prepared so that you may win more quickly.
LBD28.note: Revisit: from Lesson LV, Exercise A 23 (the passive periphrastic and a purpose clause).

LBD29.la: Timeō nē mala facta antīqua mea sint inventa omnia.
LBD29.en: I fear that all my old misdeeds have been discovered.
LBD29.note: Revisit: from Lesson LI, Exercise A 5 (a fear clause).

LBE1.la: Vārus mē meus ad suōs amōrēs vīsum dūxerat ē forō ōtiōsum.
LBE1.en: Varus had led me, at leisure, from the forum to see his girlfriends.
LBE1.note: From Catullus, Carmen 10.1–2; vīsum is a supine of purpose; Vārus is a proper name; ōtiōsum “at leisure.”

LBE2.la: Glōria in altissimīs Deō et in terrā pāx hominibus bonae voluntātis.
LBE2.en: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.

LBE3.la: Et eadem fortūna, quae necessitātem pugnandī imposuit, praemia vōbīs ea victōribus prōpōnit quibus ampliōra hominēs nē ab dīs quidem immortālibus optāre solent.
LBE3.en: And the same fortune that imposed the necessity of fighting offers you, as victors, rewards greater than those that men are accustomed to wish for even from the immortal gods.
LBE3.note: From Livy, ab Urbe Condita 21.43.5; imposuit = in + pōnō “impose.”

LBE4.la: Hī sunt quī, nisi mē cīvitāte expulissent, obtinēre sē nōn putāvērunt posse licentiam cupiditātum suārum.
LBE4.en: These are the men who, if they had not expelled me from the state, did not think they could maintain the license of their desires.
LBE4.note: From Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum 10.4.1; obtinēre = ob + teneō “obtain.”

LBE5.la: Et omnia quae dēsīderāvērunt oculī meī, nōn negāvī eīs; nec prohibuī cor quīn omnī voluptāte fruerētur.
LBE5.en: And all that my eyes desired I did not deny them; nor did I keep my heart from enjoying every pleasure.

LBE6.la: Complūribus expugnātīs oppidīs, Caesar ubi intellēxit frūstrā tantum labōrem sūmī neque hostium fugam captīs oppidīs reprimī neque iīs nocērī posse, statuit exspectandam classem.
LBE6.en: Several towns having been stormed, when Caesar understood that such great labor was being taken up in vain and that the enemy’s flight could not be checked by the capture of towns nor could they be harmed, he decided to wait for the fleet.
LBE6.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 3.14.1; reprimī = re + primō “check.”

LBE7.la: Sī in Britanniam quoque profectus essēs, profectō nēmō in illā tantā īnsulā perītior tē fuisset.
LBE7.en: If you had also set out for Britain, surely no one on that great island would have been more skilled than you.

LBE8.la: Nēmō fuit omnīnō mīlitum quīn vulnerārētur, quattuorque ex ūnā cohorte centuriōnēs oculōs āmīsērunt.
LBE8.en: There was altogether no one of the soldiers who was not wounded, and four centurions from one cohort lost their eyes.

LBE9.la: Itaque aedificiīs omnibus pepercit quasi ad ea dēfendenda cum exercitū, nōn oppugnanda vēnisset.
LBE9.en: And so he spared all the buildings, as if he had come with an army to defend them, not to attack them.

LBE10.la: Nunc est bibendum; nunc pede līberō pulsanda terra.
LBE10.en: Now is the time for drinking; now the earth must be struck with free foot.
LBE10.note: From Horace, Carmina 1.37.1–2, his ode celebrating the death of Cleopatra.

LBE11.la: Caesar respondit sī populus Rōmānus alicuius iniūriae sibi cōnscius fuisset, nōn fuisse difficile cavēre.
LBE11.en: Caesar replied that if the Roman people had been conscious of any wrong, it would not have been difficult to be on guard.
LBE11.note: From Caesar, de Bello Gallico 1.14.2; cōnscius “conscious, aware.”

LBE12.la: Ita mihi nōn sōlum cōpia sed etiam modus in dīcendō quaerendus erat.
LBE12.en: And so not only an abundance but also moderation in speaking had to be sought by me.

LBE13.la: Cum dēfendī urbem posse spēs nūlla sit, discēdendum est nōbīs cum fēminīs ac līberīs in arcem.
LBE13.en: Since there is no hope that the city can be defended, we must withdraw with the women and children into the citadel.

LBE14.la: Servī meī sī mē metuerent, domum meam relinquendam putārem.
LBE14.en: If my slaves feared me, I would think my house must be abandoned.

LBE15.la: Ab deīs immortālibus pars utraque hostiīs mactandīs fēlīcitātem petīverat.
LBE15.en: Each side had sought good fortune from the immortal gods by sacrificing victims.

LBE16.la: Utinam ille ea quae dē īnsidiīs sciēbat sine timōre dīxisset!
LBE16.en: If only he had said without fear what he knew about the ambush!

LBE17.la: Dī ipsī immortālēs tribuant ut nostrā virtūte tot ac tanta perīcula superentur!
LBE17.en: May the immortal gods themselves grant that so many and such great dangers be overcome by our courage!

LBE18.la: Testēs dīxērunt Orestem ad mortem patris persequendam supplicium dē mātre sūmpsisse.
LBE18.en: The witnesses said that Orestes had taken vengeance on his mother to avenge his father’s death.
LBE18.note: Orestes, who killed his mother, Clytaemnestra, to avenge her murder of his father, Agamemnon.

LBE19.la: Dē huius hominis fēlīcitāte hāc ūtar facultāte dīcendī.
LBE19.en: Concerning this man’s happiness I shall use this ability of speaking.

LBE20.la: Cicerō in sententiā haesit sē omnibus cīvibus cōnsulere etsī complūrēs questī sunt eum immortālitātem suam reī pūblicae salūtī antepōnere.
LBE20.en: Cicero persisted in the opinion that he was looking out for all citizens, although several complained that he put his own immortality before the safety of the republic.

LBE21.la: Hostibus resistendī cupidior iūdicātus est hic fuisse quam cēterī.
LBE21.en: This man was judged to have been more eager than the rest for resisting the enemy.

LBE22.la: Hic vōbīs vincendum aut moriendum, mīlitēs, est simul atque hostibus occurrerītis.
LBE22.en: Here you must conquer or die, soldiers, as soon as you meet the enemy.

LBE23.la: Sī quid dē hīs rēbus senātōribus dīcere velit, eum ut ante cōnsulat ōrāculum horter.
LBE23.en: If he wishes to say anything to the senators about these matters, I urge him to consult the oracle first.

LBE24.la: Mīror eum veniam eīdem hominī dare quem ambitūs heri accūsāverit.
LBE24.en: I am amazed that he gives a pardon to the same man whom he accused of bribery yesterday.

LBE25.la: Nūllum aliud mihi praemium sī ab senātū populōque Rōmānō nisi ōtium postulārem, quis nōn daret?
LBE25.en: If I asked for no other reward for myself from the Senate and the Roman people except leisure, who would not give it?

LBE26.la: Līberī ad templa nōbīs mittendī sunt ōrātum deōs nē calamitātem reī pūblicae īnferant.
LBE26.en: The children must be sent by us to the temples to pray to the gods not to bring disaster on the republic.
LBE26.note: ōrātum is a supine of purpose.

LBE27.la: Rēs prō salūte patriae gestae senātōrum iūdiciō probābuntur.
LBE27.en: Deeds done for the safety of the fatherland will be approved by the judgment of the senators.

LBE28.la: Per speciem officiīs fungendī, opēs suās nūllō negōtiō cōnsul auxit.
LBE28.en: Under the pretext of performing his duties, the consul increased his wealth with no effort.

LBE29.la: Quibus enim nihil est in vītā ad bene vīvendum, eīs omnis aetās gravis est.
LBE29.en: For those who have nothing in life for living well, every age is a burden.

LBE30.la: Sī praemium prō meīs labōribus accēpissem, dē cēterīs crīminibus taceam.
LBE30.en: If I had accepted a reward for my labors, I should be silent about the other charges.

LBE31.la: Nec vērō corporī sōlum nōs subvenīre oportet, sed mentī multō magis.
LBE31.en: And truly it is not only the body that we must help, but much more the mind.

LBE32.la: Cum ab eō quaererem quid accidisset novī, dīxit eōs quibus pepercisset amīciōrēs populō Rōmānō esse factōs.
LBE32.en: When I asked him what news had happened, he said that those whom he had spared had become friendlier to the Roman people.

LBE33.la: Hominēs quaerunt quid optimum factū sit.
LBE33.en: People ask what is best to do.
LBE33.note: Revisit: from Lesson LVI, Exercise A 1 (a supine of specification).

LBE34.la: Libyae magnās it Fāma per urbēs, virīsque adquīrit eundō.
LBE34.en: Rumor goes through the great cities of Libya, and gains strength by going.
LBE34.note: Revisit: from Lesson LV, Exercise A 4 (the gerund).

LBE35.la: Sī mē incolumem servāverīs, aeternum exemplum beneficiī tuī erō.
LBE35.en: If you save me unharmed, I shall be an everlasting example of your kindness.
LBE35.note: Revisit: from Lesson LIV, Exercise A 22 (a future more vivid condition).

worksheets.title: The Language of Ancient Rome
worksheets.kind: Written responses, plus a few auto-graded answers
worksheets.intro: Answer these questions after reading the lesson text and doing the guided notes.

items.q: Who were the Latins, and where did they originally settle in Italy?
Of the sister languages of Latin mentioned in the text, which one do you find most or least surprising? Explain your answer.
Why are these languages more closely related to Latin than the rest of the Indo-European languages?
Why do you think Latin remained a widely used language among scholars well after the fall of the Roman Empire?
Why might the study of Latin be considered valuable for modern students? Provide at least three reasons.
What factors (historical, geographical, and so on) led to the unique position that English has on the Proto-Indo-European chart (figure 2)?
How did the invention of the alphabet give Carthaginian merchants an advantage over other merchants?
What is the primary limitation of the Carthaginian system of writing?
Which consonants in Latin are always “hard”?
Which letters are “missing” altogether from the Latin alphabet?
What are the other primary oddities of pronouncing Latin?

items.h: Word Laboratory: Taking a Closer Look

items.ph: Terrarium = terra ‘earth’ + arium ‘a place for’

Row K on the previous page features the English word, ‘terrarium’. -arium is a noun-forming suffix, derived from Latin, used to indicate ‘a place associated with a particular function, thing, or group.’ For example, a planetarium is ‘a place for projecting images of planets (and other heavenly bodies) onto the inner surface of a dome.’
Can you think of any other English words that use the -arium suffix? You can use an English to Latin dictionary to help translate the ‘hint’ word into Latin, if you get stuck:

The -arium suffix appears in several variant forms in English. For example, due to a ‘euphonic change’, i.e. a spelling change that comes about naturally to make a word or phrase easier to pronounce (e.g. ‘want to’ → ‘wanna’), -arium shortens to -ium in such words as gymnasium, ‘a place for exercise’ or ______ ‘a place to listen to’ (Latin: audiō).
In Spanish and Italian -arium shifts its vowel to ‘e’, resulting in -eria. Can you think of some examples of English words adopting this suffix?

Often the -arium / -eria suffix is ‘Anglicized’ to -ery / -ary / -ory to sound more like a native English word. Strangely, however, sometimes the root word in English still derives from Latin, as in the third entry below:

worksheets.title: Fīat Deus
worksheets.introH: A project on the gods and goddesses of the Classical world and a new Olympian deity of your own. Read the project description, objective, and instructions, then enter your work below.

items.ph: The gods and goddesses worshipped in the Classical world were reflections of ancient peoples’ views and experience ‘of reality’ in the broadest sense of that term. They were composed of those forces—love, war, wisdom, time, etc.—that continue to have a ‘spiritual’ reality in the sense that they profoundly affect the direction of our will and/or our ability to realize our will in the world. For example, the ancients had river gods. A river may affect one’s ability to cross over to a desired location, or a river may facilitate the transportation of people and goods. In other words, a river may affect how we plan and realize our actions in the world. In that sense, we can understand how an ancient person may regard a river as divine in that it is endowed with a ‘willful’ or ‘spirited’ nature. If we felt powerless or insignificant in respect to the river, we can also understand why that river may be worthy of our worship or reverence.

With that broad definition of deity in mind, you are asked to imagine one new Olympian deity who can augment or update the traditional canon of deities worshipped by the Greeks and Romans (consult Lesson III, p. 12 of your texts for a table of the Greek and Roman Pantheon). In devising your new deity, consider ‘the blind spots’ that exist in the ancient Pantheon given how much our world has changed since then. What forces or ideas or phenomena or technologies exist today that did not exist in antiquity that may be considered ‘god worthy.’

To deepen your understanding of how the gods and goddesses of ancient Greece and Rome reflect the cultural and spiritual realities of their time. You will creatively extend this understanding by inventing a new Olympian deity that reflects a modern force or concept relevant to the 21st century.

items.html:
1. Research: Review the Greek and Roman pantheon (refer to Lesson III, page 12 of your textbook) and the roles the gods played in shaping human interactions with the forces of nature and the universe.
  2. Deity Creation:
    • Imagine a modern force or concept that significantly impacts life today, which did not exist or was not understood in antiquity.
    • Create a new Olympian deity to represent this modern force. Be sure to include the following: Name; Attributes; Domain of influence; Symbols; Mode of worship.
  3. Creative Component: You may choose one of the following options to present your deity:
    • Write a short myth (like Ovid’s Metamorphoses) in English about your deity. Perhaps it is a story of their birth or a particularly significant exploit in their lives. Perhaps it is an interaction with a person, or hero, or whole civilization. Be creative.
    • Compose a hymn or poem dedicated to this deity (use the style of a Homeric Hymn as a guide, if you like), or to tell a story about your god.
    • Create a visual representation (drawing, painting, or digital art) of the deity along with a brief explanation of the symbols you included.

items.qh: Deity’s Name: a meaningful name rooted in Latin or Greek, reflecting the force they represent.
Domain of Influence: describe what domain this deity governs (e.g., earthquakes, commerce, etc.).
Attributes: Identify 3-5 key attributes of your deity (e.g., wisdom, power over a certain technology, etc.).
Symbols: Choose at least two symbols for your deity and explain their significance.
Worship: Explain how modern society might worship this deity. How does it differ from ancient practices?

Creative Component: Create a story, poem, or visual representation of your deity. Name the option you chose (myth, hymn or poem, or visual), then present it here. For a visual, give your brief explanation of the symbols and your instructor will tell you how to hand in the artwork.

items.html:
Grading rubric

CategoryExcellent (90-100%)Proficient (80-89%)Basic (70-79%)Needs Improvement (60-69%)Points
Quality of ConceptDeity is highly original and thoughtfully connected to modern forces.Deity is creative and has some clear connections to modern forces.Deity is somewhat creative, but connections to modern forces are unclear.Deity lacks creativity or fails to connect with modern forces./15
Creativity ComponentWell-written / designed, highly imaginative and well-executed and thoroughly explains/portrays the deity’s role, attributes, and symbols.Clear explanation / execution with some minor gaps in clarity or development.Adequate explanation /execution but lacks depth or has significant errors.Explanation / execution of concept is unclear, missing key details, or poorly developed./35
Connection to Classical WorldStrong connection to ancient Greek/Roman deities and mythological tradition.Some connection to classical themes, though not fully explored.Limited connection to classical themes, with minimal detail.Lacks significant connection to classical themes or tradition./10

TOTAL: ____/60

worksheets.introH: Follow Io’s encounter with Jupiter and Juno as you practice vocabulary, prepositional phrases, and commands from Lessons IV–V.

items.ph: The Latin uses only the vocabulary and grammar of Lessons I through V, plus a few glossed words.
Io, a young woman, lives near a river. She is carrying water to her family, and Jupiter, king of the gods, sees her. Read the Latin. Words you may not know are in the glossary below.

items.qh: Iō habitābat in ____ (house) prope ____ (woods). Saepe Iō ambulābat per ____ (grasses) ad ____ (shore) flūminis. Portābat aquam ____ (for the farmers) et ____ (for the slave-girls).

items.ph: Jupiter hurries after her and calls out.

items.qh: Iuppiter puellam spectat et mox amat. Iuppiter ad ____ (girl) vocat: “Salvē, ō puella! Sum deus. Properā ad silvam!”

items.ph: Io is afraid. She does not wait for Jupiter. She hurries away, but the god hides her in a cloud.
Iō nōn exspectat. Properat trāns herbās per silvam. Sed Iuppiter puellam sub nūbe cēlat.
Juno, Jupiter’s wife, sees a strange cloud in the middle of a bright day. She suspects that her husband is hiding something. Jupiter senses her coming, and in a panic he does something strange.
Interea Iūnō in caelō stat et nūbem spectat. Dē caelō ad terram properat. Iuppiter Iōnem in vaccam mūtat! Iūnō vaccam spectat: “Vacca est formōsa!”
Juno asks for the cow as a gift. Jupiter cannot refuse without seeming guilty. Juno then sets a guard, Argus, to watch over Io.
Iūnō Argum, custōdem, vocat: “Servā vaccam, ō custōs!”

items.html:
Glossary

worksheets.title: Vestis Loquitur: The Language of Roman Dress

items.ph: As you have read in your textbook, Roman clothing—more so than clothing today—was not simply a matter of comfort or personal taste. Rather, it had a pronounced social function, serving to indicate status, citizenship, gender, profession, and moral identity.

The toga, for example, was a simple rectangular piece of woolen cloth; however, symbolically it indicated that the men who wore it were free citizens, bound by civic duty and granted certain rights. Similarly, the stola distinguished the respectable Roman matron from other women, particularly those women compelled to wear the toga due to their disreputable profession.

In this way, Roman clothing functioned almost like a language: a system of symbols through which individuals communicated their identity and through which society enforced its values, particularly those embedded within its social hierarchy. As you consider your choice of project below, you are asked to explore Roman fashion not merely as costume, but as cultural expression, and to demonstrate how clothing reveals the social and symbolic realities of Roman life.

To deepen your understanding of how Roman clothing reflects social hierarchy, cultural values, and personal identity, and to demonstrate this understanding through a creative and historically grounded project.

items.html:
Review the Roman clothing chapter carefully, as well as the Roman Dress chapter from The Private Life of Ancient Romans. Pay particular attention to:

  • Types of garments (e.g. tunica, toga, stola, palla)
  • Materials and production
  • Social distinctions in clothing
  • Footwear, hairstyles, and accessories

Examples of “characters” to convey differences in Roman dress:

  • Senator (tunica with latus clavus, toga, calceī)
  • Equestrian class man (narrow stripes)
  • Roman matron (stola and palla)
  • Athlete (subligāculum and strophium)
  • Roman soldier (cloak, caligae)
  • Roman candidate (toga candida)
  • Mourner (toga pulla)
  • Young man (toga praetexta and bulla)
  • Wealthy matron
  • Gladiator or gladiator trainer
  • Roman general
  • Freedman
  • Slave in a wealthy household

items.h: Option 1: Roman Fashion Show (performance and design)

items.html:
Students work in small groups to create and present a Roman fashion show that demonstrates historically accurate clothing and explains the social meaning of Roman dress.

Group roles (3–5 students): Historian (researches the garment and ensures accuracy); Designer or costume maker (plans or creates the clothing using fabric, sheets, paper, etc.); Model (wears and demonstrates the clothing); Narrator (explains the garment and its social meaning); Director, optional (coordinates staging and timing).

Requirements: Each group must present two Roman outfits that represent a specific social identity.

Presentation structure:

  • Runway walk (30 seconds). The model walks while the narrator introduces the character.
  • Explanation (2–3 minutes). Name of the clothing; who wore it; materials; social meaning; when it was worn; accessories (hairstyle, jewelry, shoes, etc.).
  • Latin component. Students must incorporate at least 5 Latin terms from the chapter (for example tunica, toga praetexta, stola, palla, caligae).

Example script: “Marcus is a Roman senator. He wears a tunica with a latus clavus, the broad purple stripe that marks his rank. Over this he wears a toga, the official garment of Roman male citizens. His calceī are leather shoes worn by the upper classes …”

Optional bonus: music; Roman procession staging; props (wax tablet, scroll, etc.).

items.h: Option 2: A Roman Fashion Museum (creative design)

items.html:
Students invent a Roman character and design their clothing, or take a deep dive into a subset of Roman fashion of their choosing (e.g. jewelry, hairstyles, military clothing, cosmetics, footwear, or a theme).

Requirements: an illustration of the character or theme (digital art is allowed if it is not AI-generated) in a format larger than a standard piece of loose-leaf paper; a written description (200–300 words) explaining the name of the clothing, who wore it, materials, social meaning, when it was worn, and accessories (shoes, jewelry, hairstyle); and labels or a legend explaining the clothing pieces.
