items.ph: Martial (c. A.D. 38–102) was a Silver Age Latin poet who wrote under the Emperors Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan. He specialized in the epigram, producing over 1,500 of these poems, and he used the form primarily to satirize the foibles and vices of his Roman contemporaries. A characteristic of Martial’s style is the use of a punchline, often in the form of a single word at the end of the poem upon which the humor of the entire piece depends.

items.html:
Step 1: Choose a poem from Martial’s collection of epigrams. Some highlights to narrow your selection: I.1, I.10, I.16, I.32, I.38, I.47, I.67, I.83, I.91; II.38, II.39, II.42; III.9, III.26, III.27; IV.69; V.43, V.47, V.58, V.64, V.66, V.81; VI.60; VII.3, VII.27, VII.69, VII.73, VII.76; X.8, X.47; XI.3, XI.13; XII.20, XII.46. Your teacher will give you the links for English translations and the Latin text.

Step 2: Translate your poem into English in trot form, that is, reorder the Latin words to reflect the exact order in which you translated it into English. Extra credit: translate your poem into rhyming verse.

Step 3: Create a SOAPSTone for your poem. A SOAPSTone is an analytical tool that can be used for virtually any work of art as a starting point for deeper analysis: Speaker, Occasion, Addressee, Purpose, Subject, Tone.

Step 1: Text (adapted). Martial, Epigramma XI.35. The Latin below is a simplified adaptation, not Martial’s original wording. Your own poem will be unadapted.

Ignōtōs mihi si vōcēs trecentōs,
Quārē nōn veniam vocātus ad tē,
Mīrāris quererisque pugnāsque.
Sed nōlō, Fabulle, cēnāre sōlus.

Step 2: Trot translation.

sī | vōcēs | trecentōs | Ignōtōs | mihiIf | you invite | three-hundred (people) | unknown | to me
Quārē | Mīrāris | nōn veniam | vocātus | ad | tēWhy | are you amazed (that) | I don’t come | (after being) invited | to | you(r house)
-que | quereris | -que | pugnāsAnd | (why) do you complain | and | quarrel
Sed | Fabulle | nōlō | cēnāre | sōlusBut | Fabullus | I don’t want | to dine | alone

Step 3: SOAPSTone analysis.

Speaker: The poet.

Occasion: The poet has received an invitation to a dinner party, along with three hundred other guests.

Addressee: Fabullus, a frequent addressee in Martial’s poetry, and the man who is throwing the dinner party. The use of the name “Fabullus” alludes to the Roman poet Catullus, who famously and jokingly invites his friend of that same name to a dinner party where he will be required to supply the food and wine, along with wit and a beautiful girl (cf. Catullus, Carmen 13).

Purpose: Martial writes to Fabullus to reject his invitation. He is also responding to his friend’s anger and surprise at his rejection by pointing out that a dinner with three hundred strangers is essentially the same as dining alone. There is a serious point to Martial’s humorous rejection: he is making the point that he should be the one who is upset, not Fabullus, because Fabullus’ invitation is not personal nor does it allow for any real intimacy or genuine connection between guest and host. Such parties in ancient Rome, exactly like big celebrity parties today, are more about building social credibility for guest and host alike. The point is to be seen among the “in” crowd for the guests and to be popular enough as the host for many people to desire coming to your party in the first place. Martial does not so much reject Fabullus, but rather the pretentious social conventions of the wealthy and popular of Rome.

Subject: Martial’s rejection of Fabullus’ invitation to a dinner party.

Tone: Like many of Martial’s poems, the tone here is humorous and ironic: the dinner party is “full” (like Catullus’ wallet in Carmen 13) “of strangers.” But in the tradition of Roman satire there is a serious bite to the humor, as elucidated in the “purpose” section above.

items.html:
Abbreviations and notes for Exercise D.
Line 2: C = GĀĪ, gen. “of Gaius”; F. = FĪLIUS. Line 3: CŌS = CŌNSUL; DICT = DICTĀTOR; INTERRĒX: an office held when the consuls were unavailable due to death or some other civic commotion. Line 4: PR = PRAETOR; AED · CUR = AEDĪLIS CURŪLIS, “curule aedile”; Q = QUAESTOR; TR · MĪL = TRIBŪNUS MĪLITUM, “military tribune.” Lines 3–5: BIS, adv. “twice”; COMPLŪRA = MULTA; SAMNĪTIBUS, “the Samnites,” a people inhabiting south-central Italy, with whom the Romans battled 344–290 B.C. in their bid to gain supremacy over the Italian peninsula. In 296 B.C. Appius Claudius Caecus and his co-consul Lucius Volumnius Flamma routed a combined Samnite and Etruscan force as part of the Second Samnite War (326–304 B.C.). Line 6: SABĪNŌRUM, “of the Sabines,” a people whom we read about in a legendary context in the story of the “Abduction of the Sabine Women” (Lesson XVI); it is unclear to which battle this refers, but likely one of several campaigns led against Sabine towns following the Third Samnite War (298–290 B.C.). TUSCŌRUM, “of the Etruscans,” Rome’s powerful northern neighbors. Line 7: FŪDIT = FUGĀVIT; PĀCEM, acc. sing. “peace”; FIERĪ, infin. “to come to be”; [P]YRRHŌ, abl. “Pyrrhus,” the Greek king of Epirus, whose forces challenged Roman dominion in the southern part of the Italian peninsula during the Pyrrhic War (280–275 B.C.). Following Pyrrhus’ victory against Roman forces at Heraclea in 280 B.C., he attempted to secure favorable peace terms with Rome. Many Senators were in favor of peace, but A. Claudius Caecus vehemently refused. Old and blind by this time, Claudius’ sons carried him in a litter to the Senate, where he gave an impassioned speech against peace, arguing that Rome must continue to fight, whatever the cost, until Pyrrhus was removed completely from the Italian peninsula. Lines 8–9: IN CĒNSŪRA “in his term as Censor”; STRĀVIT = AEDIFICĀVIT. Line 10: ADDŪXIT = DŪXIT; BELLŌNAE: “Bellona,” a Roman war goddess, to whom Appius Claudius Caecus vowed a temple in 296 B.C., during the Third Samnite War (298–290 B.C.).

ladder.title: Masada
ladder.sub: Adapted from Josephus, Bellum Iudaicum 7
lines: Hierosolymā captā, Iūdaeī ultimī in arce Masadā, quae in monte altō stat, manēbant.
Dux Rōmānus, Flāvius Silva, mūrum circum arcem aedificāvit nē quis fugeret.
Deinde agger ad mūrōs arcis crēscēbat.
Mūrō tandem ignī incēnsō, Rōmānī nocte quiēvērunt, postrīdiē arcem ingressūrī.
Sed in arce Eleazār suīs dīxit: “Nōn serviēmus Rōmānīs. Līberī moriāmur!”
Itaque multī, uxōribus līberīsque interfectīs, ipsī sē interfēcērunt.
Postrīdiē mīlitēs Rōmānī arcem intrāvērunt. Silentium erat; nēmō vīvus appārēbat.
Tum duae fēminae et quīnque puerī, quī in cavō sē cēlāverant, ex latebrīs exiērunt.
Ex eīs Rōmānī cognōvērunt quid in arce factum esset.
Nisi fēminae et puerī sē cēlāvissent, nēmō rem nārrāvisset.
Rōmānī, quamquam hostēs vīcerant, nōn gaudēbant, sed tantam audāciam mīrābantur.

incēnsō from incendō; quiēvērunt from quiēscō “rested”; ingressūrī “about to enter”
Eleazār: the Jewish commander; moriāmur from morior
silentium, -ī n. silence; appārēbat from appāreō “appear”

to set the wall on fire

Līberī is nominative plural “free”; moriāmur is a hortatory subjunctive.

Quamquam: concessive; they marveled (mīrābantur) at the daring.

lines: Marcus Aurelius, imperātor Rōmānus, trāns Danuvium contrā Quadōs bellum gerēbat.

Dīcunt quōsdam mīlitēs deōs ōrāvisse ut sibi aquam darent.

Cōnstantīnus, quī nōn dubitābat quīn deus vērus eum monēret, mīlitibus statim dē somniō nārrāvit.
Signum erat littera X, cuius summum caput in orbem flexum erat.
Mīlitēs signum in scūtīs suīs pīnxērunt, et proelium sine morā commissum est.
Maxentius ex urbe contrā cōnsilium suum ēgressus est; pōns nāvium frāctus est, et in Tiberim cecidit.
Cōnstantīnus victor Rōmam intrāvit, et Christiānī, quī multōs annōs persecūtiōnem passī erant, laetī erant.
Annō proximō Cōnstantīnus et Licinius, imperātōrēs, omnibus lībertātem religiōnis dedērunt.

Ratēs lentē trāns flūmen trahēbantur, sed aliī elephantī aquam vīdērunt et ācriter clāmāvērunt.

Elephantī tamen in imō flūmine stābant et proboscidēs super aquam tenēbant.

ladder.title: The Death of Cicero
ladder.sub: Adapted from Plutarch, Cicero 47–48, and Livy (in Seneca the Elder, Suasoriae 6)
lines: Antōnius, Octāviānus, et Lepidus nōmina inimīcōrum in tabulā scrīpsērunt; Cicerō prīmus in tabulā erat.

ladder.sub: Adapted from Plutarch, Antony 76–86

ladder.title: The Dinner of Nasidienus
ladder.sub: Adapted from Horace, Sermones 2.8
lines: Nasidiēnus, vir dīves sed rīdiculus, Maecēnātem et Horātium ad cēnam invītāvit.
Cum hospitēs vēnissent, servī aprum ingentem in mēnsā posuērunt.
Nasidiēnus, quod omnia cibōrum nōmina scīre cupiēbat, longē dē vīnō et dē aprō disputāvit.
Cum maximē disputāret, subitō aulaeum ē tēctō cecidit et pulverem nigrum super cēnam effūdit.
Nasidiēnus flēvit; hospitēs, cum rīdēre vellent, tamen tacuērunt.
Cum cēnam dēlētam vidērent, nihil ēdērunt et mātūrē domum rediērunt.
Horātius, quī hanc cēnam ipse vīderat, versibus nārrāvit; ita Nasidiēnus omnibus Rōmānīs nōtus est.
lineGloss: Nasidiēnus, -ī m. “Nasidienus, a rich host”; Maecēnās, -ātis m. “Maecenas, Horace’s patron”; invītō (1) “invited”

ladder.title: Silius Italicus and the Tomb of Vergil
ladder.sub: Adapted from Pliny, Epistulae 3.7
lines: Silius Italicus, vir dīves et ōlim cōnsul, Vergiliō maximē studēbat.

Diem nātālem Vergilī magis celebrābat quam suum.

ladder.title: Mushrooms and Gods
ladder.sub: Adapted from Suetonius, Nero 33, and Seneca, Apocolocyntosis

Illa eī fungōs dedit, in quibus venēnum īnfūsum erat.

Senātus Claudium deum esse dēcrēvit; Nerō tamen iocum fēcit.
“Fungī,” inquit, “cibus deōrum sunt; Claudius enim per fungum deus factus est.”
Seneca, philosophus, fābulam rīdiculam dē morte Claudī scrīpsit; ea Apocolocyntōsis appellātur, id est “Claudius Cucurbita Factus.”

lines: Plīnius ad Calpurniam, uxōrem suam, quae in Campāniā aegrōtābat, epistulam scrīpsit.

Sī valēs, laetus sum; sī aegrōtās, anxius sum.

Sī litterās tuās lēgerō, timēre dēsinam; sed statim rūrsus timēbō.”

Hector rīdet et galeam in terrā pōnit.
“Ō Iuppiter,” inquit, “fīlius meus fortis et bonus erit!”

lines: Tarquinius Superbus, rēx Rōmānus, in rēgiā sedēbat.
Subitō anus ignōta ad rēgem ambulāvit et novem librōs portābat.
“Hōs librōs,” inquit, “tibi vendō. In hīs librīs fāta Rōmae sunt.”
“Pretium nimis magnum est!” clāmāvit rēx.
Anus trēs librōs in ignem iēcit et: “Nunc sex librōs habeō,” inquit; “pretium idem est.”
Rēx iterum clāmāvit; anus alterōs trēs librōs combussit.
“Trēs librī sōlī manent,” inquit anus, “et pretium idem est.”
Rēx stultus nōn erat; augurēs vocāvit et eōs rogāvit.
Augurēs respondērunt: “Deī tibi dōnum dedērunt, sed tū id nōn accēpistī! Nunc librōs tuōs emere dēbēs.”
Rēx tōtum pretium dedit, sed anus statim discessit et numquam iterum vīsa est.
Librī in Capitōliō servābantur; Rōmānī, in magnīs perīculīs, eōs spectābant.

Ibi Lucrētia, uxor quam omnēs laudābant, lānam texēbat.
Sextus, vir malus, Lucrētiae iniūriam fēcit.
Lucrētia patrem et virum et Brūtum vocāvit: “Iniūriam, quam Sextus mihi fēcit, vōbīs nārrō.
Nōn sōlum mē sed etiam vōs omnēs iniūriā laesit.”
Deinde cultrō sē necāvit.
Brūtus, quī prope erat, cultrum ē vulnere extrāxit et: “Per hunc sanguinem iūrō mē rēgēs ē Rōmā expulsūrum esse!”

ladder.title: Brutus at Delphi

lines: Fīliī Tarquiniī ad Delphōs īre cōnstituērunt; ibi erat templum Apollinis.
Cum eīs ībat Brūtus, quem omnēs stultum esse putābant.
Brūtus Apollinī baculum aureum dōnum dedit; baculum cavum erat.
Fīliī Tarquiniī ōrāculum rogāvērunt: “Quis post patrem nostrum Rōmae rēgnābit?”
Ōrāculum respondit: “Quī prīmus mātrī suae ōsculum dabit, is Rōmae rēgnābit.”
Fīliī inter sē rogāvērunt: “Quis prīmus mātrem ōsculābitur? Cūr nōn sortem iacimus?”
Sed Brūtus, quī verba ōrāculī melius intellēxit, in terram cecidit et eam ōsculātus est.
“Terra,” inquit, “māter omnium hominum est!”

lines: Māter Poena sum, in urbe Karthāgine habitō. Urbs nostra erat magna et dīves.
Per trēs annōs Rōmānī urbem obsidēbant. Scīpiō, dux Rōmānus, mūrōs altissimōs oppugnābat.
Fāmēs erat gravior quam gladius; multī līberī et senēs periērunt.
Quīnque diēs et noctēs in viīs pugnābāmus.

In urbe magnā, ubi līber fuī, nunc serva sum.

ladder.title: Gate: Caesar and the Pirates, as a Slave Tells It
ladder.sub: Adapted from Suetonius, Divus Iulius 4, and Plutarch, Caesar 1–2. Grammar through Lesson XLI.
lines: Servus sum Caesaris. Caesar iuvenis erat; vīgintī annōs habēbat.
Ad īnsulam Rhodum nāvigābāmus; Caesar ibi artem ōrātōriam discere cupiēbat.
Subitō nāvēs pīrātārum nōs cēpērunt.
Pīrātae, quī Cilicēs erant, vīgintī talenta prō Caesare postulāvērunt.
Caesar rīsit et dīxit sē plūris esse. “Quīnquāgintā talenta dabitis,” inquit.
Mē et aliōs servōs ad urbēs maritimās mīsit; pecūniam portāre dēbēbāmus.
Trīgintā diēs inter pīrātās mānsit. Cum eīs lūdēbat, et ōrātiōnēs aliquās eīs recitābat.
“Ego vōs in crucem agam!” inquit, rīdēns.
Pīrātae putābant eum iocum facere. Quīdam rīsit.
Ubi pecūnia vēnit, Caesar līber erat et ad Mīlētum nāvigāvit.
Ibi nāvēs parāvit et ad pīrātās rediit.
Eōs cēpit et in Asiam dūxit; ibi in crucem ēgit.
Mīsericordiae causā, prīmum eōs gladiō necāvit; deinde corpora in cruce fixit.
Ego omnia vīdī, sed nēmō mē rogāvit.
Servus sum; nōn iocum sed vērum vīdī: Caesar dīxit, et fēcit.

lines: Mandubiī sumus, cīvēs Alesiae. Ego, mulier pauper, cum parvō fīliō in oppidō habitābam.

Itaque nōs, mulierēs līberīque, per portās ēiectī sumus.
Ad mūnītiōnēs Rōmānōrum vēnimus ut cibum acciperēmus.

Caesar custōdēs in vallō posuerat nē quis nōs admitteret.

lines: Calpurnia sum, uxor Caesaris. Nocte ante Īdūs Mārtiās somnium terribile vīdī.
Caesarem in sinū meō morientem vīdī, et ūnā cum eō domus nostra cecidit.
Māne Caesarem ōrāvī, “Nōlī hodiē exīre, marīte!
Tot praesāgia fuērunt ut animus meus perterritus sit.”
Haruspex Spurinna dīxerat perīculum in Īdibus Mārtiīs esse.
Caesar tamen, “Nōlō timidus vidērī,” inquit.
“Quid Rōmānī dīcent sī domī manēbō propter somnium mulieris?”
Ego eum retinēbam. Ōrābam, “Maneāmus domī hodiē!”
Sed Dēcimus Brūtus, amīcus Caesaris, domum vēnit ut eum ad Cūriam dūceret.
Brūtus eum dēridēbat et dīcēbat sē mīrārī cūr uxōris verbīs crēderet.
Caesar, cum haec audīvisset, ex domō exiit.
Ego in domō mānsī et exspectābam dum nūntius venīret.
Mox servus ad mē cucurrit et, “Caesar in Cūriā occīsus est,” inquit.
Tum vīdī somnium meum vērum esse.
Corpus Caesaris ad domum nostram ferunt.

lines: Vigil sum. Augustus nōs creāvit ut urbem ab ignī servārēmus.
Nocte mēnsis Iūliī, cum in Circō Maximō tabernae ārdērent, ignis ortus est.
Ventus magnus flammās per urbem ferēbat; ignī resistere nōn poterāmus.
Cīvibus subvenīre cōnābāmur.
Timēbāmus nē ignis ad Forum et templa perveniret.
Praefectus nōbīs imperāvit ut domōs dēmolīrēmus, nē ignis latius ērumperet.

Multī cīvēs in viās fūgērunt; aliī, cum parentēs reperīre nōn possent, flēbant.

lines: Senex sum et in urbe Rōmā habitō. Avus meus sub Antōnīnō Pīō vīxit, quī pācem et ōtium cīvibus dedit.

Cum Alexander Sevērus ā mīlitibus necātus esset, imperātōrēs complūrēs ab exercitibus creātī sunt, quī paucōs mēnsēs rēgnābant.
Pestilentia magna Rōmam premēbat; multī cīvēs ob morbum periērunt.
Gothī Danuvium trānsiērunt et prōvinciās vāstāvērunt.
Imperium in trēs partēs scissum est: Galliae, Rōmae, Palmyrae.
